title: Ravens news: NFL downplays concerns about Brazil field conditions
summary: Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of all of the latest news and analysis regarding the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover recent concerns about field conditions for the team’s upcoming trip to Brazil, early-season concerns after Sunday’s loss to the Saints, and the officiating pool report on Tyler Shough’s controversial game-winning […]
full_text: This general view shows players on the pitch during the Copa Libertadores quarter-final second leg football match between Brazil's Flamengo and Ecuador's Independiente del Valle at the Maracana stadium in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, on September 17, 2026. (Photo by MAURO PIMENTEL / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of all of the latest news and analysis regarding the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover recent concerns about field conditions for the team’s upcoming trip to Brazil, early-season concerns after Sunday’s loss to the Saints, and the officiating pool report on Tyler Shough’s controversial game-winning touchdown. Ravens’ Week 3 trip to Brazil to proceed as planned Multiple reports over the weekend raised concerns about the field conditions at Maracaña Stadium in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, where the Ravens are scheduled to take on the Cowboys next Sunday. Members of CR Flamengo, the home soccer team, have criticized the playing surface, but NFL field director Nick Pappas said on Monday that there are “no concerns right now.” NFL: ‘No concerns’ over field conditions in Rio for Cowboys-Ravens – Jamison Hensley (ESPN) ‘Look, there’s the realities of managing any playing surface and then there’s also the realities of managing a grass playing surface that’s being used midseason,” Pappas told ESPN on Monday. “So it’s all about monitoring it. It’s all about having a plan in place and then being able to react to anything that maybe comes our way.’ Pappas added, ‘So what we’ve seen in Rio is a significant amount of rainfall, a record kind of rainfall over the last six weeks. And that obviously poses challenges just from a management perspective, but nothing that we’re not capable of managing or prepared to take.’ Ravens-Cowboys in Brazil ‘full speed ahead’ despite field concerns, Stephen Jones says – Jeff Howe, Mike Jones and Dan Pompei (The Athletic) ‘I don’t have concerns only because the league has said full speed ahead. … I think if there was a real concern, there would have already been contingent plans being made,’ [Cowboys co-owner Stephen] Jones said. ‘I know how the league works, about where we play the game if it weren’t there, and there’s none of that. So, I think we’re full speed ahead.‘ ‘Whatever work needs to be done on the field to make sure that it’s safe and great for our players, no one understands that more than the league, that we’ve got to have great surfaces and great playing fields that are very safe for our players. As far as I’m concerned, we’re full speed ahead and we’re ready to go to Rio.’ Let’s be realistic here. The NFL has invested heavily in expanding football’s international appeal. It would take something extreme for the league to change their plans for a game featuring one of the most recognizable teams in the world and one of the sport’s biggest stars. The Ravens and the Cowboys will simply have to prepare and adjust. For Baltimore, that could mean a conservative approach with players dealing with lower-body injuries like Zay Flowers (hamstring) and Ronnie Stanley (toe). Teddye Buchanan (knee) and Nnamdi Madubuike (neck) could also have to wait another week to make their 2026 debuts after months away from the field. Ravens expected to rebound from Week 2 loss to Saints NFL Week 2 panic meter: Caleb Williams’ injury, another Chargers no-show shake up early season – Jeff Howe, Mike Jones and Dan Pompei (The Athletic) Which version of the Baltimore Ravens is closer to reality? The team that blew out the Indianapolis Colts in Week 1 or the group that blew a second-half lead and lost 24-17 to the New Orleans Saints on Sunday? Pompei: The Ravens’ collapse was rough with self-inflicted wounds, and head coach Jesse Minter’s leadership will be tested early. Their performance was sloppy — not unusual for many teams early in the season. The Ravens have committed 17 penalties in two weeks. That cannot continue if the Ravens are going to be contenders. But this is a talented team that’s capable of high-end football, as they showed in Week 1 against the Colts. It will be a surprise if the Ravens don’t rebound and remain one of the better teams in the AFC. They just need to get in a groove. Jones: The Ravens are somewhere in the middle, but a smidge closer to the Week 1 product. Many elements of Sunday’s performance resemble the Ravens of last season (penalties and ill-timed turnovers, a couple of head-scratcher offensive play calls, late-game defensive collapse). But the roster and energy within the organization improved. It’s important to remember that Baltimore has a 30-year-old rookie offensive coordinator in Declan Doyle, and that the unit wasn’t at full force with two of Lamar Jackson’s top wide receivers injured. There were some drops (even one by the reliable Mark Andrews) that, if caught, could have extended drives, and extended drives lead to heavier emphasis on the run. And had Doyle displayed more discipline/patience by giving Derrick Henry the ball on third-and-1 late rather than calling a deep shot downfield, perhaps the Ravens would have kept moving the ball and eventually scored. The Ravens hurt themselves on Sunday, but they’re still one of the better teams in the AFC. Howe: The Ravens’ inconsistent start is reminiscent of issues with blown leads under the previous regime, ceding control of a winnable game while falling out of sorts in the second half. Jackson and the offense went three-and-out on back-to-back drives while the Saints orchestrated consecutive touchdowns. The Ravens should be in the playoff conversation throughout the season, but I’m curious to see if this team can distinguish itself from past incarnations. NFL explains officiating call on Tyler Shough’s controversial game-winning touchdown Pool report with NFL Vice President of Instant Replay Mark Butterworth – Jamison Hensley (ESPN) Question : Was there clear evidence that Tyler Shough crossed the goal line on the fourth down quarterback sneak (1:32 remaining, New Orleans 4th and 1, Baltimore 1 yard-line)? Mark Butterworth : “The key here is the ruling on the field is a touchdown. So, we need clear and obvious video evidence that he didn’t score in order to reverse the on-field ruling. We stopped the game, it’s a high-leverage play, we wanted to make sure to either find clear and obvious video evidence that he didn’t score or to confirm the call on the field. We exhausted all available angles and could not prove clear and obvious that he did not break the plane of the goal line.” Question : During any of the replays, did it show that Tyler Shough lost control of the ball at any point while trying to get the ball across the goal line? Butterworth : “No. If he did lose control of the ball, we would need to find, after he regained possession, if the ball broke the plane of the goal line. In that mass of players, we weren’t able to find clear and obvious video evidence that the ball did not break the plane of the goal line. Therefore, the ruling on the field stands.” Ravens get ‘C’ grade for Week 2 showing NFL Week 2 grades for all 32 teams: Rams earn an ‘A’ for steamrolling Giants on Monday night – John Breech (CBS Sports) The Ravens’ new offense looked unstoppable in Week 1, but it came crashing back to earth on Sunday. The Ravens had multiple chances to put this game away, but the offense was only able to muster a total of 32 yards on Baltimore’s final three possessions of the game combined. The Ravens also seemed to forget that Derrick Henry existed. Their star running back had just five carries in the second half, including just one in the fourth quarter. With the Ravens leading 14-3 at halftime, it’s surprising that they didn’t lean on Henry more in the second half. One reason the Ravens got rid of John Harbaugh is because of the blown leads in the second half. Well, in his second game on the job, Jesse Minter now has a blown fourth-quarter lead on his resume.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens Snap Count Analysis, Week 2: Low usage for rookie pass-catchers and Chidobe Awuzie
summary: The Baltimore Ravens dropped to 1-1 after losing at home to the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense from the 24-17 defeat. Offense Jackson was protected by his starting offensive line for the entire game with the exception of Ronnie Stanley, […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Juwan Johnson #83 of the New Orleans Saints runs after catch against Malaki Starks #24 of the Baltimore Ravens in the fourth quarter of a game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens dropped to 1-1 after losing at home to the New Orleans Saints in Week 2. Here is a breakdown of the team’s player snap counts on offense and defense from the 24-17 defeat. Offense QB: Lamar Jackson 58 RB: Derrick Henry 31, Justice Hill 27 WR: Rashod Bateman 54, Chris Moore 32, LaJohntay Wester 31, Devontez Walker 17 TE: Mark Andrews 41, Durham Smythe 32, Matthew Hibner 19, Josh Cuevas 5 OL: Ronnie Stanley 46, John Simpson 58, Jovaughn Gwyn 58, Vega Ioane 58, Roger Rosengarten 58, Carson Vinson 13 Jackson was protected by his starting offensive line for the entire game with the exception of Ronnie Stanley, who was replaced by Carson Vinson for the last 13 snaps. Stanley’s toe injury forced him to exit the game early and he was the only injury casualty for the offense. Derrick Henry was nearly matched in snaps by Justice Hill and played 53% of the share. Henry notably only received five carries in the second half with the Ravens trying to protect a lead. He had 87 scrimmage yards and a touchdown. Rasheen Ali has not been a factor in the running back rotation to begin the season. At wide receiver, Chris Moore (32 snaps) and LaJohntay Wester (31 snaps) saw elevated playing time with Zay Flowers absent. Devontez Walker returned from injury and only received 17 snaps despite making a long 47-yard reception in the first half. Rookie Elijah Sarratt was activated to play but did not receive any offensive snaps. Rashod Bateman played all but four snaps and had a team-high seven catches for 88 yards with a touchdown. Like Sarratt, fellow rookies Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas played limited roles on offense. Hibner’s 19 snaps were slightly down from last week and neither saw a target in the passing game. Mark Andrews dominated the snap share (71%) at the position and caught six passes for 49 yards. Durham Smythe played over 50% of snaps as a blocking piece. Defense DL: Calais Campbell 40, Travis Jones 38, Broderick Washington 27, John Jenkins 21, Aeneas Peebles 8 EDGE: Tavius Robinson 53, Trey Hendrickson 36, Mike Green 32, Zion Young 23 ILB: Roquan Smith 68, Trenton Simpson 42, CB: Nate Wiggins 67, Marlon Humphrey 67, Chandler Rivers 24, Keyon Martin 1, Chidobe Awuzie 1 S: Malaki Starks 68, Kyle Hamilton 67, Jaylinn Hawkins 64, Keondre Jackson 1 Veteran Calais Campbell led all defensive lineman in snaps with 40, closely followed by Travis Jones (38). The Ravens distributed defensive reps to all five players in the rotation again, with Aeneas Peebles bringing up the rear with eight snaps. Broderick Washington and John Jenkins ate up a combined 48 snaps. On the edge, Tavius Robinson’s 53 snaps were by far the highest of the group. Trey Hendrickson played 53% of defensive plays while nursing a broken finger injury, but still managed to record a sack — as did Robinson. Mike Green saw a huge jump in playing time from last week (32 snaps) and made an impact with a team-high two quarterback hits, two tackles for loss and a sack. Zion Young saw a slight uptick in playing time (23 snaps). Roquan Smith did not leave the field. Next to him, Trenton Simpson’s 62% snap share saw him make a couple notable plays including a big tackle for loss. It will be interesting to see how Simpson’s playing time changes when Teddye Buchanan makes his return from injury soon. Nate Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey each played all but one play at cornerback. Rookie nickel Chandler Rivers jumped Keyon Martin in the pecking order in this game, playing 24 snaps with a tackle for loss. Surprisingly, veteran Chidobe Awuzie was once again iced out of the defensive game plan and saw just one snap. The Ravens seem to be opting for three-safety looks and giving their young slot corners reps over Awuzie. Malaki Starks played the entire game and Kyle Hamilton left the field for one play. Jaylinn Hawkins had another near every-down role with 64 snaps. The Ravens struggled with missed tackles on defense in this game, particularly over the middle of the field.
author: Frank Platko

title: Ravens vs. Saints: 4 winners and plenty of losers
summary: The Baltimore Ravens fell back to earth this week with a humbling loss to the New Orleans Saints. There was plenty of blame to go around in this one, with a few bright spots mixed in. Winners Rashod Bateman: The Ravens needed their former first-rounder to step up in Zay Flowers’ absence this week, and […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Rashod Bateman #7 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens fell back to earth this week with a humbling loss to the New Orleans Saints. There was plenty of blame to go around in this one, with a few bright spots mixed in. Winners Rashod Bateman: The Ravens needed their former first-rounder to step up in Zay Flowers’ absence this week, and Bateman answered the call with 88 receiving yards and a touchdown on seven catches. Bateman was the intended target on Lamar Jackson’s game-sealing interception, leading to questions about whether he ran the correct route, but both players were quick to shut such speculation down after the game. Trenton Simpson: Simpson’s contract season is off to a strong start through two games. The athletic linebacker was everywhere against the Saints, making six tackles and one tackle for loss. Simpson helped end several plays close to the line of scrimmage throughout the game. Mark Andrews: Andrews started the game on the wrong foot with a drop on third down, leading to a three-and-out on the offense’s first series. The veteran tight end rebounded afterwards, though, moving the chains on multiple plays and helping to spring several runs with key blocks. Andrews finished the day with 49 yards on six catches. While he may not be the explosive threat he once was, Jackson’s career go-to target can still be a reliable option through the air. Devontez Walker: Walker had just one catch on the day, but it was a big one. Backed up in their own end zone, Jackson connected with Walker on a 47-yard bomb. Walker has done nothing but make big plays when called upon so far in his career. Losers Secondary: Just about every member of the secondary shares some blame, from allowing Chris Olave to convert multiple key first downs to missing crucial tackles throughout the game. Safeties Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins seemed to be the worst offenders, with both missing tackles that led to extended drives for New Orleans. Starks appeared to be responsible for Olave’s touchdown catch as well. Special teams: The Ravens’ special teams had multiple gaffes on the day, the first being a blocked field goal that would have given Baltimore a 10-0 lead in the second quarter. Perhaps the bigger blunder, though, was allowing a 53-yard kick return before the end of the first half that allowed the Saints to cut the lead to eight with a field goal. Coaching staff: The honeymoon period for the Ravens’ new coaching staff is officially over. Sunday’s loss featured multiple questionable decisions on both sides of the ball. Possibly the biggest head-scratcher of the day was opting for a deep shot to wide receiver Chris Moore on third-and-one instead of handing the ball to Derrick Henry. The incomplete pass led to a three-and-out while the game was tied in the fourth quarter. Jesse Minter also had a questionable challenge on an Olave catch on the previous drive, which led to the Ravens only having two timeouts with just over a minute left on their final drive of the game. Chris Moore: Moore was the surprising hero of Week 1, but things did not go as well this week for the veteran receiver. Moore was the intended target on the aforementioned third-and-one deep ball, failing to haul the pass in. Moore was also flagged for holding earlier in the game, which negated a signature Jackson scramble for a first down. Moore nearly fumbled on a kickoff return as well, but he was ruled down on replay.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens Report Card, Week 2: Coming up short across the board in upset loss
summary: The Baltimore Ravens suffered an upset defeat in Week 2, falling to the New Orleans Saints at home by a score of 24-17. The Ravens led for most of the game before being outscored 15-0 in the fourth quarter and squandering an eight-point lead. It was a disappointing follow up to a resounding victory in […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens scores a touchdown against the New Orleans Saints during the first quarter of the game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens suffered an upset defeat in Week 2, falling to the New Orleans Saints at home by a score of 24-17. The Ravens led for most of the game before being outscored 15-0 in the fourth quarter and squandering an eight-point lead. It was a disappointing follow up to a resounding victory in the regular season opener. Here are report card grades for each position group from the losing effort. Quarterback: C+ Lamar Jackson was mostly sharp throwing the ball in this game. He wound up connecting on 67% of his 31 pass attempts for 235 yards through the air with a touchdown, while adding 34 running yards on four rushes. The game-sealing interception to end the game leaves a sour taste, however. Whether it was simply a bad throw or a case of route miscommunication with Rashod Bateman is unclear — either way it erased the chance of a vintage game-winning drive or game-tying drive. Jackson played a fine game within structure, but the Ravens could have used more off-script magic from him without Zay Flowers on the field. Running Back: B Derrick Henry’s longest run of the game went for only eight yards. He averaged 4.3 yards per rush with a touchdown and 87 scrimmage yards. The Ravens puzzlingly only gave Henry five carries in the second half when they were leading by more than a touchdown. He likely would have been able to grind out some much-needed first downs to help sustain drives. Justice Hill turned four touches into 18 total yards behind him. Wide Receiver: B In the first game without Flowers or Ja’Kobi Lane, Bateman stepped up with a team-high seven catches on nine targets for 88 yards — the most of any player on both teams — and a touchdown catch. Bateman unfortunately was the target on Jackson’s intercepted pass to end the game. Devontez Walker had a highlight reel 47-yard catch early in the game in his season debut but was targeted only one either time. Walker’s involvement likely should have been greater. LaJohntay Wester and Chris Moore each had one catch. Rookie Elijah Sarratt was not involved in the game plan and was out-snapped by both Moore and Wester. Tight End: C+ Mark Andrews had an effective pass-catching game with six catches, second-most on the team. Andrews recorded 49 receiving yards for the second straight game and had multiple first down conversions over the middle. Rookies Matthew Hibner and Josh Cuevas were not targeted at all. Some anticipated more tight end usage given the wide receiver deficit from injuries, but that was not the case. Durham Smythe was targeted one time but did not have a catch. The tight ends collectively did not seem to make a huge impact in the run game, as Henry was not able to hit any significant running lanes on the outside. Offensive Line: D+ It was another uneven performance from the Ravens’ offensive line. Their pass protection was shaky for the second straight week, and this time the run blocking was not as dominant to compensate. Jackson was sacked three times and the Ravens surrendered six quarterback hits as well. The Saints were able to generate pressure to make key plays in the second half. Ronnie Stanley was replaced by Carson Vinson after he aggravated a toe injury and the interior of the offensive line was suspect. Jovaughn Gwyn and Vega Ioane each allowed multiple pressures and John Simpson had a notable missed block as well. Defensive Line: C The front seven did a good job against the run, limiting the Saints to only 65 rushing yards on 27 carries. Alvin Kamara and Travis Etienne Jr. were held in check. They were not able to create much interior pressure against Shough in the pocket. Travis Jones, Calais Campbell, Broderick Washington and company were quiet in the box score. Jones did have one pass breakup, but there were not any notable plays in terms of pass rush. Edge Rusher: B The Ravens were able to get pressure against Tyler Shough but allowed him to evade sacks a few times. Trey Hendrickson had his first sack as a Raven to accompany a tackle for loss. Mike Green had a big performance with a team-high two tackles for loss and two quarterback hits, along with a sack as well. Tavius Robinson had another sack for the second straight game. It wasn’t the best showing for rookie Zion Young, who missed a couple notable tackles. The Ravens’ edge rushers did a good job containing outside runs and limiting any explosive rushing plays. Linebacker: C + Roquan Smith had eight total tackles but the impact plays he made last week were not there to the same degree. Trenton Simpson had a tackle for loss and a huge stop on the Saints’ two-point conversion attempt, which would have been a game-altering moment if not for a holding penalty that negated the play. The Ravens’ linebackers similarly deserve credit for the defense’s effectiveness against the run, but also share blame for missed tackles over the middle of the field. Saints’ tight end Juwan Johnson had 66 receiving yards. Cornerback: C + The Ravens had some difficulties covering Chris Olave, who made big catches and conversions in one-on-one situations. Olave finished with eight receptions for 86 yards and a late fourth-quarter score. Marlon Humphrey was beaten a couple times in lone coverage. Devaughn Vele, the Saints’ No. 2 wideout, also had a couple notable catches and finished with 64 receiving yards and a long catch of 29 yards. Humphrey had one pass breakup and Nate Wiggins finished with six tackles and was solid in coverage again. Rookie Chandler Rivers had a huge tackle for loss attacking a screen pass from the nickel spot. Safety: D+ Kyle Hamilton easily led the defense in tackles with 13 (seven solo tackles), one of which was a tackle for loss. It was not the most memorable performance for Malaki Starks and Jaylinn Hawkins, who appeared to miss multiple timely tackles in open space. Hawkins was called for a holding penalty on the Saints’ unsuccessful two-point conversion attempt, which they then converted on the re-try to knot the game up at 17-17. The Ravens need Starks to make more impact plays on the ball consistently. Special Teams: D + This was a forgettable game for the Ravens’ special teams unit and a disappointing follow up to a great outing in Week 1. Tyler Loop’s first 49-yard field goal attempt was partially blocked, forcing a miss that would have given the Ravens a 10-point lead in the second quarter. Just before halftime, their kick return coverage unit gave up a huge return that put the Saints in position to add another field goal, which made it a one-possession game.
author: Frank Platko

title: Greg Rousseau taking game to new heights early in 2026 season for Buffalo Bills
summary: Greg Rousseau is becoming a huge win for age-related draft analysis. Even after sitting out his second season at the University of Miami due to COVID, the Buffalo Bills selected Rousseau with one of the final picks in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft just a few weeks after his 21st birthday. He […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NY - SEPTEMBER 17: Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills looks on from the field during an NFL game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Greg Rousseau is becoming a huge win for age-related draft analysis. Even after sitting out his second season at the University of Miami due to COVID, the Buffalo Bills selected Rousseau with one of the final picks in the first round of the 2021 NFL Draft just a few weeks after his 21st birthday. He was one of the youngest players in that draft, and surprisingly was able to shoulder a full-time workload as a rookie at defensive end. Since then, he’s been a steady yet mostly unspectacular edge rusher in Buffalo. His regular-season pressure rate has hovered between 14.0% and 14.9%. Quite impressive, really. That is until the first two games of 2026 within Jim Leonhard’s scheme. Rousseau’s pressure rate is a massive 23.1% entering Week 3, and he already has four sacks on the year, matching his rookie-year total and just one shy of the five he accumulated as a 23-year-old in 2023. Just 26 years old, Rousseau has probably just entered the the prime of his career, and he’s already played 3,507 snaps — counting playoffs — in his NFL career. Along the way, he’s learned a variety of ways to collapse the pocket, work around tackles, and track the quarterback behind the line of scrimmage. Like on his first sack of the season, a strip-sack of C.J. Stroud in the first quarter of opening weekend against the Texans, watch how he swiped away the chipping tight end, then worked back to the inside as he felt the quarterback stepping into the pocket. pic.twitter.com/AKyqtmiHjX — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 Textbook. The clean, around-the-corner wins are flashy. The big-time sack producers understand how to follow the quarterback as he glides around in the pocket. The game-sealing sack late in the fourth quarter was a tremendous display of his maturity rushing the quarterback. Against the impossibly large and lengthy Trent Brown, Rousseau used an inside-arm stab before climbing around Brown’s outside shoulder before getting his right arm on the football as Stroud unsuccessfully attempted to evade the rush again. pic.twitter.com/CGbgryC1jX — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 That play was a fine example of why length matters along the defensive line. Not only to establish first contact at the point of attack… but to have the reach to get your hands on the football once you enter the pocket. Right when Rousseau has the offensive tackles thinking he’s a lanky-ish, finesse rusher… he can deploy a nasty straight-arm bull rush, like he did hear against the typically serviceable swing tackle Larry Borom. pic.twitter.com/Jo85WftYOA — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 His second sack against the Lions was the byproduct of bad offensive schematics from the Lions — as Rousseau was left with a tight end on him in pass pro. Obviously, Rousseau quickly worked through the tight end and forced another fumble on a sack. pic.twitter.com/LgzghItwoD — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 22, 2026 Referencing yesterday’s article on Buffalo’s pass rush converting pressures to sacks at a much higher clip than at any stage of the Sean McDermott era, Rousseau is a key aspect of that. Rousseau entered this season with a career 14.6% pressure-to-sack rate himself, and only in 2023 was that single-season rate higher than 15% — it was 21.4%. Thus far in the 2026 campaign, Rousseau has four sacks on 16 pressures, good for a 25% pressure-to-sack rate in Leonhard’s new scheme. And check where he is in the Pass-Rush Win Rates as compiled by PFF and SumerSports. By year No. 6 in the NFL, we almost always know precisely who a player is. But at his age, Rousseau has ample experience and really is entering the peak physical timeframe of his professional career. And, this season, he looks well on his way to realizing all the upside that was a key element of his draft profile all the way back in 2021.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Jim Leonhard’s defense offers mixed bag of early returns
summary: The Buffalo Bills surrendered over thirty points for the second straight game, allowing the Detroit Lions to score 31 in what was an entertaining 41-31 victory to open new Highmark Stadium in style. That 31-point result from the defense followed a similar outing from four days prior, as the Bills’ stop unit allowed 31 points […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Bradley Chubb #9 and Greg Rousseau #15 of the Buffalo Bills walk off the field after an NFL football game against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills surrendered over thirty points for the second straight game, allowing the Detroit Lions to score 31 in what was an entertaining 41-31 victory to open new Highmark Stadium in style. That 31-point result from the defense followed a similar outing from four days prior, as the Bills’ stop unit allowed 31 points to the Houston Texans in what was a 36-31 victory. The biggest change in Buffalo’s personnel from last season to this season relates to the defense. Former head coach Sean McDermott was a defensive coordinator prior to earning the Bills’ top job, so Buffalo’s defense was molded in his image throughout the last nine seasons. With Joe Brady, McDermott’s offensive coordinator since midway through the 2023 season, taking over as the head man, a new defensive boss was coming into town regardless. That new boss, Jim Leonhard, runs an entirely different system from McDermott’s. Whereas McDermott preached players doing their “one-eleventh,” sticking to fundamentals, principles, and areas on the field, Leonhard has tried to allow Buffalo’s defenders the freedom to go make a play. McDermott’s scheme generally included zone coverages in the back end, and if there wasn’t a blitz, there was a four-man rush where the main goal of those four rushers was to maintain their gap integrity. Conversely, Leonhard’s system has introduced more man coverage, more blitzing, and more movement along that front seven. One of the biggest questions from the offseason was just how well-suited to a more aggressive scheme Buffalo’s defensive personnel is this year. And, as could reasonably be expected, the answer so far is mixed. Leading off with the negative, we’ve seen a lot of miscommunication in the defensive secondary. On Thursday night against the Lions, we saw nickel corners Dee Alford and Jordan Hancock lose their mark. We also saw linebackers crashing to players in the middle of the field, leaving the seams open for some bigger chunk plays for Detroit. After Buffalo raced out to a 21-0 lead in the first 25 minutes of play, the Lions were able to outscore the Bills 31-20 the rest of the way. There is some legitimate concern about the defensive secondary’s ability to handle the assignments Leonhard is giving. On the flip side, though, the front-seven of the defense has looked dominant at times. Buffalo had Lions quarterback Jard Goff under pressure on well over half his snaps, as he took four sacks and 11 hits on the night. Goff was pressured on 22 dropbacks, per Pro Football Focus . Greg Rousseau had two more sacks and another forced fumble, and Bradley Chubb added 1.5 sacks on the night, as well. Buffalo’s front was even excellent against the run, holding stud running back Jahmyr Gibbs to 52 yards and 3.3 yards per carry just one week after he gained 156 yards and averaged 5.4 yards per carry in a win over the New Orleans Saints. The Bills had a defensive stuff rate of 45% in the game, just a phenomenal number Has the Buffalo defensive front benefitted from two subpar offensive lines to begin the season? Perhaps, as the Lions started three backups on Thursday and the Texans were widely regarded as possessing the worst offensive line in the NFL heading into the season. However, it’s encouraging to see a Buffalo front willing to attack rather than sit back and react. For years, we’ve waited for the Bills to show a return on investment along the defensive line, as general manager Brandon Beane continuously has tinkered with the front in search of a solid pass rush. The best part of this early season showing is just how many of the players central to it are home-grown players. Nose guard Deone Walker is rapidly developing into one of the best interior defensive linemen in the NFL. We’ve already talked about Rousseau, but he’s been so good early on that he’s looking like a whole new player. Ed Oliver missed Week 2, but he was disruptive in the victory over Houston. Even DeWayne Carter, who was written off and figuratively left for dead after a horrendous rookie season and a lost second year spent dealing with an Achilles tear, looked disruptive on Thursday night. Free agent signings like Chubb and Michael Hoecht, who is also coming off an Achilles tear and looked much better against the Lions, have only added to the good vibes up front. Then, we have the linebacker group. Dorian Williams is flying around making run stops and big hits. He has 15 tackles and two tackles for loss. Terrel Bernard has transitioned to the new defense well, registering 17 tackles and two tackles for loss in two games. Rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr hasn’t looked as dynamic as he did in the preseason, but he hasn’t looked lost in his first two real NFL games. Right now, the defense hasn’t quite found its footing overall. Leonhard himself said that the unit is too “boom or bust” after the win over Detroit. However, some of what they’re doing up front gives me hope that, once the back end of the defense figures itself out, that this unit has more “boom” potential than it does “bust.” My favorite thing that’s happened so far this season is the use of stunts and games up front. Maybe it was just a feel thing, but under McDermott, it felt like we always knew exactly where the defensive linemen were going based on where they linedup before the snap. Through two games with Leonhard at the helm, Buffalo is showing that it won’t do that anymore. Leonhard’s Bills are third in the league in passing down stunt rate thus far, and I expect that they’ll either stay right around there or continue to use it even more as they play more games. The Bills have 7 sacks in two games and are third in passing down Stunt% behind the 49ers and Seahawks. DC Jim Leonhard is using a "speed" package on passing downs, amplified by movement, to wreak havoc on opponents' pass protections. Clip 1 illustrates how Buffalo can build… pic.twitter.com/prsOC16IpN — Cody Alexander (@The_Coach_A) September 21, 2026 The front of the defense is showing multiple encouraging signs. The back of the defense has enough talent that they’ll figure something out, and while concerns that the team has a lot of square pegs for round holes in the defensive secondary are valid, the hope is that with more time on task, they’ll round into shape as the season goes on. I’m not worried about the points Buffalo has allowed so far because the offense has scored more; however, we all know that the first time Buffalo loses a game 35-31 this season, the focus will fall squarely on the defense if it doesn’t round into shape. Early on in the seaosn, we’ll take the good with the bad. What’s going right for this team so far, though, is that they finally seem to have the makings of a truly formidable pass rush. The secondary will find its footing. For now, though, keep watching those glorious stunts ( and fake stunts! ) up front pay dividends for a Buffalo defense that has been searching for juice in that area of the game for a long time.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Buffalo Bills will face a Los Angeles Chargers team thin at TE in Week 3
summary: The Buffalo Bills are getting ready to host the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday for a classic AFL matchup that should feature plenty of fireworks by quarterbacks Josh Allen and Justin Herbert. Both teams are dealing with injuries to key offensive starters, but Los Angeles that may have the hardest path to carve out to […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 13: David Njoku #83 of the Los Angeles Chargers runs after a catch during a 26-14 loss to the Arizona Cardinals at SoFi Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills are getting ready to host the Los Angeles Chargers on Sunday for a classic AFL matchup that should feature plenty of fireworks by quarterbacks Josh Allen and Justin Herbert. Both teams are dealing with injuries to key offensive starters, but Los Angeles that may have the hardest path to carve out to earn the team’s first win of the season due to a shortage of pass catchers. On Monday afternoon, ESPN senior NFL insider Adam Schefter reported that the Chargers are placing tight ends David Njoku (fibula) and Charlie Kolar (forearm) on Injured Reserve . With each missing at least next four games, that leaves Los Angeles with only tight end Oronde Gadsden II on the team’s active roster. The son of former Miami Dolphins wide receiver Oronde Gadsden, the younger Gadsden attended Syracuse University from 2021 through 2024. It’s likely the Chargers make roster moves to reinforce the tight end position, but it would appear that Gadsden is in line for featured snaps at tight end. Patrick Herbert (brother to Justin) is currently on Los Angeles’ practice squad, and seems to be a likely candidate to be called up in Week 3. Bills reporter Sal Capaccio of WGR 550 also reports that the Chargers are likely to “be without starting LG Kayode Awosika and starting DT Dalvin Tomlinson” following comments head coach Jim Harbaugh shared with the media saying “both will miss some time.” Los Angeles has also seen wide receiver Ladd McConkey miss time to start the season thanks to a ribs injury, but he was able to return for the team’s Week 2 game against the Las Vegas Raiders. Safety Derwin James Jr. is also dealing with a broken thumb that will see him playing with a protective cast beginning in Week 3. Buffalo will monitor wide receiver DJ Moore this week to see how the AC joint sprain he suffered in Week 2 responds ahead of Sunday’s game. Additionally, the Bills are also managing a hip injury with defensive tackle Ed Oliver.
author: Matt Byham

title: Bills vs. Chargers odds: Opening lines for Week 3 matchup
summary: The Buffalo Bills enter Week 3 riding a two-win wave to start the 2026 NFL season. With quarterback Josh Allen locked in and playing at an MVP level, the team has taken down a tough Houston Texans team on the road, and dealt the potent Detroit Lions a humbling defeat. Next up and heading to […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - DECEMBER 23: Josh Allen #17 of the Buffalo Bills passes the ball during the first quarter against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on December 23, 2023 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Katelyn Mulcahy/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills enter Week 3 riding a two-win wave to start the 2026 NFL season. With quarterback Josh Allen locked in and playing at an MVP level, the team has taken down a tough Houston Texans team on the road, and dealt the potent Detroit Lions a humbling defeat. Next up and heading to Highmark Stadium are the Los Angeles Chargers, a team reeling with two very ugly 26-14 losses to its name. Will it be a one-sided affair in Buffalo this coming Sunday? It’s trending that way with odds makers, where opening odds at FanDuel Sportsbook have the Bills as 7-point (-7/-112) over the Chargers (+7/-108) . As of publishing, the moneyline sat at -370 for Buffalo and +295 for Los Angeles, with the over/under at U50.5/-115 (Bills) / O50.5/-105 (Chargers). This will be the Bills’ second of a three-game home stand at their new stadium, which features an even louder Bills Mafia than ever before. It’s going to be tough sledding for Los Angeles, which must also adapt to jet lag and a 1 p.m. EDT start. However, an 0-2 team is among the most dangerous early season opponents and the NFL is famously a week-to-week league. The last time these teams met, the game was played in SoFi Stadium for a primetime Peacock-exclusive matchup on December 23, 2023. Buffalo won a tough-fought game, 24-22, with Josh Allen completing 15-of-21 passes for 237 yards with a touchdown and interception; adding five rushes for 15 yards and two more ground scores. It was wide receiver Gabe Davis’ last spectacular game with the Bills, as he finished with four catches for 130 yards — including a 57-yard touchdown. Overall, the Chargers lead the all-time series 25-14-2, which dates back to October 2, 1960 when both teams first joined the newly formed American Football League. Buffalo is 2-1 against Los Angeles since Josh Allen took over as the team’s starting quarterback. Interestingly, that loss came in his first NFL start and second professional game back in 2018. Despite the odds and current situation, the Chargers come to Bills Country looking to make a statement and fully capable of making life miserable for Bills Mafia if things click. The Bills are in the midst of a defensive overhaul that’s seen the defensive backfield struggle to contain pass catchers. Buffalo is managing injuries to two key players this week. Wide receiver DJ Moore suffered an AC joint sprain in his shoulder, while defensive tackle Ed Oliver is dealing with a hip injury. The status for both players remains up in the air as of publishing. Additionally, there are existing injuries to continue monitoring for defensive tackle T.J. Sanders and running back Ty Johnson. Key injuries to monitor for Los Angeles are safety Derwin James (broken thumb, to be fitted w/cast), tight end David Njoku (knee), defensive tackle Dalvin Tomlinson (hamstring), offensive guard Kayode Awosika (leg), and tight end Charlie Kolar (forearm). You can bet that it’s likely to remain the Josh Allen & James Cook III show on Sunday. Think you’ve got what it takes to make a play with the Buffalo Bills in 2026? title: Buffalo Bills off to an elite pace disrupting quarterbacks
summary: Just to start off a candid note, nothing you’re about to read suggests that the Buffalo Bills’ defense doesn’t have room for improvement. It very obviously does, allowing 31 points in both of their first games. Now Week 1 is known for “lying” about a team’s identity, and Thursday Night Football is similarly wonky, but […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Greg Rousseau #15 and Bradley Chubb #9 of the Buffalo Bills sack Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions during the first quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just to start off a candid note, nothing you’re about to read suggests that the Buffalo Bills’ defense doesn’t have room for improvement. It very obviously does, allowing 31 points in both of their first games. Now Week 1 is known for “lying” about a team’s identity, and Thursday Night Football is similarly wonky, but neither is wonky enough to make me dismiss all that. They’ve also not recorded an interception yet, have the sixth worst points per drive in the league, and the ninth worst scoring rate; allowing their opponents to score 50% of the time. But the pass rush! That’s been a delight and something to build off of. Buffalo has seven sacks on the season so far and 19 QB hits. It’s early yet and forecasts should be considered as accurate as the weather ones in Western New York, but that would put Buffalo on pace for about 60 sacks and 160 quarterback hits. Those numbers aren’t unachievable, with the Broncos breaking the 60-sack mark the last two seasons (63 and 68) and 164 QB hits last year. Let’s take a look at some of their work so far this and see if it’s a lucky streak, or likely to be replicated.. The Film! pic.twitter.com/Bshv0SAIG0 — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 20, 2026 Alright, so the question was if what was happening can be replicated and the answer so far seems to be “yes.” Breaking down the plays, here’s a quick rundown of what I see. Greg Rousseau is leading the way for the team. His success is largely dependent on his use of space and subsequent ability to disengage from the block to get after the quarterback. Rousseau’s long arm has been his bread and butter but as seen in the plays above, he’s been able to generate leverage and collapse the pocket. That’s benefitted himself directly and doesn’t exactly hurt the chances for the rest of the team either. Groot is currently on pace for 34 sacks this season which would shatter the current single-season mark of 23. I don’t expect that to continue, but would clearly be happy if it did. Deone Walker has been the talk of the town, and for good reason. For a big man, he’s been showing off good finesse techniques. The shimmy and swim move in the clips above are good examples of that with Walker starting to get a reputation as a menace up the middle. Bradley Chubb I described earlier this year as “capable” which was in no way intended as an insult. While I didn’t gush over anything I felt was “elite” I did indicate he could make a bigger impact than Von Miller or Joey Bosa if he remained healthy. Put differently, I felt he might be a tier below those players’ peak, but actually being present snap-to-snap would elevate him higher than those guys. So far I’m not backing off that analysis and his steady presence has been paying off for himself directly, but also the rest of the team. Chubb is currently trending toward double digit sacks himself. Michael Hoecht is a player I was excited to see suit up for Buffalo, feeling he could become the chaos piece like Lorenzo Alexander used to be. He had a great debut last year, and was sadly injured pretty much right away. So far this season, he’s been living up to what I hoped for and he’s another player that a full season of play from would likely pay off in a big way. The Final Straw Yeah, it’s way too early to make sweeping declarations, but as of right now the defensive front seems legit. The team may have an emerging star in Greg Rousseau, and a strong supporting cast around him. If they can keep it up, it’ll be the first time they broke the 50-sack mark since 2023 when Leonard Floyd and Ed Oliver led the team’s 53-sack campaign. That was the only time they hit the 50s in the McDermott era, despite several years with excellent pass rush rates.

title: Derwin James provides injury update before game against Buffalo Bills
summary: The Los Angeles Chargers have started 0-2 after consecutive 26-14 losses to the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, and in Week 2, their superstar safety Derwin James injured his hand. The six-time All-Pro updated his injury on Monday as the club begins preparations for the cross-country trip to take on the Buffalo Bills in […]
full_text: Inglewood, CA - September 20: Los Angeles Chargers safety Derwin James Jr. (3) takes the field for a game against the Las Vegas Raiders at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood on Sunday, September 20, 2026. (Photo by Jeff Antenore/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images) | MediaNews Group via Getty Images The Los Angeles Chargers have started 0-2 after consecutive 26-14 losses to the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, and in Week 2, their superstar safety Derwin James injured his hand. The six-time All-Pro updated his injury on Monday as the club begins preparations for the cross-country trip to take on the Buffalo Bills in Week 3. Derwin James said he fractured his pinky finger on his left hand. He’ll play the rest of the season in a cast — Kris Rhim (@krisrhim1) September 20, 2026 Despite fracturing the pinky against the Raiders, James still appeared on 52 defensive snaps, the second-most of any Chargers player on that side of the ball. He’s always been one of the tougher defensive backs in football. He’s regularly been darn disruptive too. Now 30, James was a second-team All-Pro the past two seasons. Through two contests this year, James has 17 tackles and one pass breakup. At 6’2” and 215 pounds, the former All-American from Florida State remains one of the NFL’s most dangerous swiss-army knives in the secondary. He’s an elite blitzer, tackler, and coverage defender. It’ll be interesting to see how sizable his cast is, and monitor whether it hinders his ability to make plays on the football against the Bills in Week 3 (and for the remainder of the season).
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills Week 2 game balls following 41-31 win over Detroit
summary: The Buffalo Bills are 2-0 after defeating the Detroit Lions 41-31 in the inaugural regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. Buffalo’s offense delivered 41 points against Detroit, led by another nearly unstoppable performance from Josh Allen. James Cook controlled the game on the ground, while Greg Rousseau continued his dominant start to the season […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are 2-0 after defeating the Detroit Lions 41-31 in the inaugural regular-season game at the new Highmark Stadium. Buffalo’s offense delivered 41 points against Detroit, led by another nearly unstoppable performance from Josh Allen. James Cook controlled the game on the ground, while Greg Rousseau continued his dominant start to the season on the other side of the ball. Following the win, head coach Joe Brady awarded game balls to all three players. Game ball: QB Josh Allen Allen completed 20 of 31 passes for 248 yards and three touchdowns. He added two more touchdowns on the ground, along with 69 yards rushing. Through two weeks, Allen has once again shown why there aren’t many (if any) quarterbacks you would take over him. Whether Buffalo needed him to deliver through the air or finish a drive with his legs, Allen found a way to keep the offense moving. Game ball: RB James Cook Cook carried the ball 21 times for 135 yards and a touchdown, averaging more than six yards per attempt. His performance gave Buffalo the offensive balance it needed against Detroit. Cook was patient when necessary, decisive when the running lanes opened, and consistently put the offense in manageable situations. Allen will understandably receive plenty of attention after accounting for five touchdowns, but Cook’s work on the ground helped make the entire offense more difficult to defend. Cook absolutely delivered. Game ball: DE Greg Rousseau As Brady prepared to present the final game ball, he explained just how rare Rousseau’s start to the season has been. “This has only happened once in history,” Brady said. “And the first one was Bruce Smith…” Rousseau recorded two sacks against the Houston Texans in Week 1 and added two more against the Lions. He became the first Bills player since Pro Football Hall of Famer Bruce Smith in 1996 to record at least two sacks in each of the season’s first two games. The four sacks are impressive enough, but they only tell part of the story. Rousseau has also forced three fumbles through two games, becoming a consistent source of disruption for Buffalo’s defense. Three game balls, one historic afternoon As Brady ended the locker room speech, Allen quickly handed his ball to Bills owner Terry Pegula in recognition of the franchise’s inaugural game in the new stadium. “I want to give my ball to Mr Pegula.” Celebrating the first win in the new stadium. It was a fitting gesture on a historic day for the organization. Allen may have led the Bills to the victory, but he understood that this game ball represented something much bigger than his performance. It was a historic evening in Buffalo, and there was no shortage of players worthy of taking home a game ball. My Honorable mentions: TE Dalton Kincaid Kincaid gave Allen a reliable target throughout the night, finishing with seven receptions for 95 yards and a touchdown. He consistently found openings in Detroit’s defense and came just five yards short of the second 100-yard receiving game of his career. Kincaid’s production was another encouraging sign of the role he can play in Buffalo’s passing attack this season. WR Keon Coleman Coleman may have been the unsung hero of the night, especially after DJ Moore left the game. He caught all six of his targets for 63 yards, with four of those receptions moving the chains. Coleman did not find the end zone, but he delivered every time Allen looked in his direction and helped keep multiple scoring drives alive. It was exactly the type of dependable performance Buffalo needed from the third year player. WR Joshua Palmer Palmer has only two receptions through the first two games of the season, but he has certainly made them count. Both catches have gone for more than 30 yards, and both have resulted in touchdowns. Palmer has not needed significant volume to make a difference. Through two weeks, every reception has produced an explosive scoring play. Bills Mafia, who earned your game ball following Buffalo’s 41-31 victory over the Lions?
author: Sara Larson

title: Buffalo Bills can’t forget about this common tendency in NFL before Chargers game
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will enter this Week 3 contested headed in diametrically opposed directions, which can often spawn a rather silly assumption. That we are sure of something in the NFL, especially in September. Now, should the Bills have confidence going into this game? Yes. Plenty of it. And, I’ll never […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 13: Offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel of the Los Angeles Chargers takes the field during a preseason game against the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium on August 13, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers will enter this Week 3 contested headed in diametrically opposed directions, which can often spawn a rather silly assumption. That we are sure of something in the NFL, especially in September. Now, should the Bills have confidence going into this game? Yes. Plenty of it. And, I’ll never blame for a team for, internally, feeling good about their chances against a team spiraling as opposed to an opponent firing on all cylinders. But we can’t simply assume this game is over before it begins. There’s too much parity in today’s NFL. And many times, right when we collectively feel like we have a team or teams figured out, the unexpected strikes. Justin Herbert defenders are going through it to begin the 2026 season. He’s completed 59.3% of his throws, with two touchdowns and three interceptions and has been sacked six times in this 0-2 start. That comes after another dud of a playoff game last January. Mike McDaniels’ widely regarded reputation as an offensive genius is continuing to lose luster, fast, and it’s fair to start to wonder if Jim Harbaugh, at this age, can be a Super Bowl-caliber coach. But Herbert has insane big-time throw ability in him. McDaniels did coach a Dolphins team that, with plenty of talent, saw Tua Tagovailoa lead the NFL in passer rating. Derwin James has been a first or second team All-Pro six times. And Harbaugh has won everywhere he’s coached, from FCS football to Stanford to Michigan to the 49ers. Heck, McDaniels’ rather hapless Dolphins trounced the Bills 30-13 in November last season. And, for the Bills, the Patriots are coming to town in Week 4. This Sunday could be referred to as a “trap game.” Buffalo can’t get caught looking ahead. Because for as much as the Chargers may very well be already into a season-long implosion with some polarizing yet previously successful characters at the top of their organization, the bounce-back tendency of the NFL cannot be forgotten before this Week 3 game. It’s very real. Sure, favorites can cruise. But more often than we initially believe, two teams playing each other one week do not resemble what we’ve previously seen from them. However, I’ll end with this — if Buffalo can get out to a sizable lead in the first half, this does feel like a Chargers team that won’t have nearly as much fight in it as the Lions showed in Week 2.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills pass rush has improved in one overlooked but key area
summary: Despite clearly not playing particularly well through two weeks, there is one vital area in which the Buffalo Bills defense has improved from years past. Converting pressures to sacks. Through the vast majority of the Sean McDermott era, the Bills pass-rush unit was rarely one of the league’s better units actually sacking the quarterback. We […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Bradley Chubb #9 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates with Greg Rousseau #15 after sacking Jared Goff #16 of the Detroit Lions during the second quarter of the game at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Despite clearly not playing particularly well through two weeks, there is one vital area in which the Buffalo Bills defense has improved from years past. Converting pressures to sacks. Through the vast majority of the Sean McDermott era, the Bills pass-rush unit was rarely one of the league’s better units actually sacking the quarterback. We never really hear or read about this metric for a defense — it’s strictly reserved for quarterbacks — and I’m not sure why. Don’t get me wrong. Disruption is production for a pass rush. But, of course, sacks are most valuable. Let’s check the Bills’ pressure-to-sack rate through two games in 2026 and compare to the last few seasons. Last season, the pressure-to-sack rate of Buffalo’s defense was 19.0% via Next Gen Stats. The season before it was only 12.8%. The best figure Buffalo’s defense managed since 2020 in this metric was 23.2% in 2023, when as a team, the Bills had 54 sacks during the regular season. It was the only time they reached or eclipsed the 20% mark in McDermott’s tenure. Two weeks into the 2026 campaign, the Bills defense has managed a pressure-to-sack rate of 29.1%. Yes, I know. Sample size. But it ranks third in the NFL behind the Texans (30.4%) and Steelers (36.8%). The Bills are currently one of five teams with a pressure-to-sack rate as a defense over 25%. In short, they’re not just pressuring quarterbacks, they’re getting quarterbacks on the ground. Leonhard’s defense has been far from stellar, allowing 31 points in each contest. And the unit’s pressure rate is only 27.1% per NGS, which is distinctly in the bottom fourth of the NFL. But if it’s felt like the Bills pass rush has been better than previous seasons through these first two weeks, it’s because they’re converting those pressures to sacks at a noticeably higher rate than the past two seasons. This is a not often used metric I’ll be tracking with the Bills throughout this season, particularly after the pass rush’s torrid start.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: What Buffalo Bills’ snap counts against Detroit Lions reveal
summary: The Buffalo Bills offense spent plenty of time on the field during their 41-31 victory over the Detroit Lions in Week 2.  Buffalo ran 74 offensive plays, compared with just 58 in its season-opening win over the Houston Texans. The Bills possessed the ball for 33:45, accumulated 34 first downs and produced touchdowns on six […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: C.J. Gardner-Johnson #22 with Damar Hamlin #3 of the Buffalo Bills celebrate a play during the first quarter against the Detroit Lions at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills offense spent plenty of time on the field during their 41-31 victory over the Detroit Lions in Week 2. Buffalo ran 74 offensive plays, compared with just 58 in its season-opening win over the Houston Texans. The Bills possessed the ball for 33:45, accumulated 34 first downs and produced touchdowns on six of their possessions. Defensively, the Bills played 65 snaps after facing 79 against Houston. Although Detroit scored 31 points, Buffalo’s improved time of possession helped keep the defense from carrying the same workload it faced in Week 1. Here is what the Bills’ Week 2 playing-time distribution tells us. Offensive Snap Counts The offensive line remains remarkably stable For the second consecutive week, Buffalo’s starting offensive line did not miss a snap. Dion Dawkins, Alec Anderson, Connor McGovern, O’Cyrus Torrence and Spencer Brown each played all 74 offensive snaps. Josh Allen was also on the field for every play. That continuity matters. Tylan Grable’s two snaps came as an additional offensive lineman. Buffalo continues to lean heavily on its tight ends For the second straight game, all four active tight ends received offensive snaps. Dawson Knox led the group with 56 snaps, accounting for 75.7% of the offense. Dalton Kincaid played 49 snaps, or 66.2%, while Jackson Hawes was on the field for exactly half of Buffalo’s offensive plays. Keleki Latu rounded out the position with six snaps. The overlap between Knox, Kincaid and Hawes reinforces how frequently Buffalo used multiple-tight-end personnel . Hawes’ 50% participation is especially notable because his role extends beyond the traditional passing-game production reflected in a box score. Kincaid made the most of his opportunities, catching seven passes for 95 yards and a touchdown. DJ Moore’s injury changed the receiver rotation DJ Moore played only 23 snaps, or 31.1%, before leaving the game with an injury during the second quarter. His early departure opened additional opportunities for Buffalo’s other receivers. Keon Coleman led the position with 55 snaps, matching James Cook for the highest total among Buffalo’s skill-position players. Coleman caught all six of his targets for 63 yards, with four of those receptions moving the chains. Khalil Shakir played 36 snaps, while Joshua Palmer logged 28. Palmer continued to make his limited opportunities count, turning one of his two receptions this season into his second touchdown of more than 30 yards. Greg Dortch received only four offensive snaps, suggesting Buffalo responded to Moore’s absence largely by leaning further into its tight ends and its top three remaining receivers. James Cook remains the clear leader in the backfield Cook played 55 snaps, accounting for 74.3% of the offense. Ray Davis received 10 snaps, while Frank Gore Jr. played nine. Cook’s workload confirms that Buffalo continues to view him as its featured back rather than the leader of a committee. Davis and Gore combined for only 19 offensive snaps despite the Bills running 74 plays. Defensive Snap Counts Three defenders remain locked into every-down roles Terrel Bernard, Cole Bishop and C.J. Gardner-Johnson each played all 65 defensive snaps. They were also Buffalo’s three every-down defenders against Houston. Christian Benford and Maxwell Hairston nearly joined them, missing only one defensive snap apiece. That gave Buffalo five defensive backs or linebackers who played at least 98% of the game. The Bills continue to build the back end of their defense around that core, with Bernard handling the every-down responsibilities in the middle. Ed Oliver’s absence reshuffled the defensive line Ed Oliver was inactive after suffering an injury during pregame warmups, forcing Buffalo to adjust its defensive tackle rotation shortly before kickoff. Rookie Deone Walker assumed the largest workload at the position, playing 44 snaps, or 67.7%. DeWayne Carter followed with 31 snaps, while Greg Gaines played 19. Walker’s usage stands out. Playing more than two-thirds of the defensive snaps is a substantial assignment for an interior defensive lineman, particularly after the rotation unexpectedly lost Oliver. The edge rotation remains deep Greg Rousseau led Buffalo’s edge defenders with 43 snaps, followed closely by Bradley Chubb with 42. Landon Jackson played 28 snaps, Michael Hoecht received 27, T.J. Parker logged 17 and Javon Solomon played 15. Mike Danna added eight snaps. That distribution allowed Buffalo to continue rotating fresh pass rushers without significantly reducing the workloads of Rousseau or Chubb. Through two games, the defense has converted 29.1% of its pressures into sacks , an encouraging rate despite surrendering 31 points in each contest. Dorian Williams sees an expanded role Dorian Williams played 37 defensive snaps, accounting for 56.9% of the defense’s workload. Kaleb Elarms-Orr received 12 snaps behind him. Williams’ participation, combined with Dee Alford playing 38 snaps, shows Buffalo moving between its linebacker and defensive back packages based on Detroit’s personnel and game situation. Damar Hamlin played 17 snaps and Jordan Hancock played in 13, giving the Bills additional flexibility in their safety packages. What stands out most Buffalo’s Week 2 snap counts reveal continuity in some of its most important areas and adjustments where injuries demanded them. The most significant changes were largely injury driven. Moore’s early exit altered the receiver rotation, while Oliver’s pregame injury elevated Walker and Carter’s snaps inside. Buffalo is 2-0, but the defense has now allowed 31 points in consecutive games. The pass rush has been efficient at finishing its opportunities, yet the broader defensive results remain a work in progress. The snap counts show a coaching staff still relying heavily on its core, can they find the right rotation capable of producing more consistent results.
author: Sara Larson

title: Panthers vs Falcons Game Review: What do we know
summary: There are now three things that I am certain of in this world: death, taxes, and the Carolina Panthers using the Atlanta Falcons for a ‘get right’ game. I don’t know why, but quite frankly I don’t care to overthink it. Whether it’s Sunday’s 34-3 blowout or 2025’s franchise record breaking performance from Bryce Young, […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Jaelan Phillips #5 of the Carolina Panthers sacks Jack Strand #18 of the Atlanta Falcons during the third quarter of the game at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Butch Dill/Getty Images) | Getty Images There are now three things that I am certain of in this world: death, taxes, and the Carolina Panthers using the Atlanta Falcons for a ‘get right’ game. I don’t know why, but quite frankly I don’t care to overthink it. Whether it’s Sunday’s 34-3 blowout or 2025’s franchise record breaking performance from Bryce Young , nothing heals the Panthers wounds like a trip to Mercedes Benz Stadium in Atlanta, Georgia. With that said, what if I told you that there’s an argument to be made that the team’s performance between Week 1’s barn burner versus the Chicago Bears and this most recent blowout of the Falcons weren’t all that different? I imagine the general reaction would range from a dismissive scoff to some choice not-safe-for-work words. Fair enough, because that’s an insane assertion for me to make and wrong on many levels. I’m going to do it anyway, though. Welcome to this week’s game review where I try to tell you how the Panthers performance against the Falcons was not actually that much better than the game that preceded using some definitely-not-cherry-picked stats. Let’s get into it. Statistic vs. CHI @ ATL Penalties on CAR offense 7-49 9-63 3rd down conversions 4-9 (44%) 6-14 (43%) Red zone TD 5-5 (100%) 3-7 (43%) Pressure rate allowed 11.6% 15.4% EPA / play 0.18 0.14 So, the Panthers offense in Week 2 were called for more penalties, slightly less efficient on 3rd down, significantly less efficient in the red zone, allowed more pressure on the quarterback and were overall efficient as an offense according to their EPA per play. Let me be clear, I am not saying the Panthers offense performed poorly. Far from it, as averaging an 0.14 EPA/Play for a season would have been good for the best offense in the NFL in 2025. As far as week-to-week comparisons go, though, the Offense was better against the Bears. Statistic vs. CHI @ ATL RB Production 28-224 (8.0 ypc) 27 – 123 (4.5 ypc) RB Production minus K. Monangai 61 yd rush 27-163 (6 ypc) 27 – 123 (4.5 ypc) NFL NGS Average receiver separation 3.14 yards 2.7 yards Completion % over expected 11.4% -14.5% Opposing QB turnover worthy plays 1 4 Listen, we’re talking about a difference of 56 points scored here so the numbers were going to be significantly improved against Atlanta. Just hear me out as I am going somewhere with this. If you take out the outlier 61 yard rush by Kyle Monangai, the Bears and Falcons had the exact same number of runs against the Panthers (27). While the Bears running backs ran for an insane 6 yards per carry, the Falcons’ backs ran for a still strong 4.5 yards per carry. This suggests that while improved, the overall rushing defense was still below average against the Falcons. However, the difference of performance between the two quarterbacks the Panthers have faced is where the crux of my argument lays. The Bears receivers had an above average amount of yards of separation. Generally, the more separation your receivers have, the more likely a quarterback is to complete a pass, and vice versa. The more likely a quarterback is to complete a pass, the higher their expected completion percentage will be. The inverse of this is also true – less receiver separation, the less likely a quarterback is to complete pass. Consider now that Caleb Williams was managing to complete 11.4% more of his attempts than expected while the Falcons gruesome twosome at quarterback completed 14.5 overall less of their attempts. This is not even accounting for the fact that Williams’ average intended air yards was literally 8 yards farther than Jack Strand. In other words, Williams made the hard plays look easy and the Falcons quarterbacks made the easy plays look hard – hard enough to sink their entire offense with poorly placed footballs and 5 turnovers. This is, of course, a fairly simplified view that does lack a some nuance. Those of you who are optimists (as I like to think I am) may believe that it takes a talented improvisor like Williams who can run 20 mph and turn off-script plays into big gains to dismantle the defense. The pessimist amongst you will wonder what may have happened if the Falcons had deployed even average quarterback play. The question I ask is did the Panthers play that much better this week, or did the Falcons just play that much worse than the Bears did in Week 1? I’d love to hear where you stand in the comments below. That’s all I have for you this week! So far the Panthers have faced against elite quarterback play and then the best efforts of Cooper Rush and Jack Strand. Who is to say what they get against the Cleveland Browns next week, though. Until then, keep pounding.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Colin Simmons
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: AUSTIN, TX - SEPTEMBER 05: Defensive end Colin Simmons #1 of the Texas Longhorns rushes around offensive lineman William Boone #71 of the Texas State Bobcats during the college football game the Texas Longhorns and the Texas State Bobcats on September 5, 2026, at Darrell K Royal-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Texas Longhorns edge defender Colin Simmons. Bio Simmons (6’3”, 240 lbs.) came into college as one of the best pass rushing prospects in the country. He led his high school to back-to-back state championships, winning Defensive MVP of the game both times. In his freshman year at Texas, Simmons posted nine sacks and 14 tackles for loss in 16 games for the Longhorns, earning him National Freshman of the Year, Freshman All America, and SEC All-Freshman honors. Heading into the following season, Simmons was named to the preseason All-SEC first team and preseason All-American first team. He improved in his sophomore season, notching 12 sacks and 15.5 tackles for loss in just 13 games, indeed being named to the All-SEC first team and to the All-American second team. The true junior has started hot for the Longhorns this year as well, already being credited with 3.5 tackles for loss and two sacks in three games so far. He is on the watchlist for many awards, including the Lott, Bronko Nagurski, Weurfful, Lombardi, Walter Camp, and Chuck Bednarik trophies. Strengths/Weaknesses Simmons is considered the consensus best pass rusher in the 2027 class (assuming he doesn’t return to school). He has an insane first step and converts that elite short area speed into power, bending around tackles with loose hips and ankles. He also has a knack for turnovers, forcing six fumbles and grabbing one interception across his first two college seasons. While not the biggest or strongest, Simmons is able to set a solid edge against the run and has the motor to chase down cutbacks and backside runs. Simmons’s size is a question mark for some NFL scouts. At just 240 lbs., stronger offensive lineman can push him around when they get their hands on him. He also has a couple discipline and technique issues to address, namely missed tackles and committing penalties. Projection Simmons will likely be the top edge defender taken in the 2027 NFL Draft baric anything drastic happening between now and April. His pass rush prowess and playmaking ability definitively outweigh some of the lack of discipline and weight questions. Simmons has the three down ability that modern NFL teams need and will likely be a day one starter. If he continues on his current trajectory, he could easily be a double digit sack player while being an above average edge setter at the next level. His abilities make him scheme versatile as a plug and play edge, so the Panthers should do their due diligence regardless of the defensive scheme and coaching staff. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Colin Simmons is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
