title: Game balls for the Broncos 20-13 win over the Jaguars
summary: A thrilling 14-point fourth quarter catapulted the Denver Broncos ahead of the Jacksonville Jaguars as both sides of the football dominated late to secure the victory for Denver. It didn’t seem possible early in the third quarter when Jacksonville added another field goal to take a double-digit lead. However, from then on out the Broncos […]
full_text: DENVER , CO - SEPTEMBER 20: Jaylen Waddle (17) of the Denver Broncos hauls in a pass from Bo Nix (10) during the second quarter against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colorado on Sunday, September 20, 2026. (Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images A thrilling 14-point fourth quarter catapulted the Denver Broncos ahead of the Jacksonville Jaguars as both sides of the football dominated late to secure the victory for Denver. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . It didn’t seem possible early in the third quarter when Jacksonville added another field goal to take a double-digit lead. However, from then on out the Broncos offense and defense controlled the game. They scored 17-unanswered and with over four minutes to go the offense controlled the clock and the downs to ensure Trevor Lawrence never saw the field again. It was a great team win and rally to avoid an 0-2 start. There were many game ball options in this game, but there were only so many of us to go around. Here’s who we’re giving our game balls to: Riley Moss I had to start with the defense. The offense were stumbling around for 2.5 quarters and if the defense hadn’t shown up with fire in the bellies, this game could have gotten out of hand early. Instead, every time it seemed the Jaguars were going to step on their throats the defense stood up and made a play. In my mind, none was bigger than this one in the late third quarter by Riley Moss. He’d already had himself a pretty good game with three passes defensed and two tackles, but with the Jaguars crossing midfield again up by a touchdown they couldn’t afford to let them add more points there. Riley Moss made a great play and turned the tide. Have a game ball, sir! – Tim Lynch RILEY MOSS INT pic.twitter.com/jjTTzYc7RN — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 20, 2026 Zach Allen Zach Allen didn’t do much that showed up on the stat sheet on Sunday. He finished the game with one tackle and one QB hit, but he was a disruptive force for most of the game. His pressure forced Trevor Lawrence off his spot multiple times and his disruption against the run allowed Malcolm Roach to get two TFL. Despite being double-teamed most of the game, Zach Allen had a dramatic impact that will go largely unnoticed on the stat sheet. For this he gets my game ball. – Joe Mahoney QUE ROBINSON AND ZACH ALLEN COMBINE FOR THE SACK pic.twitter.com/zReoz7tTTu — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 20, 2026 Bo Nix The Broncos quarterback showed some serious bounce back and resiliency in his play on Sunday. In the process, we saw the type of play we’ve grown accustomed to seeing from Nix. He was confident and making great decisions with his arm and legs. He was accurate. He and Jaylen Waddle showed the type of dangerous attack they can have. You could also see Nix and Davis Webb got into rhythm in the second half. Nix finished the game 22-for-31 passing for 288 yards, one touchdown, and one interception. This is the type of game and win that could propel Nix and the Broncos. – Ian St. Clair BIG PLAY JAYLEN WADDLE 🐧 pic.twitter.com/FLI7iIbGD1 — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 20, 2026 Jonah Coleman Jonah Coleman played a pivotal role in helping the Broncos to their first win of the season. His first opportunity to make a play as a running back resulted in the game winning touchdown. It was the first of his young career, but he wasn’t done yet. As time ran toward the 2 minute warning, Coleman made a veteran play. As he busted into the open field he found the first down marker and then immediately got down. A big heads up play to stay in bounds and essentially end the game. Big game ball for the rookie. – Adam Malnati JONAH COLEMAN'S FIRST CAREER TOUCHDOWN GIVES THE BRONCOS THE LEAD pic.twitter.com/GY72InQjjt — MileHighReport (@MileHighReport) September 20, 2026 Jaylen Waddle Now THAT is what we all expected when Denver traded a first round pick for Jaylen Waddle. After just three targets and one catch on Monday, seeing Waddle pick up 10 targets, 8 catches for 138 yards and look absolutely dominant was extremely refreshing. Waddle showed what his full potential could be in this offense and the explosive element he brings with his 49 yard downfield catch. I was really excited to see him used on deep crossers and shaking DBs out of their socks up the sideline. This is just the beginning of a massive season for him and I’m sure the first of many gameballs. – Jeff Essary #Broncos Payton on Waddle. "Significant. Just gave him game ball. Could see his explosiveness." — Troy Renck (@TroyRenck) September 20, 2026 Vance Joseph We’ve talked about the players who performed well on defense, but shoutout to Defensive Coordinator Vance Joseph. He gets my game ball for having a tremendous gameplan. Outside of a few busted plays, the players executed it tremendously. Everyone looked better prepared than what we witnessed versus the Kansas City Chiefs in Week 1. Last year, the Broncos gave up 34 points to the Jaguars in December’s matchup. This time around it was only 13 and held them to less than 275 yards of total offense. Trevor Lawrence had a rough day completing less than 60-percent of his passes and throwing for under 200 yards. Limiting Lawrence’s impact was huge and Joseph’s coaching played a big role in that. – Chris Hart Who gets your game ball for the Broncos-Jags game? Share in the comments section below.
author: Tim Lynch

title: Lions bring back veteran safety to practice squad
summary: The Detroit Lions made a minor move on Monday, signing safety Jalen Mills to their practice squad. He takes up the vacant spot on the 16-man squad after the Lions signed Levi Onwuzurike to the 53-man roster over the weekend. Mills’ signing is a direct reaction to the Lions losing starting safety Avonte Maddox for […]
full_text: Dec 15, 2024; Jacksonville, Florida, USA; New York Jets safety Jalen Mills (35) celebrates after an interception against the Jacksonville Jaguars in the first quarter at EverBank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Nathan Ray Seebeck-Imagn Images | USA TODAY Sports via Reuters Con The Detroit Lions made a minor move on Monday, signing safety Jalen Mills to their practice squad. He takes up the vacant spot on the 16-man squad after the Lions signed Levi Onwuzurike to the 53-man roster over the weekend. Mills’ signing is a direct reaction to the Lions losing starting safety Avonte Maddox for the entire season due to a foot injury that will require surgery . On Monday afternoon, Lions coach Dan Campbell noted that the team was in the market for a veteran safety—and possibly more. “We had a workout this morning just looking for a veteran guy,” Campbell said. “And then we’re looking for some of these safeties that are on other teams right now that are promising young players that we could potentially poach and bring in and let them compete.” As of the release of Monday’s transaction wire, the Lions had not made any additional moves in their secondary. Mills, 32, will now be entering his 11th NFL season, starting first as a seventh-round pick of the Philadelphia Eagles back in 2016. Over the course of the next decade, Mills would start 92 games, make 122 game appearances, and play for five different teams, including the Lions last year. Detroit picked Mills up on waivers after Brian Branch’s injury, and the veteran ended up playing three games for the Lions down the stretch. Though Mills entered the league as a cornerback, he’s been playing at either nickel or safety since 2023. He’s a willing run defender and plays with some swagger. Mills will have to work his way into the lineup. For now, it appears Detroit will move forward with Chuck Clark, Thomas Harper, and Christian Izien as their three safety options on the 53-man roster.
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Everywhere the Detroit Lions need to improve, per Dan Campbell
summary: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell started his Monday press conference with a lengthy self-scouting report after the team’s 1-1 start. Coming off a hugely disappointing loss to the Buffalo Bills, Campbell had no shortage of things he felt the team needed to improve upon. So here, in order, are the things Campbell listed that the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell watches a play against Buffalo Bills during the second half at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, NY, on Thursday, Sept. 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell started his Monday press conference with a lengthy self-scouting report after the team’s 1-1 start. Coming off a hugely disappointing loss to the Buffalo Bills, Campbell had no shortage of things he felt the team needed to improve upon. So here, in order, are the things Campbell listed that the team needs to improve, along with statistics to back his case and his specific comments. Third- and fourth-down conversion rates Lions offense: 9-of-24 on third down (37.5%, 17th), 2-of-2 on fourth down (100%, t-first) Lions defense: 17-of-29 on third down (58.6%, 30th), 2-of-2 on fourth down (100%, t-last) Campbell made the interesting note that Detroit’s defense is actually first in second-and-7+s forced, but they are failing on other downs “We’re putting them in tough positions right now. That’s the whole point of why we do what we do, but we’re losing them because we still, they’re converting 66% of the time. So, all of this that we’ve gained on first down, we are losing on second and third down. ” Run game on both sides of the ball is “inconsistent” Lions run offense: 13th in EPA, 10th in success rate Lions run defense: 31st in EPA, 26th in success rate Campbell was happy with how both looked against the Saints, but both took a step back vs. the Bills “We get into this game and we don’t run it well enough on offense. And then defensively obviously gave up a lot of yards, gave up 80 to that quarterback, 40 in the first drive, lost contain three times. That’s discipline.” Losing explosive play battle Lions offense: Seven plays of 20+ yards (t-10th) Lions defense: 13 plays of 20+ yards allowed (32nd) “We’re not explosive enough on offense right now, and we’re bleeding them out on defense. Same thing, man. Be where you’re supposed to be when you’re supposed to be there. Do it with urgency.” Red zone offense/defense Lions offense: 7-of-9 TDs, 77.8% (seventh) Lions defense: 9-of-10 TDs, 90% (30th) Campbell noted the offense percentage is good, but points to their first-and-goal situation vs. the Saints that turned into a field goal after a goal-line holding penalty as another conversion that should’ve happened. “We should be 90% at worse right now after two games.” Penalties: 18 penalties (sixth most) “Right now, we have 18 penalties. 14 of those to me are, they’re not okay, man. They’re not okay. Four false starts. We have got three offensive holdings from poor fundamentals, three defensive holdings, poor fundamentals, one defensive offsides, a blatant face mask, delay a game that was off of seeing if they get them to jump and they jumped and we don’t react. . And then the landing zone infraction, we missed the landing zone and it wasn’t even close. So, those are unacceptable. The other four, hey, it’s cost of doing business. And those are all correctable. Every one of them is correctable.” Punt coverage 8.1 yards per punt return allowed (eighth best) “We’ve got to get out of there. Our interior, our core, we’re getting hung up too much. We’re tripping on each other. We’re not shooting our way out.” Kick return 24.1 yards per return (24th) “We’re leaving a lot of meat on the bone on kickoff return right now.”
author: Jeremy Reisman

title: Lions safety Avonte Maddox out for year, as Detroit seeks DB ‘shake up’
summary: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell delivered tough injury news on Monday, noting that veteran safety Avonte Maddox will miss the rest of the 2026 season after suffering a foot injury on Thursday night that will require surgery. “That hurts a little bit,” Campbell said. “Maddox is a good player for us. Good solid football player, […]
full_text: Detroit Lions cornerback Avonte Maddox (29) practices during training camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Monday, July 28, 2025. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell delivered tough injury news on Monday, noting that veteran safety Avonte Maddox will miss the rest of the 2026 season after suffering a foot injury on Thursday night that will require surgery. “That hurts a little bit,” Campbell said. “Maddox is a good player for us. Good solid football player, headsy. I hate that for him. But that’s the hand that we’re dealt, and we move forward.” Maddox was starting for the Lions at safety for the first two weeks of the season while Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch remain on the Physically Unable to Perform list (PUP). Both Joseph and Branch are eligible to return to practice this week, but Campbell noted that both still need more time . That leaves the Lions in a bit of a precarious spot at safety moving forward. Detroit has Chuck Clark and Thomas Harper capable of stepping in and starting, but the depth behind that only currently includes Christian Izien—who has been playing more nickel lately. The Lions have reportedly been in search of some veteran safety help on the free agent market , and held a workout on Monday morning that reportedly included Jordan Fuller, Jalen Mills, and Mike Edwards, among others. Campbell noted that the search won’t just be limited to available veterans, either. “We had a workout this morning just looking for a veteran guy, and we’re looking for some of these safeties that are on other teams right now that are promising young players that we could potentially poach and bring in and let them compete,” Campbell said. “Right now, we’ve got Chuck and Izzy and Harper, but we need to bring in some fresh players and get a look at them.” Beyond just being shorthanded at safety, the Lions also clearly need to shake up their secondary after two rough defensive performances to start the season. Campbell certainly hinted that some depth chart reorganization could be on the horizon. “We’re going to do a couple of things defensively, we’re going to move some guys around, we’re going to give some guys some more opportunities to play here and shake it up a little bit,” Campbell said. “And because they’ve earned that. We’ve got some guys in here that have earned some play time that they deserve a chance to do more for us.” Campbell was asked specifically about two players who have started the season on the inactive list: defensive end Ahmed Hassanein and cornerback Ennis Rakestraw. The Lions coach didn’t exactly sound eager about throwing them into the lineup, but didn’t count it out either. “Right now I’m open to everything,” Campbell said. “I’m open, and we’re looking at everything. So, yeah, there’s always a chance.”

title: Detroit Lions safeties Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph won’t return to practice this week
summary: Due to a new NFL rule, the Detroit Lions could return both Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch to practice this week, despite the fact that both players will remain on the Physically Unable to Perform list through Week 4. However, coach Dan Campbell noted on Monday morning that both players will remain sidelined for the […]
full_text: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31), left, and safety Brian Branch (32) walk off the field after practice during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Due to a new NFL rule, the Detroit Lions could return both Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch to practice this week, despite the fact that both players will remain on the Physically Unable to Perform list through Week 4. However, coach Dan Campbell noted on Monday morning that both players will remain sidelined for the time being. “I don’t see it for either one,” Campbell said. Branch is out while recovering from a torn Achilles he suffered late last season, and he is not eligible to play until the Lions’ Week 5 game against the Arizona Cardinals. Kerby Joseph is eligible along the exact same timeline as Branch, but Campbell noted that he’s not quite ready to return to practice while he continues to navigate a knee injury that last lingered for over a full year now. Campbell wouldn’t give a timeline for either’s return, but it certainly sounds like Branch is closer to coming back. “It’s tough to say. It really is,” Campbell said. “I think Branch has a chance to be back sooner than Kerby, but it won’t be this week.” Joseph’s injury has been more enigmatic than Branch’s, as the Lions have been saying they need to build enough strength around his knee in order to be able to test it and see whether his knee can withhold the punishment of an NFL season. Campbell was asked when they were going to feel comfortable enough to try that, and he gave a little more context on his situation—seemingly referring to Joseph’s time outside of the facility during training camp. “Nothing I’m gonna say is going to make anybody feel better about anything. I just know we were strengthening the knee, and it wasn’t a setback, but there was a little time there where we weren’t able to do everything that we needed to do and so now we’re back at it,” Campbell said. “Until we can get the knee to a certain point where it feels strong, as strong as we can possibly get it, and he feels comfortable, we’re not going to put him out there.” Detroit is in need of all the safety help they can get right now. Starter Avonte Maddox suffered a foot injury on Thursday and is out for the season . The Lions are reportedly working out a stable of defensive backs to help them in the interim.

title: Lions reportedly working out ‘group’ of defensive backs
summary: According to a report from ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, the Detroit Lions will be working out a group of defensive backs when the team reconvenes from their extended break on Monday. Fowler doesn’t have an exhaustive list of those players, but it will include two known names: Jordan Fuller and Jalen Mills. UPDATE: Fowler added one […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - DECEMBER 21: Jordan Fuller #4 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the New Orleans Saints at SoFi Stadium on December 21, 2023 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to a report from ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, the Detroit Lions will be working out a group of defensive backs when the team reconvenes from their extended break on Monday. Fowler doesn’t have an exhaustive list of those players, but it will include two known names: Jordan Fuller and Jalen Mills. UPDATE: Fowler added one more name to the list: Mike Edwards Lions general manager Brad Holmes is likely very familiar with Fuller, as he was drafted by the Los Angeles Rams in the sixth round of the 2020 NFL Draft, when Holmes served as the Rams’ director of college scouting. Fuller would start 12 games his rookie season at safety, logging three interceptions and five passes defended. He continued to be a full-time starter in 2021, but a hamstring injury held him out of the majority of 2022. After another 17 games started in 2023, he ended up signing with the Panthers on a one-year, $3.25 million deal. Another hamstring injury sidelined him for about half of that season. And last year, he played just six games with the Falcons. While Fuller has dealt with a lot of injuries in his career, he’s an aggressive player that doesn’t mind getting active in the run game. He’s posted a PFF run defense grade above 68 in every year of his career, but he’s been comfortable playing both in the box and as the deep safety. Jalen Mills may sound familiar, because he was with the Lions briefly last season. The 32-year-old safety joined the Lions off waivers in December after Brian Branch suffered his Achilles injury, and he played 65 defensive snaps for the Lions over the final two games of the season. Edwards is a former 2019 third-round pick who spend his first four season with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. He’s split time since with the Chiefs (2023, 2025), the Bills (2024), and Buccaneers again (2024). In total, he’s started 30 games and made 89 game appearances. Edwards is described as a “ ball hawk ” and is a two-time Super Bowl winner (Chiefs, Buccaneers). In addition to these two safeties, the Lions have also reportedly shown some interest in free agent cornerback Kenny Moore. The Lions searching for defensive backs could mean two things. For one, it could be a response to Avonte Maddox’s injury. The Lions’ veteran safety left Thursday’s game early with a foot injury, and he did not return. While coach Dan Campbell didn’t have a definitive update on Maddox after the game, he was not optimistic about the outlook of his injury. “I don’t know. Maddox is pretty tough, so when he doesn’t come back, that makes me nervous,” Campbell said. “But I won’t know until tomorrow for sure.” Detroit may also be in the defensive back market because their play in the secondary has been troublesome through two games. Saints quarterback Tyler Shough threw for 410 yards in Week 1 against the Lions, and Bills quarterback Josh Allen through for 248 yards and three touchdowns on Thursday. One other thing to keep in mind: Lions safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph started the season on the Physically Unable to Perform list. They cannot play until Week 5 at the earliest, but they can return to practice this week, if ready. We should have more clarity on this situation Monday, when Campbell is expected to speak with the media.

title: How often NFL teams recover from a terrible defensive start
summary: The Detroit Lions defense is in trouble. After two extremely troubling performances, fans and analysts are already wondering if Detroit needs to make massive changes on the defensive side of the ball, while others are already claiming defeat for the team. The silver-lining crew points to the fact that it’s early in the season. September […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard, left, and head coach Dan Campbell watch practice during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions defense is in trouble. After two extremely troubling performances, fans and analysts are already wondering if Detroit needs to make massive changes on the defensive side of the ball, while others are already claiming defeat for the team. The silver-lining crew points to the fact that it’s early in the season. September is for ugly football and correcting those mistakes. So Detroit has plenty of time to right the ship. But what is the historical context of massive improvement when it comes to terrible play on defense? Does it actually happen a lot, or is it something coaches simply try to manifest by saying they’re all correctable mistakes? For this exercise, I looked at the bottom-five defenses (by points allowed) after two weeks over the last five seasons, exploring where each started and where it ended the season. We’ll start with the most recent data points from the 2025 season and work our way back to 2021. For context, the Lions have allowed 71 points through two games, which currently ranks 31st (before Monday night’s game). 2025 season After 2 weeks: 32. Bears — 79 points allowed (39.5 PPG) 31. Dolphins — 66 points allowed (33.0 PPG) 30. Jets — 64 points allowed (32.0 PPG) 29. Steelers — 63 points allowed (31.5 PPG) t-28. Cowboys — 61 points allowed (30.5 PPG) t-28. Giants — 61 points allowed (30.5 PPG) At the end of the season Bears: 24.4 PPG allowed (23rd) 25th in DVOA 21st in EPA/play Dolphins : 24.9 PPG allowed (24th) 24th in DVOA 25th in EPA/play Jets: 29.6 PPG allowed (31st) 31st in DVOA 20th in EPA/play Steelers: 22.8 PPG allowed (17th) 11th in DVOA 19th in EPA/play Cowboys: 30.1 PPG allowed (32nd) 32nd in DVOA 32nd in EPA/play Giants: 25.8 PPG allowed (26th) 26th in DVOA 27th in EPA/play Of these six teams, only the Steelers really pulled themselves out of the basement, which is kind of incredible, because you may remember they started the season by giving up 32 points to the lowly Jets. However, they bounced back nicely and held each of their last six opponents to 26 points or less. What was the reason for their improvement? A big schematic shift, moving from single-high safety looks to a two-high shell . Everyone else showed their true colors early. 2024 season After 2 weeks: 32. Panthers — 73 points allowed (36.5 PPG) 31. Rams — 67 points allowed (33.5 PPG) 30. Cowboys — 61 points allowed (30.5 PPG) 29. Commanders — 55 points allowed (27.5 PPG) 28. Ravens — 53 points allowed (26.5 PPG) At the end of the season: Panthers: 31.4 PPG allowed (32nd) 32nd in DVOA 32nd in EPA/play Rams: 22.7 PPG allowed (17th) 26th in DVOA 23rd in EPA/play Cowboys: 27.5 PPG allowed (31st) 24th in DVOA 28th in EPA/play Commanders : 23.0 PPG allowed (18th) 23rd in DVOA 22nd in EPA/play Ravens: 21.2 PPG allowed (9th) 6th in DVOA 11th in EPA/play There’s a little more hope in this data set. The Commanders and Rams were able to climb toward average, while the Ravens arguably turned into a top-10 defense. But there’s an interesting story to the 2024 Baltimore Ravens. At the start of the year, the defense was coordinated by former NFL linebacker Zach Orr—his first year as a coordinator. In October, the Ravens added senior defensive assistant Dean Pees to the staff. The actual defensive turnaround didn’t come until weeks later—and some coaches denied that Pees was the catalyst for the improvement —but it’s something to consider. Despite the turnaround, Orr would only last one more season as Ravens defensive coordinator. Again, however, it’s worth pointing out that the Panthers and Cowboys defenses were exactly as they seemed after two weeks. 2023 season After two weeks: 32. Giants — 68 points allowed (34.0 PPG) 31. Bears — 65 points allowed (32.5 PPG) 30. Chargers — 63 points allowed (31.5 PPG) 29. Seahawks — 61 points allowed (30.5 PPG) 28. Lions — 57 points allowed (28.5 PPG) At the end of the season: Giants: 23.9 PPG allowed (26th) 21st in DVOA 22nd in EPA/play Bears: 22.3 PPG allowed (20th) 17th in DVOA 16th in EPA/play Chargers: 23.4 PPG allowed (24th) 26th in DVOA 24th in EPA/play Seahawks: 23.6 PPG allowed (25th) 28th in DVOA 30th in EPA/play Lions: 23.2 PPG allowed (23rd) 13th in DVOA 21st in EPA/play Most of these defenses were able to climb out of the bottom five, but not much further. All remained in the bottom half of the league except arguably the 2023 Lions (by DVOA), coincidentally enough. The Bears managed to become an average defense, as well. Two things worth noting in the Bears’ turnaround: defensive coordinator Alan Williams resigned after two games due to health and family reasons. Additionally, they traded for Montez Sweat at the deadline, and he provided 6.0 sacks in the final nine games. 2022 After two weeks: 32. Cardinals — 67 points allowed (33.5 PPG) 31. Lions — 65 points allowed (32.5 PPG) 30. Titans — 62 points allowed (31.0 PPG) t-29. Falcons — 58 points allowed (29.0 PPG) t-29. Rams — 58 points allowed (28.0 PPG) t-29. Commanders — 58 points allowed (28.0 PPG) At the end of the season: Cardinals 26.4 PPG allowed (31st) 26th in DVOA 20th in EPA/play Lions 25.1 PPG allowed (t-30th) 27th in DVOA 31st in EPA/play Titans 21.1 PPG allowed (t-14th) 19th in DVOA 21st in EPA/play Falcons 22.7 PPG allowed (23rd) 31st in DVOA 29th in EPA/play Rams 24.6 PPG allowed (26th) 18th in DVOA 22nd in EPA/play Commanders 20.2 PPG allowed (7th) 10th in DVOA 5th in EPA/play Again, there is some hope here. The Titans, Rams, and Commanders all pulled themselves out of the bottom-10 by most metrics. Washington, in particular, turned into a top-10 defense. It’s interesting because Washington had one of the worst defenses in 2021 and 2023, but this one haven of a season under defensive coordinator Jack Del Rio worked with no clear reason why. He was fired the next year. 2021 After two weeks: 32. Falcons — 80 points allowed (40.0 PPG) 31. Lions — 76 points allowed (38.0 PPG) 30. Titans — 68 points allowed (34.0 PPG) 29. Ravens — 68 points allowed (34.0 PPG) 28. Chiefs — 65 points allowed (32.5 PPG) At the end of the season: Falcon s 27.0 PPG allowed (30th) 31st in DVOA 28th in EPA/play Lions 27.5 PPG allowed (31st) 29th in DVOA 30th in EPA/play Titans 20.8 PPG allowed (6th) 10th in DVOA 10th in EPA/play Ravens 23.0 PPG allowed (19th) 28th in DVOA 27th in EPA/play Chiefs 21.4 PPG allowed (8th) 22nd in DVOA 23rd in EPA/play We have one more example of a team pulling themselves out of a bottom-five performance and climbing to a top-10 defense by the season’s end: the 2021 Titans. They looked like a completely different unit after their Week 13 bye, allowing 24.2 points per game before the bye week and just 13.8 points per game in the six games after the bye (including playoffs). It’s hard to point to exactly what helped the turnaround, but in a funny coincidence given how many Lions fans want a similar move, it is worth noting that Jim Schwartz was added as a senior defensive assistant prior to the 2021 season. Only one other bottom-five defense was able to pull themselves out of the basement—the Chiefs, who remained in the bottom-10 in efficiency numbers, but the scoring defense jumped into the top-10 likely due to some help from a top-five offense. Conclusions Of the 27 teams that started the season in the bottom-five of scoring defense after two weeks: Only eight (29.6%) finished in the bottom-five in scoring defense However, 17 (63.0%) finished in the bottom-10 in scoring defense Similarly, 17 (63.0%) finished bottom-10 in DVOA, but, oddly, only 14 (51.9%) finished bottom-10 in EPA/play. As for the positive finishes, of the 27 teams: Only five (18.5%) finished in the top half of the league in scoring Five (18.5%) finished in the top half of the league in DVOA Four (14.8%) finished in the top half in EPA/play Of this…

title: Lions vs. Jets odds: Opening lines for Week 3 matchup
summary: The Detroit Lions (1-1) are back inside the comfy confines of Ford Field in Week 3, welcoming coach Aaron Glenn and the New York Jets (1-1 back to town, and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -7.5 points. In 2025, Glenn stepped away from his defensive coordinator […]
full_text: Lions coach Dan Campbell talks to defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn during minicamp in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 8, 2022. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (1-1) are back inside the comfy confines of Ford Field in Week 3, welcoming coach Aaron Glenn and the New York Jets (1-1 back to town, and the folks over at FanDuel Sportsbook have set the opening betting line at Lions -7.5 points . In 2025, Glenn stepped away from his defensive coordinator position with the Lions and accepted a head coaching position with the Jets, the team that drafted him in 1994. Unfortunately, his rookie season as head coach was rough, starting 0-7 before finishing 3-14. Glenn opened the offseason by revamping his coaching staff, beginning with the firing of both offensive coordinator Tanner Engstrand and defensive coordinator Steve Wilks. Former head coach Frank Reich was hired as the Jets’ new offensive coordinator, and Brian Duker—who coached under Glenn with the Lions from 2021-23—was named the new defensive coordinator. Several other coaching positions were also overhauled to match the new coordinators. The Jets were also aggressive with their roster, giving running back Breece Hall a contract extension, trading away quarterback Justin Fields, and acquiring quarterback Geno Smith, safety Minkah Fitzpatrick, and defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat. In free agency, the Jets signed several new starters, including left guard Dylan Parham, EDGE Joseph Ossai, linebacker Demario Davis, defensive tackle David Onyemata, and safety David Belton. In the draft, the Jets used three first-round picks to acquire three more starters: EDGE David Bailey, tight end Kenyon Sadiq, and wide receiver Omar Cooper; they also snagged corner D’Angelo Ponds in the second round and defensive tackle Darrell Jackson in the fourth. In Week 1, the Jets’ offseason moves looked like they paid off, as New York easily handled the Titans 23-10 in Tennessee. Then, in Week 2, the Jets and Packers traded blows in a defensive battle that opened up in the second half and eventually went to overtime. Glenn surprisingly had the Jets take the ball first in overtime, and when the offense went three-and-out, the Packers got the ball in great field position and easily kicked a field goal to secure the win. Detroit’s defense has been struggling, but their offense has been putting up points in volume. And although the Jets’ defense looks like it could give the Lions problems, Vegas doesn’t seem to think it will be enough to affect this game. title: Packers Film Room: Dashing for a dagger
summary: Last week, we talked about the Green Bay Packers’ use of Dash motion and how they used the Vikings defensive tendencies to hit a play behind it. Today, we’re looking at that same motion and a play the Packers hit off of it in Week 2 against the New York Jets. Before we get started, […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 20: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers passes the ball against the New York Jets during the first half of the game at MetLife Stadium on September 20, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Elsa/Getty Images) | Getty Images Last week, we talked about the Green Bay Packers’ use of Dash motion and how they used the Vikings defensive tendencies to hit a play behind it. Today, we’re looking at that same motion and a play the Packers hit off of it in Week 2 against the New York Jets. Before we get started, let’s talk about the type of motion. “Dash” motion is something we’ve been seeing quite a bit of around the league this year. It’s a type of slow motion that arcs behind the line, then run towards the line at the snap for a block. Over the first two weeks of this season, the Packers have used this motion 10 times. They have run on 8 of those for an average gain of 6.5 yards, and they have run the same power concept on every one of those runs. The Dash motion man kicks out the EMOL (End Man on Line), the right guard pulls and works as a lead, the rest of the line blocks down. (I have the pullers in blue to make it easier to see.) Last week, the Packers hit a backside slant late, as the Vikings were blitzing the backside every time the Packers showed that motion. This week, they had the backside WR run a Bubble. That Bubble tag was on the backside of every one of these plays this week. Last week the only time we saw a route run on the backside of one of these plays was the slant to Matthew Golden that we covered last week . The Jets played this route a couple different ways. When they aligned a man tight to Golden, that defender aligned outside and shadowed the bubble. (Bottom of the screen on the next clip.) When the Jets were in off coverage, the safety over Golden would shadow the bubble motion. (Top of the screen on the next clip.) Now, to the last play. After stopping the Jets on their first possession of overtime, the Packers drove down the field. With 5:47 remaining in overtime, they were facing 1st & 10 at the Jets’ 22 yard line. With the Jets already having had a possession, a field goal would win it, but you want to drive a little closer. Trey Smack had been a perfect 3/3 on field goals and extra points up until that point (due in some part to a great snap-and-hold operation ), but you want to make this a little easier on him. The Packers come out in 12 personnel (1 RB, 2 TE, 2 WR) in a completely balanced set: one wide receiver split to each side, an in-line tight end to each side, and a single back behind the QB. Matthew Golden [0] is split wide to the left and Christian Watson [9] is wide to the right. The cornerback over Golden is shaded to the inside shoulder and the safety is playing on the hash. This is important. Before the snap, Mark Redman [86] starts his Dash motion, triggering the play. At the snap, Golden bubbles out. Instead of handing it off – or throwing to Golden on the Bubble – Love throws a lollipop up the field. The cornerback is blitzing off the edge to try to stop the run from the backside, so he’s in no position to make a play on this ball. The safety playing so far inside is also in no position to make a play on this. By throwing it over the top, Love avoids any opportunity for the defender to that side to make a play. A couple interesting things here. The Jets did not really blitz their cornerbacks in this game. They blitzed on 31.25% of their defensive snaps (per SumerSports ), but, unless I missed some, this was the only time they blitzed a cornerback in this game. More than anything, I think the alignment of the cornerback and safety is what informed the decision to throw this. If the cornerback was playing on Golden’s outside shoulder, I think Love hands the ball off. If the Jets are in off coverage and the safety is over the top, I think Love throws this to Golden on the bubble. With the cornerback playing the inside shoulder and the safety playing on the hash, Love makes the decision to throw to Golden, but throw further outside and up-field than simply throwing the Bubble (since the cornerback could have a chance to knock down a throw to the flat). And, since Golden is running a Bubble, Love puts enough air under this ball to allow Golden to adjust as the ball is in the air. The cornerback blitzing makes this more open than it would have been, but even if that cornerback simply played how he had been playing this – a soft mirror on the Bubble – he still would not have been in a great position to defend this. I love the call in this moment (it was the best run concept on the day for the Packers), but I love seeing the recognition from Love at the line and the adjustment from Golden to be able to make this catch and pick up yards afterwards. By the time the dust had settled, it was a 14 yard gain, setting up a 26 yard field goal, which Smack knocked through. FOR THE WIN! 📺: FOX pic.twitter.com/6SaV3LwqmI — Green Bay Packers (@packers) September 20, 2026 Albums listened to: Nicole Atkins – Drama ; Beck – Ride Lonesome

title: Green Bay Packers News: Lukas Van Ness has arrived
summary: Lukas Van Ness had an inauspicious start to his NFL career. Through two seasons, he’d produced just seven sacks and 16 quarterback hits. He was solid against the run, but you don’t pick an edge rusher 13th overall because he’s stout in the ground game. Year three was promising, but then the injuries came. Nagging […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NJ - SEPTEMBER 20: Lukas van Ness #90 of the Green Bay Packers defends during the second quarter of the game against the New York Jets on September 20, 2026 at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Lukas Van Ness had an inauspicious start to his NFL career. Through two seasons, he’d produced just seven sacks and 16 quarterback hits. He was solid against the run, but you don’t pick an edge rusher 13th overall because he’s stout in the ground game. Year three was promising, but then the injuries came. Nagging issues limited Van Ness to just nine games in 2025, and for more than a few of those nine, he clearly wasn’t quite himself. And then the Packers picked up his fifth-year option this past offseason. I was a fan of the move, but I can understand anybody who was skeptical. Injuries and a lack of production are a recipe for some negativity, and Van Ness had plenty of both of those things. But through two weeks, Van Ness has paid off every bit of faith the Packers have had in him. Two weeks does not a season make (and the Packers are thanking the ghost of Lombardi for that), but the start for Van Ness is about as promising as things could be. Hopefully this turns into a season-long trend. The Van Ness ascension may just have begun. title: Scouting Report: How the Green Bay Packers’ offense performed in Week 2
summary: I’m going to put a quick post together explaining what I saw from the Green Bay Packers’ offense on Sunday, after watching the film of the game. In short, there was some good and some bad. Obviously, you want to put up more than 17 points in regulation, but I want to explain some of […]
full_text: (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’m going to put a quick post together explaining what I saw from the Green Bay Packers’ offense on Sunday, after watching the film of the game. In short, there was some good and some bad. Obviously, you want to put up more than 17 points in regulation, but I want to explain some of the positives and negatives that I saw and some differences between Week 1 and Week 2. General Notes The Packers’ passing game changed a good amount, as they relied on moving the pocket (with sprintouts or play-action bootlegs) against the Vikings. Versus the Jets, it was a lot of quick game passing, which put a lot less stress on the offensive line, as quarterback Jordan Love got the ball out quicker. That’s good and bad. Good, because it was a short-term solution for their line issue. Bad, because now the running game and passing game are sort of divorced, rather than building upon each other. The Packers still run outside zone in the ground game, but did you see the team pull it and pass off the same look much on Sunday? No? Edge defenders, who are usually unblocked on the backside of outside and are supposed to be held by the threat of a bootleg, probably will notice that. Linebackers, who are the players put in the most pass-run conflict when facing zone/boot teams, will also probably respect the pass threat less. There were also injuries. Receiver Jayden Reed (neck) and offensive linemen Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), Aaron Banks (knee/toe) and Donovan Jennings (hand) all left action and did not return, leaving the Packers with just five active offensive linemen for the end of the game. Despite the injuries, I think you can make the argument that Jager Burton, who was the third left guard option, and Anthony Belton, who subbed in at right tackle for Bako-Bewele, played better than the starters. Passing Game Despite the horror show in Week 1, I actually think the pass protection unit did fine in Week 2. To be fair to the Week 1 players: They didn’t go against Brian Flores in Week 2. The Packers made the OL’s jobs a lot easier in Week 2 by leaning into the quick passing game instead of using longer developing plays. Green Bay slides left here (empty) and Kraft is out quick on a route. Ends up being 3 OL vs defender left and 2 OL for three defenders right pic.twitter.com/66K7WNnm8l — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 21, 2026 The line wasn’t perfect, but I really only thought they “killed a play” three times. One was a weird pressure that they were caught off-guard for (but a play they should have made), one was a bad call on which way to slide (you can see the screenshot of that above) and the other was left tackle Jordan Morgan letting his man cross his face on the Hail Mary. Belton still has some issues with an anchor, which might be surprising considering his size, but that doesn’t make a play dead in the water by any means, and there were a lot of plays that died within the first step of the down against Minnesota. In general, we’ll consider it improved, especially their ability to pass off stunts correctly. Honestly, if you want to know why I think the passing game sputtered a bit this week, it’s drops and Jordan Love. To be fair to Love, it looked like a lot of the issues stem from him playing spooked. For example, there was one play where he recognized a stunt from the interior line and immediately started bailing…but Burton simply went through his rules and picked up the stunt correctly on his blind side. After the Vikings game, I’m not going to blame Jordan for being a little panicky, but he was certainly panicky on Sunday. The overhead shot when Love starts to move on the sack-fumble. It's first down (clock not a factor in the mid-third). Just take the drag pic.twitter.com/M0tBxRuZyd — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 21, 2026 The best example of this is the sack-fumble, where Love, on first down, had a good pocket, bailed out of it and just didn’t throw to the wide-open drag. He didn’t think the pocket was gonna hold up (it did, but again, we all saw the Vikings game), and tried to make a play he didn’t need to, r esulting in him losing feeling in his throwing hand . Hopefully, he gains trust in his line again soon, because he was playing really good football for the Packers (including in the 2025 season) before it all went to hell late against the Vikings. Love also missed some throws that he tends to make. A lot of shorter routes, like swings, curls and drags, were missed short, resulting in incompletions. There was weather, and he was dealing with a numb hand, but some of these passes were made before that sack-fumble, which is when Love said he got injured. For what it’s worth, Love wasn’t on the Packers’ injury report on Monday . When Love did make some plays, his receivers didn’t really help him out. I counted at least four times when either Matthew Golden or Christian Watson had drops, potentially five (the final one was a bang-bang play for Watson on a corner route). There was the play on the Bako-Bewele injury where Golden had a drop, and then Watson dropped passes on the play that was flagged for an illegal formation, a third-and-seven in the red zone and then the play where he took a shot in the mid-section over the middle late in the fourth quarter. You can blame weather, Love’s hand or whatever on the passing game, but to me, I think the skill players just needed to make more plays — and I think one reason Love ran why he didn’t need to was that he didn’t trust his line, not because they were actually losing blocks quickly or blowing assignments. Running Game Here is where we can blame all sorts of stuff on the offensive line. I cut up all the carries, by individual running backs, in Week 2 for a post we made earlier . The ground game is still very much an issue from a line execution issue, unlike the passing game. Guys aren’t getting tight on double teams, they’re climbing to wrong defenders, they’re still late off the ball and they’re not trusting their rules/footwork. Look how tight one double team is (supposed to be hip to hip) compared to the other. Jennings just steps the wrong way and it gets split so easily https://t.co/VdkYkSpzFN pic.twitter.com/PmEHOP547o — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 21, 2026 1: Johnson's fumble was on duo. Kraft/Watson were just late off the ball. 2: This probably pops if 65/TE don't both end up on 44. No one accounted for the Mike LB. 3: Kraft missed assignment, letting 44 be a free runner. 4: Monk chases a slanting NT, allowing an unblocked tackle. https://t.co/XTmzN9a3by pic.twitter.com/x3SszXeXHo — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 21, 2026 Green Bay’s backs are making some bad decisions right now, like MarShawn Lloyd passing over an open point of attack on the first carry of the video below, but much of the running game’s woes are because blockers (this includes tight ends and receivers) aren’t doing their job. MarShawn Lloyd carries Week 2 pic.twitter.com/fbFPYlYQ9I — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 21, 2026 Guys like Watson and tight end Tucker Kraft, who are usually really good as blockers for their positions, were making mental mistakes in this game. Watson’s father even took to Twitter to criticize him. That was the laziest approach to blocking I’ve ever seen from Christian… Gotta wake his ass up! — Tazim Wajid Wajed (@TazimWajidWajed) September 20, 2026 There was some good in the ground game. I thought the tackles all did their jobs, as did center Sean Rhyan, but the guards were incredibly inconsistent outside of Burton. Banks, Jennings and Jacob Monk all struggled when the Packers ran the ball, though Monk did have some good plays where he was able to build up some steam as a puller to actually get some knockback. The problem is that Banks and Jennings got stuck up in the hole by off-ball linebackers when they pulled, so the line is only successful running some concepts to one side of the field. — Overall, I thought the offensive line’s…

title: Green Bay Packers release first injury report of Week 3
summary: The Green Bay Packers did not practice on Monday as they go into a short turnaround to play the Atlanta Falcons, while the Falcons had a walkthrough, according to the NFL’s official injury reports. The coaching staff did not talk to the press today, but they will field questions on Tuesday. The non-participants on Monday’s […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers did not practice on Monday as they go into a short turnaround to play the Atlanta Falcons, while the Falcons had a walkthrough, according to the NFL’s official injury reports. The coaching staff did not talk to the press today, but they will field questions on Tuesday. The non-participants on Monday’s estimated injury report (participation obviously has to be estimated when there wasn’t a practice) were right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele (knee), left guard Aaron Banks (knee/toe), defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf), defensive lineman Anthony Campbell (ankle), offensive lineman Donovan Jennings (hand) and receiver Jayden Reed (neck). This shouldn’t be surprising, considering these players were either not healthy enough to play in Week 2 (Brinson’s case) or dropped out of Week 2’s action. The cluster of injuries on both lines is a bit of a concern, but the Packers can handle the numbers game with their practice squad , at least for now. It’s assumed that Bako-Bewele and Reed will eventually go on the injured reserve for their injuries. There have been no updates on the status of Banks, Campbell or Jennings, nor timelines for when we’re supposed to expect to see them back. Players estimated to be limited for a Monday practice, had the Packers had one, are cornerback Brandon Cisse (teeth), linebacker Edgerrin Cooper (shoulder) and defensive lineman Javon Hargrave (knee/concussion). Both Cisse and Cooper were able to finish the game on Sunday, while Hargrave was unable to play in Week 2. Hopefully, this means that Hargrave will pass the concussion protocol before Thursday’s action. On Friday’s practice, the final practice before the team’s trip to New York, Hargrave was a non-participant — so there is progress there. The full participants in Green Bay, beyond players not listed on the injury report, were receiver Bo Melton (neck) and cornerback Benjamin St-Juste (hamstring). Melton’s injury had not previously been reported or announced by the team, while St-Juste did not play on Sunday. Hopefully that’s a good sign that St-Juste will be able to put on the pads on Thursday. It’s worth mentioning here that quarterback Jordan Love, who said that his throwing hand went numb after a hit to the elbow in the mid-third quarter against the Jets , was not on the Packers’ injury report at all. The non-participants for the Falcons, the players most at risk of missing the game, were edge defender Samson Ebukam (hamstring) and cornerback A.J. Terrell (groin), who are both preferred starters for the team. Packers-Falcons injury report estimation for today. Neither team actually practiced. pic.twitter.com/5NIRQkc5Vd — Matt Schneidman (@mattschneidman) September 21, 2026

full_text: (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have worked out three players following their win against the New York Jets, according to the NFL transaction wire. Generally, the Packers do workouts on their “off” day on Tuesday, but with them playing a Thursday Night Football game this week, Green Bay will be cramming all week. The players brought in are safeties Chris Edmonds, Wande Owens and Juanyeh Thomas. Chris Edmonds Chris Edmonds is a FS prospect in the 2024 draft class. He scored a 5.60 #RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 477 out of 1082 FS from 1987 to 2024. https://t.co/S2eAcsE9m0 pic.twitter.com/qc3hVSRo89 — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 6, 2024 Notably, Chris Edmonds is a former pre-draft visitor with the Packers. Already this season, Green Bay has added two players to their practice squad who were previously visitors: running back Damon Bankston and defensive tackle Eric Johnson II. Usually, they’re much more interested in visitors than non-visitors, when they become available (either when they’re coming out of college or down the line). Edmonds is a third-year player who was waived by the Cleveland Browns at the cutdown deadline. While the former undrafted player played 11 regular-season games over two seasons in Cleveland, he only got on the field for 11 defensive snaps compared to 175 special teams looks. Assume that he’s more of a special teams player than a defender. This appears to be Edmonds’ first workout since being let go by the Browns. Wande Owens I think y'all should read this short excerpt on Wande Owens, but for those of y'all who love your RAS scores, here's what his looks like https://t.co/nyRQOAg2CA pic.twitter.com/mXfPHJfKpB — Sabre (Go Bills & Cardinals) (@sabre_gaming_) April 29, 2025 It appears that Wande Owens, who signed with the Buffalo Bills as an undrafted free agent, tore his ACL back in 2025 , which led to him being placed on the injured reserve before his rookie preseason was even over. He was let go in late July of 2026, but re-signed with the Bills before this year’s preseason after workouts with several teams . He hasn’t played in a regular-season game, and this appears to be his first workout since he was waived at the cutdown deadline. Juanyeh Thomas Juanyeh Thomas is a SS prospect in the 2022 draft class. He scored a 8.46 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 131 out of 843 SS from 1987 to 2022. https://t.co/4l7NNjyVQa #RAS pic.twitter.com/ABYttn1xSb — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 8, 2022 Juanyeh Thomas, like Chris Edmonds, is another special teams contributor, but he’s played significantly more defense than Edmonds in his NFL career. Thomas signed with the Dallas Cowboys as an undrafted free agent back in 2022 and stuck on the team for four seasons before being signed by the Indianapolis Colts. He was waived by the Colts at the cutdown deadline. In total, Thomas played 36 games and made 4 starts on defense with the Cowboys. Over his entire NFL career, he’s played 550 snaps of defense and 706 snaps of special teams. Over the 2023 and 2024 seasons, he played some of the most special teams reps in the league (599). Juanyeh Thomas (1) Dallas Cowboys 43 yards, Kick Return pic.twitter.com/tPfmPwBmzh — NFL Touchdown Videos (@NFLTDsVideos) November 24, 2024 The highlight of his special teams career, at least so far, was him returning an onside kick for a touchdown back in 2024. Funny enough, he’s the brother of Azareye’h Thomas, a cornerback who just played against the Packers yesterday. Since being released by the Colts, Thomas has visited the Pittsburgh Steelers, Houston Texans and Cleveland Browns before his stop in Green Bay. — The Packers currently have a full 53-man roster and practice squad (though that might change if WR Jayden Reed and RT Zach Bako-Bewele end up going on the injured reserve), so they’ll need to make corresponding roster moves to sign any of these players. For reference, here’s how Green Bay’s practice squad looks right now: QB Kedon Slovis RB Pierre Strong Jr. RB Damon Bankston WR Isaiah Neyor WR Quincy Skinner Jr. OT/OG Dalton Cooper OG Josh Gesky OG/OC Dillon Wade OG Cordell Volson DL Eric Johnson II ED Nyjalik Kelly ED Arron Mosby (really a special teamer) LB Kristian Welch (really a special teamer) CB Domani Jackson S Khalef Kailassie K Lenny Krieg (international exemption) Kailassie, the Packers’ current practice squad safety, was added to the team during Week 1, so they have committed little to him. For what it’s worth, Green Bay is a little short on defensive back bodies, though, as they only have 11 players in the secondary, despite having 70 players on the 53-man roster and practice squad, barely more than the two-deep once you include the nickelback. Below is the positional breakdown of the Packers’ roster, including their practice squad: QB: 3 RB: 5 (1 exempt) WR: 8 (1 IR-DFR) TE: 5 (1 PUP) OL: 14 DL: 8 (1 PUP) ED: 6 (1 IR-DFR, 1 PUP) LB: 6 CB: 6 S: 5 K: 2 P: 1 Here are all of the players the Packers have worked out since the cutdown deadline: QB Jack Plummer QB Cam Miller RB Phil Mafah (signed by Giants) RB Damon Bankston (signed by Packers) RB Ian Wheeler WR Nick Nash WR Bryce Oliver (signed by Texans) WR Quincy Skinner Jr. (signed by Packers) TE Cody Hardy OL Cordell Volson (signed by Packers) DL Zxavian Harris ( they got in trouble for this ) DL Eric Johnson II (signed by Packers) DL Jalen Hunt ED Cruz Smith ( international exemption player from Australia, per sources ) CB Ambry Thomas S Sanoussi Kane S Kahlef Hailassie (signed by Packers) S John Saunders Jr. (signed by Jets) S Chris Edmonds S Wande Owens S Juanyeh Thomas

title: The Packers will face Falcons QB Michael Penix on Thursday
summary: After much debate on the will-he, won’t-he, the Atlanta Falcons have named Michael Penix Jr. their starting quarterback against the Green Bay Packers on Thursday Night Football. Both Penix and Tua Tagovailoa, the team’s number two quarterback, have missed the first two weeks of the season, forcing Cooper Rush and Jack Strand to play under […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images After much debate on the will-he, won’t-he, the Atlanta Falcons have named Michael Penix Jr. their starting quarterback against the Green Bay Packers on Thursday Night Football . Both Penix and Tua Tagovailoa, the team’s number two quarterback, have missed the first two weeks of the season, forcing Cooper Rush and Jack Strand to play under center for the Falcons. Penix tore his ACL in Week 11 last year, was doing limited work with Atlanta starting in May and was able to participate in full practices after the preseason. This was his third ACL tear, the first in his left knee, after he tore his right ACL twice in college. Penix hasn’t been great in the NFL, even when healthy, as he’s posted a 4-8 record. He’s completed less than 60 percent of his passes overall, has a 12-touchdown-to-6-interception ratio and has a career 85.8 passer rating. For perspective, Packers quarterback Jordan Love has a 96.5 rating in his career, an 89.6 rating this season and has been above Penix’s career average in both of Green Bay’s games this season, despite the offense struggling. Still, Penix will be a notable upgrade over Cooper Rush and Jack Strand. The Falcons haven’t even been to the red zone this year, making them the first team since the 2008 St. Louis Rams to not make a trip going into Week 3. Those Rams ended up going 2-14. Rush and Strand have combined to go 30 of 54 for 247 yards (just 5.3 yards per pass) to go along with one touchdown and five interceptions. Together, they have a passer rating of 38.2 on the year, which doesn’t even include the fact that they’ve already taken seven sacks for 41 yards. They have two notable pass-catchers in Drake London and Kyle Pitts, but those two have combined for just seven receptions for 95 yards (1.8 receptions per game, 23.8 yards per game, individually) in 2026. We’ll see how much Penix can move around, but the Falcons’ passing game has been the absolute worst in the NFL through two weeks, so a quarterback change can really only be a positive thing for them. title: Christian Watson, Jordan Love adjust for a touchdown
summary: Last week we looked at two Christian Watson TDs. If we have a space that is simply “Let’s break down however many TDs Christian Watson scored this week,” I would not be mad at it. This was a really fun TD, so I bookmarked it as something to break down before the game was over. […]
full_text: (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) Last week we looked at two Christian Watson TDs . If we have a space that is simply “Let’s break down however many TDs Christian Watson scored this week,” I would not be mad at it. This was a really fun TD, so I bookmarked it as something to break down before the game was over. So let’s get to it. Packers get the ball with 10:58 remaining in the 4th, down 17-7. After a drive that was aided by a (legitimate) Defensive Pass Interference call, the Packers were facing 2nd & goal at the 3 yard line with 8:02 remaining in the game. The Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR), starting in a 2×2 formation. Before the snap, Matthew Golden [0] shifts to the left, putting him at the #3 in a Trips set to that side. That puts the Packers in Nub formation (3 receivers to one side, in-line TE the only receiving option on the other side). The Jets defender travels with Golden on the shift, giving the Packers a Man coverage tell. This is an Inside Zone RPO (Run Pass Option), with the initial pass tag likely being a WR Screen. Christian Watson [9] and Skyy Moore [23] would fire out and block for Golden, who is running to the flat underneath. Before the snap, Jordan Love [10] gives a hand motion to Watson, who in turn passes it to Moore on the outside. With the Jets in Man coverage and the safety squatting in the middle of the field, Love adjusts to a Stalk-and-Go release. Watson & Moore will both sell an initial block, then Watson will release on a slant and Moore on a fade. This changes the play from a pre-snap read RPO to a post-snap read RPO. On the WR Screen, Love would be reading the numbers pre-snap on the Trips side and decide to hand off or throw depending on if the Packers have a numbers advantage. The Jets have 3 defenders over 3 receivers, so Love would hand the ball off. By changing the routes, Love is now reading the safety post-snap. As he puts the ball into the stomach of the running back, he’s reading the safety (that would make the safety the “conflict defender” if we’re using the terminology). If the safety drives on the run, that means the middle of the field is open so Love will pull and throw. If the safety stays in place, that means he’s not part of the run fit so Love will hand it off. At the snap, the safety fires down at the line (he’s leaning a bit before the snap, giving away his intentions), so Love pulls and fires. Watson does a good job releasing at the outside shoulder on the fake block. The defender fades back with that block look, giving up the inside on the slant. Good recognition from Love and a great route from Watson. If you’re wondering if we’ve seen this kind of thing before the answer is yes. Yes we have. full_text: (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers’ running back situation is certainly unsettled right now, as the rotation opened up even more in Week 2 with the addition of Kaleb Johnson to the committee. Between Johnson, MarShawn Lloyd and Chris Brooks, the team is splitting touches three ways now, as the Packers attempt to find an answer at the position post-Josh Jacobs’ placement on the commissioner exempt list. So who is doing well or poorly with their opportunities? You decide! Below are videos of all the carries each back has taken this season. Let us know in the comments section who you think should be getting more or fewer opportunities moving forward. MarShawn Lloyd MarShawn Lloyd carries pic.twitter.com/soRjAkagKB — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 14, 2026 MarShawn Lloyd carries Week 2 pic.twitter.com/fbFPYlYQ9I — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 21, 2026 Lloyd is currently leading the team with 19 carries and 57 rushing yards (3.0 yards per carry), but he most recently played as many snaps as Johnson (tied for second/last among the backs) against the New York Jets. title: Packers Film Room: Long snapping on kicks in Week 2
summary: We’re back for Week 2 to look at special teams. There were not nearly as many snaps to look at here compared to in the Packers’ Week 1 game, but we get to look at them through the lens of a win, which is exciting. We kicked this series off in earnest last week. In […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 28: Long snapper Matt Orzech #42 of the Green Bay Packers warms up prior to an NFL game against the Miami Dolphins at Lambeau Field on November 28, 2024 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Brooke Sutton/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re back for Week 2 to look at special teams. There were not nearly as many snaps to look at here compared to in the Packers’ Week 1 game, but we get to look at them through the lens of a win, which is exciting. We kicked this series off in earnest last week. In this space, we’re talking about every long snap on a field goal and extra point and looking at the placement of the snap. I made a beautiful and complex image to help us track and visualize the location of the snaps. Because we are in a constant state of learning, I have slightly updated the template we’re using, based on a comment on last week’s article . In the comments of that article, 31-Wedge had this to say: I held for kicks two years in HS, and my only ultra-small quibble on the chart would be that a low or ground-ball snap into the body was, for me at least, easier to handle than a low snap away, if only because you’re more prone to lose balance reaching away from your body and trying to draw the ball back into place. A stable base is everything to a holder. 31-Wedge, thanks for your input. As you can see, the area on the ground in the place where the hold is to be placed has been changed to a light red. How did Matt Orzech do this week? All four snaps (2 extra points, 2 field goals) are in the green zone: 2 to the body, 2 over the hold spot. I will admit that the second extra point felt a bit dicey – it was right on the line of being too low – but it was up off the ground so I ultimately put it in the green area. For the sake of transparency – and also in an attempt to keep improving – here are all the videos, with the snap-to-hold operation slowed down to 30% speed. Kick 1: Extra Point (Made) This is just about perfect. Laces rotated slightly towards Whelan so he can easily catch it and spin it on the hold. With the rain and a little wind, it looks like the ball is leaned forward a bit more and the lean away from Smack isn’t quite as extreme as we see in perfect conditions. Kick 2: Extra Point (Made) Harder to see from this angle (I wish we still got both angles available through NFL Pro). Snap is a bit low, but off the ground and into the body. Slightly less than ideal, but still more than good enough. Kick 3: Field Goal – 34 yards (Made) Like the first one, this is just about perfect. Whelan seems to have a slight issue on the catch-to-hold. Ball looks like it slips a bit, but it was a rainy day and he still gets the hold down. Kick 4: Field Goal – 26 yards (Made) Game-winner. Snap into the body in a good spot, with the laces in a good spot for Whelan to catch and get the ball down. Albums listened to: Lizzy McAlpine – Angel ; Babehoven – I see them, I see me

title: Jager Burton was entirely fine in relief duty
summary: The Green Bay Packers offense line management continues to completely befuddle me beyond belief. After Aaron Banks had to leave the game on Sunday due to a toe injury, which, as of the writing of this article, we still do not know the severity of, the Packers went back to Donovan Jennings at left guard […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers offense line management continues to completely befuddle me beyond belief. After Aaron Banks had to leave the game on Sunday due to a toe injury, which, as of the writing of this article, we still do not know the severity of, the Packers went back to Donovan Jennings at left guard again. Jennings’ insertion promptly led to the Packers’ run game getting stuck in park. Jennings then had to leave the game due to injury, so Green Bay gave rookie Jager Burton, who had received most of the first-team snaps at left guard all pre-season, the remainder of the snaps in that position. And he was fine. Not great, but he was fine. He looked like an NFL player. I’m not going to highlight every snap he played, but there are a few good and bad ones worth pointing out. The first one here is a good one, as he and center Sean Rhyan pass off a T/T stunt cleanly. pic.twitter.com/BEBU3Eh0ch — rcon14 (@rcon14) September 21, 2026 On the flip side, here is the entire offensive line contributing to a play dying. pic.twitter.com/ZacXo9rjMB — rcon14 (@rcon14) September 21, 2026 Burton’s anchor here is pretty poor, and he loses so much depth that he then gets steamrolled by the end. Despite the left side kind of goofing the whole thing, the primary issue on the play is Belton just losing his one-on-one rep, but no one covered themselves in any glory on this play. pic.twitter.com/g1EDAMbgpT — rcon14 (@rcon14) September 21, 2026 Inside zone or duo? Probably duo based on the attack angles of the double/combos. Burton and Morgan don’t get the type of displacement they’d ideally like on this one, but the run still goes for four. Burton’s man does make the first initial tackle, but the run didn’t have a destiny much longer than that with multiple Jets showing up at the same time. This play kind of encompasses most of Burton’s reps in the run game: Just sort of fine. Tyler Brooke and I had a disagreement on the value of Burton but we saw the same thing, and you can see both sides of it in this play. Burton completes the assignment and doesn’t lose the rep, per se, but also just doesn’t have much physical juice after the point of contact to give you any splash. pic.twitter.com/K2hXRRcVZL — rcon14 (@rcon14) September 21, 2026 This isn’t stonewalling, but this is a pretty clean pass between Burton and Rhyan when the Jets run a mike/will stunt. These can be particularly hard games for interior offensive linemen because they’re usually at a pretty distinct athleticism disadvantage, but this little game doesn’t beat them. Despite Morgan washing out the edge around the loop and Burton being able to toss the linebacker out of the pocket, this is where you can see Jordan Love still be affected by the disaster from last weekend. He bails out of a pocket that was clean if he just steps up to his right, and basically kills the play with what is effectively a dirted ball. One big hop step up and to his right and Matthew Golden probably walks in with a touchdown as he roasted his man on a crosser. Unfortunately, we have to close on what is probably Burton’s worst rep of the day. pic.twitter.com/8gQKbQMwDn — rcon14 (@rcon14) September 21, 2026 To be fair to Burton, this is a tough spot for him to hang. T’Vondre Sweat is listed at 366 pounds and has alignment leverage on Burton before the ball is snapped. Because Morgan has to work up to the second level off the snap, and Rhyan is a full gap-and-a-half away from Sweat, Burton just has to take the big man one-on-one. While Burton gets nice initial contact, Sweat has him set up from the get-go. He keeps his helmet on the outside, baiting Kaleb Johnson to cut off Burton’s behind, and then chucks Burton out of the play entirely to make the tackle. This is just kind of what happens when a slightly undersized guard is matched up with an athletic nose tackle without a leverage advantage. Sometimes you just get beat. Even here, though, on a bad play, Green Bay still picked up three yards, so it doesn’t throw things completely off-schedule. I think the story of Burton’s snaps in this game are exactly what you’d hope for for a day three rookie. He was fine. The pass protection looks ahead of the run blocking, but Green Bay’s running game wasn’t necessarily setup for his game. While they ran a lot of outside zone early, by the time Burton got into the game, it was more duo and inside zone. There was one outside zone rep that went for a nice gain, but Burton’s man tried to jump the gap and basically washed himself entirely out of the play. I don’t see any reason, regardless of injury status for Donovan Jennings, and assuming Banks will be out for Thursday, why Burton shouldn’t be the starting left guard this week. And depending on how he looks in future snaps, could earn himself a full-time starting role at one of the guard spots for the long haul.
