title: The Day After the Day After: Reliving the Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals
summary: The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 2: Houston’s D-Line was Good; Cincinnati’s was Better: The Texans generated 5 sacks, held the Bengals […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 20: Safety Jordan Battle #27 of the Cincinnati Bengals runs down the field after breaking up a pass as defensive tackle Kris Jenkins Jr. #90 of the Cincinnati Bengals signals incomplete during the NFL football game between the Houston Texans and Cincinnati Bengals on September 20, 2026, at Reliant Stadium in Houston, TX. (Photo by David Buono/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Day After the Day After…when the raw, immediate emotions from the aftermath of a game diminish into the realm of clarity and the proverbial (or literal) hangover no longer haunts the mind. With that, a review of Week 2: Houston’s D-Line was Good; Cincinnati’s was Better: The Texans generated 5 sacks, held the Bengals to 80 yards total rushing and made the Bengals work for everything. Will Anderson and Danielle Hunter upped their play. Yet, it was the Bengals’ D-Line that ruled the game. They held Houston to only 60 total yards rushing, with RBs Marks and Montgomery only managing 18 combined. They obliterated the Houston interior, and it was all Stroud could do to keep out of their way until the 4th Quarter, when the Bengals sacked him four times. They surrendered over 350 yards in the air, but only 6 points. Dexter Lawrence took whatever Texans’ interior player he faced and made them into a glorified blocking dummy. How dominant was that Bengals’ interior? Houston only attempted four designed running plays in the 2nd half. 0-4: Box Scores aren’t the end-all/be-all for a game. They can’t always tell the full story. However, there are times when they can say everything. If you had not watched the game and just went to the box score to see how this game played out, you would find this for Houston: 4th Down Conversions: 0/4 Red Zone (Attempts/Makes): 0/4 Last season, a big reason why the team struggled to that 0-3 and 3-5 start was that the offense could not convert on 3rd/4th Down and they couldn’t convert in the Red Zone. Houston was 5 of 17 on 3rd Down, so they were already in pain there. Yet, to go 0 for 4 on a follow-up 4th Down…not good at all. This included the 4th and 4 at the CIN 16 when the muffed FG snap happened; a 4th and 1 at the CIN 16, resulting in a stuff by Dexter Lawrence; a 4th and 1 at the HOU 41 in the 4th Quarter resulting in an incomplete pass; a 4th and 17 sack at the CIN 19 that ended the game for Houston. Just a critical in those data points, three of the four 4th Down conversion failures happened in the CIN Red Zone. 4 total trips into the CIN Red Zone with ZERO points scored. For reference, the Bengals only got into the Red Zone once, but they made it count with a TD pass to Chase in the 3rd Quarter. Special Teams…Yikes!!!: This was a game to forget for that unit. Fairbairn went 2-for-3, including missing a 58-yarder, which he can normally make. P Kai Kroeger’ punting was solid for the most part, but his most notable play was a botched snap in the 2nd quarter, which deprived Houston of a key scoring opportunity. The coverage units for punts and kickoffs were not all that impressive, and a critical 15-yard penalty after a 15-yard punt return by the Bengals early in the 3rd quarter set up a Bengals’ scoring opportunity. The Kroeger muff was not helped by a less-than-ideal snap from Austin Brinkman. As a long-time Texans fan, one thing that is not a common occurrence is a bad kicking snap/hold. The Critical Plays: 2 nd Quarter (6:58): 4th and 1 at the CIN 16: David Montgomery -1 yard rush (Dexter Lawrence on the stop) 3 rd Quarter (5:56): 3rd and 7 at the HOU 49: Joe Burrow pass to Samaje Perine for 16 yards (HOU 33) There were two critical conversion plays in this game. Both went against Houston. The first one not only dented a Houston drive, but it seemed to alter the decision-making process of the Texans. The running game struggled even before that stuff, but it seemed to confirm to Houston that they were not going to get much of anything on the ground. You wouldn’t think that much could scare Ryans, but that play did. In the third quarter, Houston faced another potential 4th and 1, but at the CIN 40. After two failed plays before, and remembering what happened in the 2nd Quarter, Ryans settled for a 58-yard FG attempt. It failed, and it set up the next situation. The second play saw Houston only down 7 (10-3). After the missed FG, the Bengals got the ball in good field position, but faced 3rd and 7 at the HOU 49. If the defense gets the stop, the Bengals likely punt and Houston gets the ball back. The Houston D-line forced Burrow to move around in the pocket. However, the secondary coverage could not hold and Burrow found his Perine to catch and run for 16 yards to the HOU 33. That conversion kept the Bengals’ drive alive, culminating in a 18-yard TD pass to Ja’Maar Chase. At 17-3, and with the running game M.I.A., this made Houston one-dimensional, and against the Bengals’ D-Line on this day, that did not bode well. FUN WITH NUMBERS: 2-6 : Houston Texans’ record in regular season games under Ryans in the Summer: Perhaps Ryans and the Texans take it literally that the NFL is a fall sport and that the games don’t really start until after the Equinox. The one exception was 2024, when Houston actually went 2-0 in Summer games. 6: Total number of sacks surrendered by Houston in the 4th Quarter this season: Houston has given up 7 sacks this season. All but one happened in the 4th quarter. The two on the final three plays against Buffalo, and then in this game, when the Bengals had no reason to worry about the Texans’ run game and Stroud was forced to make all of the plays with his arm, all four of the Bengals’ sacks came at that time. 37.5%: Conversion percentage for Houston’s offense when facing 3 yards or less: Houston faced 8 total plays needing 3 yards or less to convert for a 1st down. They only converted on 3 of those. On plays where Houston only needed 1 yard to convert: 16.7%. GAME BALLS DE Will Anderson, Jr: He was back to his usual relentless self, abusing the Bengals with 8 total tackles (4 solo)/1.0 sack/3.0 TFLs/2 QB hits/1 PD. On his credited sack, he was effectively embraced by the tackle, but it made no difference. Anderson also set up another sack by Hall, as he bulled all the way to Burrow, grabbing his foot and allowing Hall to clean-up. TE Dalton Schultz: No Nico Collins hurt, especially in the Red Zone. However, Stroud had a dependable backup security blanket in Schultz. 12 receptions for 140 yards will do that. SHOULD BE FORCED TO EAT ONLY SKYLINE CHILI, WITH BEANS AND STALE SPAGHETTI, FOR THE REST OF THE FALL SEASON Texans’ Interior O-line players: The whole of the O-line could live here, especially in the 4th quarter, but the interior was completely overwhelmed by the Bengals’ D-Line. Houston could not stop Lawrence and many times Stroud had to roll out of the pocket or could not step into his throws as the center was collapsing too quickly. Officials’ UCLs : 21 total flags between both teams. For Cincinnati, their 12 penalties did a lot to keep Houston in this matchup. Not that Houston was playing that much cleaner, as they lost more yards in penalties (83 to CIN’s 78). Houston’s Sporting Teams: You know about the Texans, but they weren’t alone. It started Friday night when the Houston Cougars went up to rival Texas Tech and couldn’t hold a double-digit lead. The Astros entered the weekend with a one-game lead in the AL West. They left down one. The Houston Dynamo didn’t technically lose but blew a 2-goal second period lead to end up with a tie. At least the Dash won, but they live at the bottom part of the table. Houston, now 0-2, will go on the road to take on their division rival, and fellow 0-2 squad, Indianapolis in what is shaping up to be a near-must win for both. Kickoff is slated for noon CDT on CBS/Paramount+

title: Texans vs. Colts odds: Opening lines for Week 3 matchup
summary: The Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals stung in a way that is a bit rattling to those that were hoping for a breakthrough season. It’s still a bit early, but maybe the Texans’ 0-2 start has shaken your faith in this team and their championship ambitions. They’ve played poorly enough to warrant […]
full_text: The Houston Texans’ 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals stung in a way that is a bit rattling to those that were hoping for a breakthrough season. It’s still a bit early, but maybe the Texans’ 0-2 start has shaken your faith in this team and their championship ambitions. They’ve played poorly enough to warrant this doubt, but one of the great things about the NFL is that they’re one good game away from turning the page on this rough start. Next week, the Texans will play their first road game when they travel up north to play the 0-2 Indianapolis Colts in an early divisional bout to determine who’s racing to the bottom of the AFC faster. It’s an early-season battle between the AFC South’s disturbing cousins, and FanDuel has got their opening odds for the game: What may have been seen as an easier game for Houston before the season started has now become far more intimidating, especially after Indy’s overtime loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. FanDuel is narrowly favoring the Texans to win over the Colts in this game, meaning the Texans haven’t quite returned to the underdog status that they occupied for the majority of last season. They certainly aren’t the world-beaters many expected of them coming into 2026, and FanDuel has taken note of the disappointing results, but despite it all, they are still favored in this game. THE SPREAD: TEXANS -2.5 Since the Texans are -2.5, FanDuel is expecting the Texans to win, but still expects the game to be close. That’s encouraging for Houston, and historically, this era of the Texans have been dominant against the Colts. They swept the Colts last year, and in his career, Texans QB CJ Stroud is 5-1 against Indianapolis, his only loss coming in 2023. This season, Stroud has been one of the few bright spots on the team thus far, and I expect him to continue his dominance over the Colts and their suspect pass-defense. Jonathan Taylor will likely feast on the Texans, but Houston’s offense should be able to maintain a lead on Indianapolis. Colts WR Pierce’s status for Week 3 following the team’s loss to the Chiefs Sunday night is in serious doubt, so I think the Texans will rebound and get this season back on track. I’m taking the spread here! Watch out! C.J. Stroud vs. the Bengals today via @NextGenStats & @SumerSports : 30/55 353 Passing Yards 29 Rushing Yards -0.08 EPA/Play 42.6% Success Rate Stroud threw the ball very well in a game where Houston did not have a successful run from an RB and had multiple opportunities from… pic.twitter.com/6hLXfJvASI — Jacob Barzilla (@JacobBarzilla) September 21, 2026 THE MONEY LINE: Texans -146 Between these two admittedly sloppy and injured squads, the Texans are narrowly favored. If you were to bet $14.60 on the Texans winning, you’d net $10.00 in return. After that Bengals game, I don’t blame you if you’re against betting on the Texans to win any game, but last time the Texans played the Colts, they won in a shootout in the 2025 season finale 38-30 on just 339 total yards – 35 less than they gained against the Bengals yesterday. That Texans win came from the efforts of a lot of backup players that Houston plugged into the game following the first half – which may bode well considering the amount of backups that will be playing next week’s game due to Houston’s alarming number of injuries. KPRC2’s Aaron Wilson reported that it’s possible both WR Nico Collins and RG Ed Ingram miss two games following their respective hamstring and groin injuries, so Houston’s depth at those positions will be tested yet again. #Texans Nico Collins has a Grade 1 hamstring injury, per league sources. Status for next week vs. #Colts still being determined. Replacing Collins is a committee approach. Ed Ingram, out vs. #Bengals and expected to miss at least two games, per sources. Next man up for Ingram:… https://t.co/hYebjZHCKx — Aaron Wilson (@AaronWilson_NFL) September 18, 2026 Still, Houston’s recent history of success against Indianapolis gives me optimism despite the critical injuries. Their history against the Colts must be influencing FanDuel since Houston is still favored despite all of their warts. They should have at least a moderately improved rushing attack against the Colts, and that should grant the Texans a far more complimentary offense – so give me the Texans to win it! OVER/UNDER: 44.5 Honestly, as much as I wish for the over to occur, I expect this game to actually stay below 44.5 total points. Both the Texans and Colts have had a lot of drives end in field goals in the first two games, and, following Colts WR Alec Pierce’s injury during Sunday Night Football, both teams will now be missing their #1 receiver in this Week 3 matchup. That means a lot more handoffs and loaded boxes. Both teams will get production from their quarterbacks, but I expect a lot of drives to stall in the red zone. Give me the Texans to win 23-20. omg this is a brutal stat is this necessary 💀💀 pic.twitter.com/hHtjbd16PW — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) September 21, 2026 Of course, this is all just my opinion, and you should take the gambling advice from me or any other sports blog seriously. Remember to gamble responsibly and, of course, go Texans! They’ll travel to play the Indianapolis Colts in Lucas Oil Stadium on Sunday, September 27th at 12:00 PM CST. title: Value of Things: In the rearview mirror
summary: Two weeks of football and two losses for your Texans. Every victory and every loss comes with its own set of circumstances. The key is to take down the data and figure out the patterns in what you see. If you see the same things in defeat then you can avoid defeat by avoiding those […]
full_text: Two weeks of football and two losses for your Texans. Every victory and every loss comes with its own set of circumstances. The key is to take down the data and figure out the patterns in what you see. If you see the same things in defeat then you can avoid defeat by avoiding those things. There are other things that are more or less random, For instance, week one was largely on the defense where week two was more on the offense and special teams. However, we can begin to see some similarities when we look at the numbers. Of course, we will also do our customary good, bad, and ugly along with our special look at C.J. Stroud. The scoreboard says it was a 20-6 game, but watching it live and the numbers in the aftermath says it was a lot closer than what the final score would indicate. These games are usually decided by a play here and a key decision there. We will get to those as well. The Numbers Total Yards: Texans 78/374, Bengals 59/267 Rushing Yards: Texans 18/60, Bengals 23/85 Passing Yards: Texans 60/314, Bengals 36/182 Third Down Conversion: Texans 5/17, Bengals 5/15 Fourth Down Conversion: Texans 0/4, Bengals 0/0 Sacks: Texans 5, Bengals 4 Penalties: Texans 9/83, Bengals 12/78 Turnovers : Texans 0, Bengals 0 Time of Possession: Texans 29:11, Bengals 30:49 So, let’s get this straight. The Texans had more yards than the Bengals. They possessed the ball for more plays than the Bengals. They had more first downs than the Bengals. They got into the red zone more often than the Bengals (called penestrations back in the good ole days). They didn’t turn the ball over. Yet, somehow did they not only lose, but they got blown out on the scoreboard. The Texans have gained 755 yards of total offense and have produced 37 points. That is over 20 yards per point scored. We are going to keep a look at that number throughout the season as it the highest sum in the league and a good predictor of team success. The Good Will Anderson got paid a lot of money to play football this offseason and he showed up to play football on Sunday. He was second on the team with eight tackles including multiple tackles for loss in the running game. He also added his first sack of the season. Anderson and Danielle Hunter both got to Joe Burrow and Burrow was harassed all game including on his two touchdown passes. Those were plays that superior players make. The second touchdown had some shaky defense from Reed Blankenship, but it was still a good play where Burrow was chased and narrowly avoided the rush. Great players make great plays. Great offenses will put some points on the board. When you hold a team like the Bengals to 20 points then you usually feel good about your chances. We can’t say great because this is still a defense that has generated zero turnovers. Sometimes a quarterback is just better and that might have been the case during these first two weeks, but the defense showed up on Sunday. The Bad It is hard to decide on what to peg here, so I will peg what is not a normal occurence for this team. Frank Bush might kill someone in practice this week if they look at him sideways. You had a muffed field goal and Fairbairn missed a 58 yarder. I’m not holding that one against him, but it is what it is. There was also a bad punt followed up by a targeting penalty that gave the Bengals the ball in Texans territory. This is a day they will want to have back, but in the grand scheme of things it wasn’t the reason why the Texans lost the football game. The Ugly I can see the wheels spinning in DeMeco Ryans head and that is the problem. On a key fourth and one play he decided to attempt a low percentage 58 yard field goal rather than go for it. The math geeks would all tell you to go for it. The math geeks haven’t tried to watch a Nick Caley offense try to gain a yard. This team was a combined five for 21 on third and fourth down. Sure, the Bengals defense is much improved, but this wasn’t the 2000 Ravens or the 1985 Bears out there. In the grand scheme of things this is probably a mediocre defense which is evidenced by the fact that the Texans gained nearly 400 yards in total offense without Nico Collins. This qualifies under the ugly column because we’ve seen it all before. We get new linemen. We get a new featured back. After year two of the Ryans era we even got a new offensive coordinator. This team is still soft in short yardage situations. I honestly don’t know how it can be fixed and whether it could during the year. I’m not happy that Ryans decided to kick in that scenario, but I can’t be mad at him either. He’s watched this team fail repeatedly in short yardage and had just seen them fail on third and one the previous play. Who wouldn’t be gun shy after watching that yet again? Focus on Stroud There are a couple of things I need to say first. First, this is one data point out of 17. No one should make any declarative statements based on one or two data points. Secondly, we live in a hot take world where people want to go with superlative statements one way or another. That is radically inappropriate in this case. Based on the two data points, Stroud has shown himself to be a good NFL quarterback. He definitely should be on the the 32 starters and would start for probably half of the teams in the league. All that being said, these first two weeks showed us something up close and personal. Two of the QBs that are considered among the elite made plays that Stroud simply did not make. We can blame the offensive line, receivers, offensive coordinator and the alignment of the planets if we wish. Some of that is valid and that is why these discussions are a lot more nuanced than we let on. Elite quarterbacks make plays to win games. Good quarterbacks don’t. It really is that simple. What makes life hard is that we have seen Stroud make plays before. We have seen those elite guys fail to make plays. Nothing is ever black and white. We are looking at rates of success and those guys just make those plays more often than Stroud. Again, we can argue the whys and what fors if we like. There are always reasons, but if you are going to pay a guy 60 million then he needs to be one of those guys that makes plays to get his team over the hump. When he is playing good football, Stroud manages a game well, but he hasn’t been that guy since his rookie season. Sometimes it really is that simple.
author: Scott Barzilla

title: Colts sign ex-Giants veteran wideout, who has great familiarity with QB Daniel Jones
summary: The Colts did not wait long to add help at receiver after the latest setback with Alec Pierce. Veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton is signing with Indianapolis, according to NFL Network’s Tom Pelissero. The move comes shortly after news that Pierce is expected to miss several weeks while rehabbing the heel injury he aggravated, with […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - JANUARY 04: Darius Slayton #18 of the New York Giants in action during the game against the Dallas Cowboys at MetLife Stadium on January 04, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The New York Giants won 34-17. (Photo by Ishika Samant/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Colts did not wait long to add help at receiver after the latest setback with Alec Pierce. Veteran WR Darius Slayton is signing with the Colts, sources tell @ringer @netflixsports . With Alec Pierce dealing with a heel injury, Indianapolis turns to Slayton, who played the past seven seasons with the Giants — and now reunites with Daniel Jones. pic.twitter.com/zcHenDO5S8 — Tom Pelissero (@TomPelissero) September 22, 2026 Veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton is signing with Indianapolis, according to NFL Network’s Tom Pelissero. The move comes shortly after news that Pierce is expected to miss several weeks while rehabbing the heel injury he aggravated, with a midseason return currently viewed as possible. Slayton gives the Colts an experienced outside receiver at a time when the group suddenly needed one. He spent the past seven seasons with the New York Giants and, more importantly for Indianapolis, played alongside Daniel Jones from 2019 through 2024. There should be far less of an adjustment period than there would be with most receivers signed this late in the season. He is not going to replace everything Pierce brings. Pierce has become one of the NFL’s better vertical threats and is coming off a 1,000-yard season, while Slayton is more of a complementary outside receiver than a featured target. Still, the Colts needed someone who could step in immediately and handle legitimate offensive snaps, and Slayton fits that description much better than simply promoting someone from the bottom of the depth chart. His speed also gives Indianapolis another receiver who can stretch the field while Pierce is out. With Josh Downs and Keenan Allen handling much of the underneath and intermediate work, Slayton should have a chance to fill some of the vertical role that would otherwise be missing. The Colts will still need to adjust without Pierce, especially if his absence extends into the middle of the season. Slayton at least gives them an experienced option who already has years of chemistry with their quarterback. Given the timing and the connection to Jones, it is a pretty logical move.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: Alec Pierce expected to head to IR, will attempt rehab before considering surgery
summary: The Colts will be without Alec Pierce for an extended stretch, but the wide receiver is going to try to rehab his injured heel before turning to another surgery. NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported Sunday that Pierce aggravated the heel injury that was surgically repaired earlier this year and is expected to miss several weeks. […]
full_text: The Colts will be without Alec Pierce for an extended stretch, but the wide receiver is going to try to rehab his injured heel before turning to another surgery. #Colts star WR Alec Pierce, who aggravated a heel injury that was surgically repaired, will attempt to rehab the ailment rather than have surgery, sources say. Pierce is slated to be out several weeks while he heals, but if all goes well, he could return midseason. pic.twitter.com/9dQR0PD7X0 — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 22, 2026 NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported Sunday that Pierce aggravated the heel injury that was surgically repaired earlier this year and is expected to miss several weeks. Pierce will attempt to rehab the injury, and if everything goes well, there is a possibility he could return around the middle of the season. Pierce is also likely to be placed on injured reserve while he recovers. It’s likely that Alec Pierce will head to IR while he recovers. If all goes well, he could recover without surgery. But it’s not a guarantee. Surgery is still possible. https://t.co/YMC8xOTV00 — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 22, 2026 There is still some uncertainty surrounding the plan. Rapoport added that avoiding surgery is not guaranteed, and another procedure remains possible if the rehab does not produce the results Pierce and the Colts are hoping for. For now, though, the plan is to give the injury time and see if Pierce can get back on the field without going through another operation. It is another frustrating development for Pierce after an offseason and training camp already dominated by the same injury. He underwent surgery in March after dealing with ankle and heel soreness during the 2025 season, then spent most of training camp on the physically unable to perform list before being activated shortly before Week 1. The Colts were careful with him in the opener, limiting his workload as he worked his way back into game shape. Now they will be without one of their biggest offensive weapons for at least the next several weeks. Pierce is coming off the best season of his career, finishing 2025 with 1,003 receiving yards on 47 catches while leading the NFL in yards per reception for the second consecutive year. His ability to stretch the field gives the Colts something that is difficult to replace, especially after the team committed to him with a four-year extension during the offseason. Indianapolis will now have to lean more heavily on Josh Downs, Keenan Allen and the rest of the receiver group while Pierce recovers. The good news is that surgery is not the immediate plan. The concern is that it has not been completely ruled out either. For now, the Colts will hope rehab is enough and that Pierce can make his way back sometime around midseason.
author: Andrew Aziz

title: The Colts squandered the perfect gift to turn their season around
summary: Heading into Kansas City to take on the Chiefs seemed rather daunting after both teams’ Week 1 performances. Then again, the Bears went from 59 points to 3 in the span of seven days, so week to week outcomes don’t always carry over. The Indianapolis Colts looked like they might be headed for slaughter. That […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Laquon Treadwell #13 of the Indianapolis Colts catches a pass against L'jarius Sneed #38 of the Kansas City Chiefs in over time at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Heading into Kansas City to take on the Chiefs seemed rather daunting after both teams’ Week 1 performances. Then again, the Bears went from 59 points to 3 in the span of seven days, so week to week outcomes don’t always carry over. The Indianapolis Colts looked like they might be headed for slaughter. That was far from the case, but they still managed to let an opportunity slip through their fingers. They had their chances. One of the biggest spots in the game found the Colts unable to convert a first down near midfield. That would have given them a potential shot at a long field goal in regulation. On the other side, they didn’t allow the Chiefs to kick a game winner either, so things headed to overtime. After the Chiefs scored three, a touchdown would have ended it and sent the Colts home 1-1. What happened next made things feel even worse. Daniel Jones threw a beautiful ball to Laquon Treadwell who was tackled at the Chiefs’ 17-yard line. What followed can only be described as chaos. A catch, followed by a punch out made a late game go even longer as a review was needed to determine if the defender was still making contact with Treadwell when he went down. Somehow, it was ruled down by contact, and the Colts maintained possession. The game ending on that note would have been devastating. What came next was still certainly painful. Two runs that went in the wrong direction preceded a quarterback scramble for five after a broken play. The problem wasn’t necessarily that the Colts didn’t go for it on fourth and eight. That is a tough down and distance. It was the approach to the set of downs after receiving the Treadwell gift and being at the 17 that disappointed. Instead of going for the kill shot and staying after it, the Colts seemed content to tie. Jonathan Taylor can always break one, but it felt like something different was needed at that point in the game. The argument could easily be made that Laquon Treadwell fumbled that ball. The ruling was a fumble and clear and obvious evidence didn’t seem to be present. It was a gift, and the Colts absolutely squandered it. The aggressiveness that got them there was abandoned, and the conservative approach sunk the Colts to 0-2. It’s a decision they might not recover from.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Horsepower or Horseplay? Colts’ performances from Week 2’s gut-wrenching loss vs. Chiefs
summary: The Indianapolis Colts narrowly fell 33-30 in overtime on the road in Arrowhead Stadium, after almost pulling off the surprising upset on Sunday Night Football. Almost is only as good in horseshoes and hand grenades, and there are no moral victories—as the Colts fall to 0-2, but it was a much more spirited performance from […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Laquon Treadwell #13 of the Indianapolis Colts catches a pass against L'jarius Sneed #38 of the Kansas City Chiefs in over time at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts narrowly fell 33-30 in overtime on the road in Arrowhead Stadium, after almost pulling off the surprising upset on Sunday Night Football. Almost is only as good in horseshoes and hand grenades, and there are no moral victories—as the Colts fall to 0-2, but it was a much more spirited performance from Indianapolis than we saw during that Week 1 home dud. I had to take an extra 24 hours last week to write about that clunker, but while this one still admittedly stings a lot right now, given how close the Colts were to toppling Kansas City in a tough road environment on primetime, I was able to recover a lot quicker. Perhaps, I’m just getting better used to the lengthy franchise disappointment. Without further ado, let’s get to it! Horsepower QB Daniel Jones : While Jones didn’t match Patrick Mahomes’ in this one, as not many NFL starting quarterbacks can, he was pretty good in this one—especially in his second game coming off a torn Achilles. The early interception arguably wasn’t his fault, as veteran Keenan Allen has to better fight for that football . Either way, Jones settled back in. He stood in the pocket and made some tough throws , and had even the biggest one of the night, a deep 48-yard pass to veteran wideout Laquon Treadwell that set up the Colts’ controversial game tying field goal in overtime . Jonathan Taylor : There’s not much else to say on the Colts star workhorse that hasn’t been already, as the future Hall of Fame running is one of the best to ever do it , and not only in Indianapolis speed blue. Taylor rushed for 92 total rushing yards on 24 carries (3.8 ypc. avg.) and 2 rushing TDs and once again, was the focal point of the Colts offense, despite the Chiefs best attempts to bottle him up. The Colts clearly rode on his back as much as they could offensively in a tough road game against a very good Chiefs defense. Colts Offensive Line: Not only did they pave the way for Taylor to have a big game on the ground as denoted, but they also largely kept Jones protected and upright. The Colts’ starting quarterback was just pressured on 27.3% of his dropbacks, which was the 5th lowest of all Week 2 starting NFL quarterbacks (via Next Gen Stats). In particular, Chiefs perennial All-Pro pass rushing defensive tackle Chris Jones had just one pressure on 23 total pass rushing snaps (4.3%) . PK Spencer Shrader: The Colts returning kicker was a perfect 3 for 3 on primetime, including a pressure filled 38-yard field goal to initially tie it 30-30 in overtime. He also nailed all 3 of his extra point attempts. Horseplay Laquon Treadwell: The well-traveled veteran wideout has been a great offseason story, fighting his way to a Colts’ final 53-man roster spot after being initially labeled a former first round bust. Treadwell finished with 3 catches for 61 total receiving yards, and his biggest, and most controversial, was his 48-yard deep reception which he bobbled, caught, and almost lost to a fumble to begin the Colts offensive OT drive. To be fair, Treadwell made the catch, but the fact that he had to bobble it, not only cost the Colts some additional yards, but his subsequent near-fumble (which was initially considered a fumble on the field before it was overturned by replay review that he was down by contact) slowed the Colts offensive momentum and didn’t allow Indianapolis to keep the gas pedal down. Instead of going no huddle, the Chiefs defense was allowed to catch its breath after replay review and better set its defense against Jonathan Taylor with a shorter field in the red zone. If Ashton Dulin was healthy, perhaps he would’ve had his number called over Treadwell. CB Justin Walley: Look, I’m not trying to kick a young defensive player, when they’re already down. After missing his entire rookie season, Walley is essentially a rookie with 2 career NFL starts under his belt. However, as opposing passers throw elsewhere from shutdown cornerback Sauce Gardner , they’re clearly looking to pick on the young slot cornerback Walley , who’s arguably not ready yet for the pro level. After a strong training camp showing from Walley, maybe we were led to believe that the Colts would miss longtime veteran standout slot cornerback Kenny Moore II less than we actually would. It wasn’t readily apparent in Colts camp, but Walley has seemed to struggle with speed and separation, as perhaps teammate slot Josh Downs, who’s a very good natural slot wideout, wasn’t the best matchup to exploit his coverage deficiencies. At any rate, it’s another reason why I continue to temper expectations from the training camp buzz we hear from certain Colts standout camp players on an annual basis. Not saying Walley can’t turn it around by any means, but it may take some patience, development, and some continued growing pains in coverage out there during the interim—until he better gets up to speed. Colts Linebackers: We’re getting to the point, where the general consensus seems to be that playing the Colts rookie linebacker pairing of CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher can’t be worse than the rather poor play that Indianapolis has gotten from the incumbent staring linebacker duo of Akeem Davis-Gaither and Jaylon Carlies . Whether it’s failing to get off of blocks, missed tackles, or blowing their run defense/coverage assignments, it’s hard to stomach much more from this unit. Heck, there’s even been questions whether they’re fully hustling out there , which is completely under their control! Colts Defense: Lou Anarumo’s defense has surrendered over 500+ total offensive yards in back-to-back games, for the first time in franchise history . Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes threw for a whopping 382 passing yards and 3 passing touchdowns on primetime, while their running back Kenneth Walker had 117 total rushing yards. It’s hard for the Colts to try to focus on either shoring up their passing or run defense right now, because both stink. All three levels of their defense need improvement, even on their defensive line where Arden Key has struggled in run defense and journeyman veteran Jerry Tillery is playing meaningful defensive snaps. There’s a lot of work for Lou and his coaching staff right now, and I don’t envy them right now. Some of it is coaching, but it also goes hand-in-hand with weaker personnel at certain spots. HC Shane Steichen: My issue is a lot less with the lack of going for it on 4th and 8 in overtime, down 30-27 in the KC red zone, but more with the called 2nd down run, where the Colts essentially ran Taylor into a brick wall again, versus the Chiefs defense that was clearly loading the box and teeing off on Taylor—after their similar 1st down run was already stifled. I don’t think the Colts would’ve converted that 4th and 8 regardless, given how shaky their offense looked collectively, and the bigger gripe is that the Colts didn’t go for it on 4th and 4 near midfield with about 35 seconds left in regulation. It’s a shorter distance to have to move the sticks and a longer field for the Chiefs to have to defend instead of within the red zone. Honestly, if the Colts couldn’t pick up 4 yards after three plays near the end of regulation, they didn’t deserve to win anyways, and I’d rather have them lose on their own terms than at the eventual hands of Mahomes & Co. Are you confident the Colts are headed in the right direction? | Stampede Blue
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts receive initial encouraging injury update on Alec Pierce, but further evaluation coming on Monday
summary: According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler (which was later confirmed by head coach Shane Steichen post-game), the x-rays on Indianapolis Colts wideout Alec Pierce’s reinjured ankle/heel were negative last night: However, further medical evaluation will be undergone on Monday, and given that Pierce was seen leaving Arrowhead Stadium in a boot and using crutches, I’m no […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 13: Alec Pierce #14 of the Indianapolis Colts is tackled by Marlon Humphrey #44 of the Baltimore Ravens during the fourth quarter of the game at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Andy Lyons/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler ( which was later confirmed by head coach Shane Steichen post-game ), the x-rays on Indianapolis Colts wideout Alec Pierce’s reinjured ankle/heel were negative last night: X-rays on Colts WR Alec Pierce's heel injury were negative, per source. Further evaluation coming Monday. — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) September 21, 2026 However, further medical evaluation will be undergone on Monday, and given that Pierce was seen leaving Arrowhead Stadium in a boot and using crutches, I’m no doctor, but him missing time here again seems like a realistic possibility. It’s the same injured ankle/heel that kept him out of all of training camp and preseason. Pierce left late in the first quarter on a non-contact play and was unable to put weight on his aggravated left ankle/heel, as he limped off to the sideline. He was eventually helped to the medical tent with the help of Colts team trainers before exiting the field entirely along the sidelines on a medical cart. While he was initially designated as “questionable,” which seemed overly optimistic for any sort of return, he was quickly downgraded to “out” by the Colts medical staff—and obviously, was not available again last night. Of course, it’s a big blow to the Colts offensively, as Pierce is one of their unit’s most explosive playmakers, and their best downfield threat—especially with their AFC South rival Houston Texans coming to town in Week 3. The Colts absolutely want to avoid an 0-3 start and make an already increasingly large loss deficit, grow even bigger. Even though the Texans defense has struggled a bit out of the gates, allowing the 24th most points (28.0 avg. ppg.) through two games in the 2026 campaign, reputationally, they’re still regarded as one of the league’s best. With Pierce potentially absent, it could mean more looks for rookie Deion Burks downfield situationally, as well as Ashton Dulin (ankle), who’s also mending from an injury which kept him out of action last night. Without Pierce’s deep speed and vertical separation, the Colts become a lot easier to cover, as none of the group of Keenan Allen, Josh Downs, or Tyler Warren are burners, which also means heavier boxes for Jonathan Taylor.
author: Luke Schultheis

title: Colts-Texans opening odds: Colts seeking lone victory against the Lone Star State
summary: The Indianapolis Colts are set to return home and begin divisional play against the Houston Texans. After these starts, this one will be huge. 0-2 starts to the year have created a sense of desperation for both teams. FanDuel Sportsbook sees the Colts as underdogs in this one at +2.5. The money line is +124 […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - AUGUST 28: A Texans helmet during a preseason NFL football game between the Houston Texans and the Carolina Panthers on August 28, 2026, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C.(Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are set to return home and begin divisional play against the Houston Texans. After these starts, this one will be huge. 0-2 starts to the year have created a sense of desperation for both teams. FanDuel Sportsbook sees the Colts as underdogs in this one at +2.5. The money line is +124 with the over/under at 45.5. Oof. That one hurt. After a rough opener, the Colts responded in Kansas City. Another beautiful drive to start the game was followed by a blow by blow affair. Each team traded punches, but the defense once again struggled immensely. It took overtime to decide this one, and after a fortuitous reversal of a fumble call, the Colts had hope. Patrick Mahomes had other ideas, however, as he swiftly worked down the field for the game-winning field goal. The Texans welcomed the Bengals into town for their second home game to start the year. So far, the season hasn’t gone as planned, but after a slow start in 2025, you can’t count them out. C.J. Stroud threw 55 times with no touchdowns as the Texans fell behind early and could never catch up. After putting up 31 on the Bills, they could only muster 6 points against Cincinnati. This is the battle for relevancy, a chance to save a season. 0-2 is a bad start. 0-3 might be a death sentence. The season and jobs could be on the line if the Colts don’t turn this one around. It’s time to get in the winning column.
author: Jon Spradley

title: Week 2 AP NFL Power Rankings: Chiefs remain top 5; Raiders rise
summary: We’re in the swing of things now. Two weeks are in the books, and once again, parity runs rampant in the NFL. It seems there is the cream of the crop in the top few teams; then there are the clear bottom feeders—and in the middle lies a bunch of teams that could win or […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Travis Kelce #87 and Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs run onto the field prior to an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images We’re in the swing of things now. Two weeks are in the books, and once again, parity runs rampant in the NFL. It seems there is the cream of the crop in the top few teams; then there are the clear bottom feeders—and in the middle lies a bunch of teams that could win or lose on any given Sunday. This week’s talking points will be the quarterback injuries that wreaked havoc across the league. Caleb Williams, Jayden Daniels, and Jaxson Dart were all forced out of their games. It remains to be seen how long each player will miss this season. For now, each team dropped in our power rankings. Injuries to the quarterback don’t spell disaster, however, as the Seahawks remain at the top of the league with Drew Lock under center, while the Vikings crash into the top of the rankings under the strong play of quarterback Carson Wentz. Let’s see how the rankings shook out this week from the crew. Biggest riser: Las Vegas Raiders +9 Biggest faller: Houston Texans -12 This week, along with myself, staff voters were: Maurice Elston, Caleb James , Ron Kopp Jr., Rocky Magana and Jared Sapp. 1. Seattle Seahawks (1st) Jaxson Smith-Njigba is the only Seahawk to score a touchdown this season. Four so far. And so far, so good. 2. Buffalo Bills (3rd) Yikes, that Bills’ defense. But when you have Josh Allen in September, it doesn’t matter. 3. San Francisco 49ers (4th) Even back on American soil, the 49ers were dominant. 4. Kansas City Chiefs (5th) Inexplicable special-teams blunders, Mahomes’ dimes, Kelce finding an open hole against zone defense, Depression-era play calls, and a weird game against the Colts. We’re so back. 5. Cincinnati Bengals (6th) The Burrow-Chase connection was renewed. And the Bengals defense looked stout against an offense that shredded the Bills the week prior. It looks like the Bengals are back in the AFC mix. 6. Philadelphia Eagles (9th) Say what you want, but all Jalen Hurts does is win football games. 7. Baltimore Ravens (2nd) It was John Harbaugh before. Who’s the scapegoat for a fourth-quarter collapse now? 8. Los Angeles Rams (11th) Now that is the Rams team we expected to see. 9. Minnesota Vikings (16th) KOC, head coach Kevin O’Connell, is putting on a coaching masterclass in Minnesota to start the year. 10. Chicago Bears (8th) You would have to take me off an NFL field in a wheelchair or ambulance if I attempted to play. But these Caleb Williams memes are hilarious. 11. Jacksonville Jaguars (10th) The Jaguars couldn’t complete the win in Denver on Sunday. But Trevor Lawrence is a different player this year. 12. New England Patriots (14th) Dominating win against the Steelers…but is anyone overly impressed? 13. Denver Broncos (12th) It took almost seven quarters, but the Broncos’ offense made their 2026 season debut. 14. Detroit Lions (13th) This team has completely lost the toughness and grit promised by head coach Dan Campbell. 15. Green Bay Packers (17th) Everything for the Packers just seems like a struggle right now. 16. Dallas Cowboys (19th) Quarterback Dak Prescott now owns every passing record in Cowboys’ franchise history. But he’s tied for fewest Super Bowl wins. 17. New Orleans Saints (23rd) “Poor man’s Josh Allen” Tyler Shough currently leads the NFL in passing yards. 18. Las Vegas Raiders (27th) Kirk Cousins’ good boy persona just doesn’t fit the vibe of the Raiders…yet, he’s turned back the clock and is balling out to start the season. 19. Houston Texans (7th) With Nico Collins on the sideline, the Texans’ offense had no juice. Lucky for them, they play in the AFC South. 20. Carolina Panthers (26th) Okay, Bryce Young…I’m starting to take notice. 21. New York Giants (15th) A hopeful start to the season took a big blow, depending on the severity of Dart’s injury. 22. Indianapolis Colts (24th) Is it the right move to actually go for it on 4th and 8 in overtime rather than giving Patrick Mahomes the ball again? 23. Pittsburgh Steelers (18th) The Steelers benefitted from playing the Falcons in Week 1… this is not a good football team. 24. Arizona Cardinals (22nd) I was convinced wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. would be an All-Pro from the beginning of his career. Right now, he looks like an all-time bust. 25. Los Angeles Chargers (20th) Their AFC West offseason crown was even shorter-lived than usual. How long will the national media make excuses for Justin Herbert? 26. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (21st) Baker has taken a two-week vacation since he got paid. 27. New York Jets (29th) Same old Jets. A 10-point blown lead in the 4th quarter. (And still no interceptions). 28. Washington Commanders (25th) Tom Brady said what we were all thinking on the broadcast. 29. Cleveland Browns (32nd) The Browns are the Browns. Or so we thought? 30. Tennessee Titans (31st) They were cooling off cleats with water bottles in Nashville on Sunday. The heat got to the Titans as their first win remains elusive. 31. Atlanta Falcons (28th) This team is going nowhere fast. Worth a call to see if Drake London is available? 32. Miami Dolphins (30th) Ryan Fitzpatrick said his former team could realistically go 0-17. It’s hard to believe that’s possible—but they look like a team tanking.

title: Chiefs Mailbag: Will the real Kansas City defense please stand up?
summary: Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs! It took a full 70 minutes, but the Chiefs are 2-0 thanks to a 33-30 overtime victory over the Indianapolis Colts Sunday night. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 20: Chris Jones #95 of the Kansas City Chiefs chases Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts during a run in the second quarter of an NFL game between the Indianapolis Colts and Kansas City Chiefs on Sep 20, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome back to the Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! Throughout the season, keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to submit your questions about the Kansas City Chiefs ! It took a full 70 minutes, but the Chiefs are 2-0 thanks to a 33-30 overtime victory over the Indianapolis Colts Sunday night. Let’s see what’s on our readers’ minds ahead of a trip to South Florida to face the Miami Dolphins in Week 3. MrAustin.Sr asks: Which defense is REALLY our defense, last week vs the Denver Broncos or the defense we ran out there for the Colts? This will sound like a cop out, but the answer is probably somewhere in between. I think there are some context factors we should consider. The Chiefs had probably been working on the Broncos game plan since midway through training camp. Also, Week 1 was defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo’s fifth opportunity to game plan against the Denver quarterback Bo Nix’s offense. He clearly made adjustments to keep Denver from repeating some of their success in the pair of 2025 matchups. Many laughed off the Colts after being blown out by the Baltimore Ravens in Week 1. However, Indianapolis was also among the league’s best offenses in the first half of last season. Indianapolis started 8-2 while averaging 32 points per game. Yes, the wheels fell off down the stretch, but the Colts have definitely shown the ability to score big early. My biggest concern coming out of the Broncos win was how the defense would react to a team that doesn’t abandon the run early, as Denver did. Hopefully, the team sees some areas to address because it did not go well. The combination of star running back Jonathan Taylor and the Colts’ offensive line is likely a challenge few opponents can replicate. The biggest issue for the Chiefs’ defense is how long the unit can afford to continue a heavy workload for cornerback L’Jarius Sneed, who surrendered a passer rating of 132.6 when targeted in Week 2. Colts quarterback Daniel Jones treated Sneed like an “easy button,” and the Chiefs’ pass rush had little to do to be effective. Like most things early on, we will need a larger sample. If the Chiefs struggle with the Dolphins — who have surrendered nine sacks through two games and needed a garbage-time touchdown to reach 13 points on Sunday — it will be more concerning. Will007 asks: Is it time to start worrying about the wide receivers room or is just the first two games the Chiefs played two teams with good secondaries? There are two possibilities to ponder with the wideouts. For many, the question is whether the Chiefs have someone in-house who can be a no-doubt No. 1 passing game option. That answer is undoubtedly no. A different assessment is whether the Chiefs have the potential to replicate the 2022 receiving corps featuring complementary pieces that propelled quarterback Patrick Mahomes to an MVP season. That one is probably a “maybe.” Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy, Tyquan Thornton and Jalen Royals combined for 200 receiving yards and a pair of touchdowns against Indianapolis. To be fair, 31 of those yards came to Rice on the final play of regulation that never had any chance of proving fruitful. But the Chiefs’ receivers did show signs of the “sum of the parts” approach that has worked well in prior seasons. While you cannot expect tight end Travis Kelce or running back Kenneth Walker to keep up their early-season pace, they are crucial to the Chiefs succeeding with an underwhelming group of wideouts. Which player gets targets will likely change weekly depending on the opponent. Second-year man Jalen Royals entered the night widely forgotten. Royals only saw two targets, but both came in key situations, and the coaches clearly saw something in the Colts’ defense they felt he could exploit. Whenever rookie Cyrus Allen’s turn finally comes, it will probably be a similar development. Andyreidsmustache_ asks: Has the coaching staff finally seen enough from Tyquan Thornton to actually make him a more prominent part of the offense, if not an outright starter? I’d already put him head and shoulders above Worthy at minimum. I think the Kansas City wideout group is so matchup dependent that I am rarely concerned with who is nominally starting. I do think Sunday previewed what can be done with Thornton. His 86 receiving yards in Week 2 were more than a tenth of his career production over his first four seasons. Thornton has never shown the yards-after-the-catch elusiveness to have the value in the short passing game that the other wideouts bring. However, he is easily the Chiefs’ most dependable deep threat since Tyreek Hill left after 2021. As Walker demands more defensive focus, Thornton should find more deep opportunities as he did on Sunday night. Worthy’s start to the season has been frustrating, but I still think it is early to write off his season. Remember that over three years with the New England Patriots , Thornton definitely looked like the far inferior player. RoyalsFanBill asks: Who is our primary kick returner going forward? The Chiefs seem to be trying to make running back Brashard Smith the focused returner. Rookie Emmett Johnson took one kickoff Sunday night. While both appear to have more juice than Remigio, I would be wary of using both backup running backs as the return tandem because of the risk of having both options behind Walker injured at the same time. Perhaps the Chiefs are seeing that Remigio’s speed limitations lead to penalties because it takes him longer to reach his blockers. Hopefully, Smith will get more opportunities on punts and kickoffs as the season goes on. FoxBot2021 asks Will AP ever just be happy the team wins? Or will everything always be nitpicked because people wamt a “perfect victory”? A long time ago — in a Chiefs Kingdom that seems far, far away — I watched the 2002 squad steal a Week 1 victory because Cleveland Browns linebacker Dwayne Rudd threw his helmet in celebration before time expired and drew an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty. An untimed down allowed a 30-yard game-winning field goal. When I see the current state of social media during Chiefs games, I wonder if we would even feel permitted to celebrate that moment if it happened today. My opinion is that now multiple generations have grown up playing Madden and believe that anything short of a three-touchdown margin of victory doesn’t truly count as a win. The truth is, the NFL is a tough business, and the margin between perceived good and bad teams is rarely as wide as fans believe. Players know how short their careers can be, and you should expect every team’s best shot every week. The first month of the season is increasingly unpredictable as teams enter the campaign with less preseason action than in previous generations. Several teams that entered 2026 with lofty expectations would have taken a tight overtime victory over how their own Week 2 contests went. Eight squads are 2-0, and the Chiefs are one of them. It would be naive to think there aren’t areas for improvement. But sometimes a game turns out closer than expected — and it’s ok just to be happy with the win. Thank you for reading this week’s Arrowhead Pride Mailbag ! We will be back after the Chiefs’ season continues with a road game in Miami on Sunday. Keep watching The Feed for an opportunity to ask your questions.
author: Jared Sapp

The latest Kansas City Chiefs news The Chiefs and Patrick Mahomes look like their old selves, but now with new help | NBC News One week after producing a career-high 191 yards from scrimmage during his Chiefs debut in Week 1, a total helped by Walker’s league-best 14 broken tackles, he finished with 117 rushing yards on 24 carries and added 61 yards receiving against the Colts. Walker has looked every bit the missing piece capable of taking pressure off of Mahomes on the ground and opening up the passing game. “We able to, I guess, freestyle it,” Walker told NBC in a postgame interview of his connection with Mahomes. “If I’m open or if somebody open, play break down, he able to make plays, so it’s great to play with him.” Travis Kelce has moved beyond football. Chiefs’ win shows football still needs him | The Kansas City Star “He’s just still doing it,” quarterback Patrick Mahomes said of Kelce. “He knows how to get open, and he can make guys miss. And so for him to go out there and make the plays that he made in the big moments of the game — that’s who he’s always been. “And I think just as much as it’s kind of cleaned up the game for me, I think having Kenneth (Walker) and the way he’s running the ball gets him into these matchups that he’s gonna win. And he showed that (Sunday night).” 5 Colts Things: Daniel Jones & offense handle Steve Spagnuolo’s blitzes, Laquon Treadwell steps up, Kapena Gushiken flashes in Week 2 loss to Chiefs | Colts.com Jones was not sacked on 35 dropbacks Sunday, and he was pressured on just nine of those plays – the third-lowest rate across Week 2 prior to Monday Night Football. Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo sent 10 blitzes, and Jones completed seven of 10 passes for 89 yards with a touchdown against those looks. Six of those seven passes went for a first down. Chiefs, Bengals, Vikings head the surprise early contenders entering Week 3 | The Athletic After two weeks, the Chiefs have scored 64 points and have the league’s most explosive rushing attack (13.9 percent). They have evolved into a varied rushing attack that can use gap-scheme and zone. They run the ball from under center and from the gun. The run blocking hasn’t been perfect, but Kenneth Walker is breaking tackles at a superhuman rate. The Chiefs average 5.96 yards after contact, which is by far the highest in the league — the next highest is the Ravens (3.95). The Chiefs ranked dead last in this metric in the last two seasons. The Chiefs’ Offense Seems to Have Solved Last Season’s Biggest Problem | Sports Illustrated The Chiefs’ offense had plenty of issues in 2025, but for at least the last two seasons, the offense simply wasn’t able to convert nearly enough explosive plays. At times, Kansas City could overcome their big-play deficiencies by playing consistent, mistake-free football, but that left them with very little margin for error, and it made quick comebacks even more difficult. Two games into the 2026 season, it seems like that won’t be an issue this year. Around the NFL Sources: Giants QB Jaxson Dart believed to have sprained MCL | ESPN “We’ll know more [Tuesday],” coach John Harbaugh said. Regarding the reported sprained MCL, he said, “That’s in the neighborhood of it. We’ll get an MRI [Tuesday] and have a real good feel for it.” Dart, who was unavailable for comment after the game, was hurt while being pressured on third-and-8. Rams linebacker Byron Young hit Dart from the quarterback’s right side, sending him into linebacker Josaiah Stewart as he tried to tackle Dart, who landed hard on the turf. Bears QB Caleb Williams considered ‘week to week’ after suffering hamstring injury in loss to Vikings | NFL.com “It sounds like it’s gonna be a week-to-week deal for him,” Johnson said. “I gotta still talk with our trainer here, we’ll do that here shortly, and I’ll have the lowdown from him, but it sounds like it’s week-to-week but will likely miss some time.” Johnson later told reporters the Bears received a “somewhat encouraging” report about Williams’ injury, adding that the QB may not practice this week. Williams exited Sunday’s 9-3 loss to the Minnesota Vikings after coming up lame on a scramble in the fourth quarter. The QB was emotional while being carted off the field but was reportedly seen in the locker room later walking without aid and only a “slight limp.” Zach Ertz is back! | Bleeding Green Nation This always made a lot of sense, even before Goedert was sidelined. The team placed rookie TE Eli Stowers on IR at the start of the season, and Grant Calcaterra was put on IR at the end of training camp. With just Johnny Mundt and E.J. Jenkins left, the TE room gets an immediate boost by adding Ertz. The former Eagles draft pick has spent his time away from Philly with the Cardinals and Commanders, and has been a consistent factor in the redzone — regardless of the overall effectiveness of those offenses. Ertz is also just 11 receptions away from breaking Harold Carmichael’s franchise record (589) in Philadelphia to become the team’s leader all-time in catches. In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride 5 things we learned from the Chiefs’ Week 2 overtime victory over the Colts Emmett Johnson will make Kenneth Walker better If you want to wear down an opposing defense, throw an absolute unit like Kenneth Walker at them 25 or more times a game and watch their will to make contact deteriorate. But if you want to absolutely obliterate them, then bring in another running back who is almost as talented as Walker. Johnson’s vision, lateral agility, and contact balance make him just as hard to bring down. The one-two punch of Walker and Johnson is only going to get better as the year progresses, and we saw tonight what happens when an opposing defense has to respect the run first when Mahomes is on the field cooking. title: Chiefs Week 2 snap count analysis: Should Xavier Worthy lead WRs?
summary: Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Full disclosure: The late, great John Dixon, our former site manager who passed in April, was the mastermind behind collecting the NFL snap-count data we would present weekly on the site in recent years. I haven’t found the same accessibility. So we’ll use Pro Football Focus’s premium stats […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Xavier Worthy #1 of the Kansas City Chiefs celebrates a touchdown with Travis Kelce #87 and Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the second quarter against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to Arrowhead Pride’s weekly snap-count analysis! Full disclosure: The late, great John Dixon, our former site manager who passed in April, was the mastermind behind collecting the NFL snap-count data we would present weekly on the site in recent years. I haven’t found the same accessibility. So we’ll use Pro Football Focus’s premium stats to collect snap-count data, a dependable database for such information that I’ve used personally for eight years covering the site. So let’s see what we can figure out about the Kansas City Chiefs when taking a closer look at playing time during the 33-30 win over the Indianapolis Colts in Week 2. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information: Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Kingsley Suamataia, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, S Jaden Hicks, CB Nohl Williams, CB Kristian Fulton, CB L’Jarius Sneed, S Alohi Gilman Did not play: CB Mansoor Delane, QB Justin Fields Inactive: TE Jared Wiley, QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), S Chamarri Conner (Knee), DE Jack Pyburn, OT Diego Pounds, LT Josh Simmons (Back), DT Byron Eason The big takeaway: Xavier Worthy leads WRs The Chiefs’ speedy third-year wideout led all wide receivers in snaps (69), ahead of Rashee Rice (63) and Tyquan Thornton (47). Worthy led the unit in run-blocking snaps (22), an interesting number compared to Rice (20) and Thornton (11). The small-bodied receiver led the way in an offensive game plan that still handed the ball off to running back Kenneth Walker and Emmett Johnson 26 times. However, Worthy produced just 25 yards over five catches; he averaged 0.54 yards per route run on Sunday night. He was tasked with stretching the defense horizontally and vertically throughout the game, but so were Thornton (2.39 yards per route run) and Rice (2.02 yards per route run). If Worthy isn’t the best blocker of the trio and isn’t as productive a receiver as the other two, why is he leading the room in snaps? The Offensive takeaway: Noah Gray plays 40 snaps After 38 snaps in Week 1, second tight end Noah Gray played 40 offensive snaps against the Colts. The 12-personnel sets kept auxiliary receivers Jalen Royals (12 snaps) and rookie Cyrus Allen (3 snaps) on the sideline. Gray blocked for a run or pass on 24 of his snaps. Over two weeks, the move speaks to the Chiefs’ commitment to running the ball against opponents they need to beat. The Broncos’ pass defense was tougher, but both opponents were asking for a downhill run game right down their faces. As the season wears on, it will be interesting to see whether Gray — who has just one catch for five yards — gets less time in favor of higher-potential playmakers in the receiving room. The Defensive takeaway: R Mason Thomas has ‘pass-rush specialist’ playing time Rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas logged 27 snaps for the Chiefs’ defense on Sunday night. Only six of those snaps were against the run, including a rep where he was washed out on the way to Colts running back Jonathan Taylor’s first of two touchdown runs. Fourth-year defensive end Felix Anudike-Uzomah out-snapped Thomas overall, but saw the field for 5 fewer pass-rush opportunities. Still, Anudike-Uzomah was a more productive pass rusher, hitting the quarterback twice while Thomas registered just one pressure. The Chiefs’ young defensive line has faced two strong units up front to start the season. Thomas stood out less against Indianapolis, and the team is clearly trying to maximize his strengths by altering the rotation to keep him fresh for pass-rush situations. title: 5 notable quotes from Andy Reid the day after Chiefs’ Week 2 win
summary: After the Kansas City Chiefs’ 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday evening, head coach Andy Reid faced local media Monday to answer questions. During his livestreamed press conference, Reid hit on a few significant storylines in Chiefs Kingdom, starting with the left tackle who hasn’t seen the field yet this season. 1. […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Head Coach Andy Reid of the Kansas City Chiefs stands on the sidelines prior to an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images After the Kansas City Chiefs ’ 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday evening, head coach Andy Reid faced local media Monday to answer questions. During his livestreamed press conference , Reid hit on a few significant storylines in Chiefs Kingdom, starting with the left tackle who hasn’t seen the field yet this season. 1. The latest on Josh Simmons “He’s doing everything,” Reid described starting left tackle Josh Simmons (Back). “He’s working his tail off. “We knew it would be a couple of, two, three or four games in here as long as he was making progress,“ Reid continued. ”We’ll just see where he’s at; he’s kind of in that ‘flex’ area there to see exactly if it’s calmed down, if some of the swelling as gone down but we’ll see.” In his place, rookie left tackle Kahlil Benson has filled in admirably. It’s also worth sharing that Reid had no further update on safety Chamarri Conner (Knee), who has also not practiced through two weeks of practices. 2. Kahlil Benson did ‘a pretty good job’ “I saw some good things,” Reid said. “He had a couple of hiccups there; mostly it was just the scheme, just adjusting to the scheme more than the one-on-one blocking part of it. “Overall, he did a pretty good job, I thought, Reid finished. “Solid.” Immediately after the game, Reid shared that he believes Benson is “winning over a lot of people.” 3. Mansoor Delane “It wasn’t coming around as fast as we wanted,” Reid said of rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane’s shoulder injury; he was questionable to play, dressed, but didn’t record a snap against Indianapolis. “He was right on the border there of ‘alright, you can get in there and play a full game,’ or, if we can, get it to calm down a little bit more and maybe he’s better this week. It was a tweener’s position to be in, but he wanted to suit up and, if needed, he could’ve gone in, but we’re trying to keep him out of playing a full game in there for sure.” 4. Anticipating more of what Tyquan Thornton did in Week 2 “Tyquan had a real good training camp,” Reid said after Thornton’s performance of four catches for 86 yards. “I think he has just carried that over into this. “I would anticipate that he would continue to make the same plays or have the same opportunities that he had yesterday,” Reid elaborated. “But you never know in these games who is going to have the opportunities and who’s not, but he is well deserving of what he got, and then he took advantage of it by making the play. “A couple of those are tough catches, and he did a great job with it; I’m sure he’s probably a little sore this morning; he took a couple of shots in there.” 5. The one-two punch is blossoming in the backfield Reid talked about the Chiefs’ backfield situation, which hasn’t looked as split as it could as the season moves forward. He commented on allowing rookie Emmett Johnson to grow with time. “I think Emmett will continue to get more snaps, and that will take a little bit of the load off [Kenneth Walker],” Reid said. “He wants the ball, he wants the ball every play, Ken does, and he’s not asking to be relieved or anything else. I think as it goes on, you get a nice balance with those two in there, and it keeps them more fresh as the season goes on.”

title: Numbers Never Lie: 3 Chiefs stats from Week 2 and their significance
summary: Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but of what to expect […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyquan Thornton #2 of the Kansas City Chiefs catches a pass during overtime of an NFL football game against the Indianapolis Colts at Arrowhead Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but of what to expect from the Kansas City Chiefs moving forward. Here are three statistics from the Week 2 win over the Indianapolis Colts and what they could mean for the rest of the season: 1. Tyquan Thornton completed both contested-catch chances downfield According to PFF , Thornton made the only two deep completions (20 or more yards in the air) for quarterback Patrick Mahomes against the Colts. Both completions had contact at the catch point, giving Thornton a chance to showcase the reliability to bring in those throws we saw all last season. It’s especially significant when compared to the lowlights from the two top wideouts in Kansas City: wide receiver Xavier Worthy was faulted with two drops, per PFF , and Rashee Rice was unable to bring in a tight-window catch late in the game that was an easier play to make than either of Thornton’s. Through two weeks, Mahomes has been tagged with five drops by PFF . Only Green Bay Packers quarterback Jordan Love has more drops this season before “Monday Night Football.” 2. None of Travis Kelce’s 9 catches were ‘tight window’ throws For the second straight week, football fans questioned how soon-to-be 37-year-old tight end Travis Kelce had so much room to rumble and stumble downfield. According to Next Gen Stats , Kelce had more than a yard of separation on each of his 11 targets, producing nine catches, 101 yards, and a touchdown; 67 of his yards came after the catch. To sum it up: Kelce is finding open windows. He avoided tight-window throws all night against Indianapolis, and that goes back to Thornton’s downfield play and the offense’s overall speed when everyone is healthy. Kelce can still work underneath and find the pockets, and Mahomes’ chemistry with the all-time tight end can still make a huge difference on crucial downs and in the red zone. Kelce is the team’s leader in receiving yards (172) through two weeks; he could continue on as the highest-volume target if Rice, Worthy and Thornton continue to share the load in the receiver room and attack downfield. The play-action game helps open things up here as well. 3. Colts receiver Josh Downs had 7 catches and 72 yards out of the slot Per PFF , the Colts’ slot receiver was very productive in the pass game, mostly against Chiefs cornerback L’Jarius Sneed; he also beat safety Christian Rolland-Wallace downfield out of the slot at one point. Six of the seven catches moved the chains. It’s a reminder that Sneed’s best trait is being physical. When a team can present this type of matchup, a shifty receiver that can win quickly out of the slot, should the Chiefs’ defense be prepared to move a stickier coverage player like Nohl Williams into the slot? It will be interesting to see if Kansas City adjusts to Downs exposing a potential hole in the secondary.
author: Ron Kopp Jr.

title: Chiefs’ Kahlil Benson is ‘winning over a lot of people,’ says Andy Reid
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs are 2-0 through two weeks of the NFL season, and that has come with rookie Kahlil Benson at left tackle in place of the injured Josh Simmons (Back). Last year’s starting right tackle at the University of Indiana has played every possible snap on the blind side so far, all 149 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - SEPTEMBER 14: Kahlil Benson #70 of the Kansas City Chiefs looks on from the field during an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Arrowhead Stadium on September 14, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs are 2-0 through two weeks of the NFL season, and that has come with rookie Kahlil Benson at left tackle in place of the injured Josh Simmons (Back). Last year’s starting right tackle at the University of Indiana has played every possible snap on the blind side so far, all 149 per Pro Football Focus , and has filled in admirably. He has allowed four hurries and two quarterback hits through two games, but hasn’t been faulted for any of the four sacks quarterback Patrick Mahomes has taken against the Denver Broncos and Indianapolis Colts . Walk-on left tackle Khalil Benson has made quite the impression against the Colts. #NextGenStats powered by @awscloud . pic.twitter.com/z8XNMhDujy — Sunday Night Football on NBC (@SNFonNBC) September 21, 2026 He has held up on pass downs, with plenty of challenges to come if he stays in the lineup, but Benson’s run blocking has made him “one of the Chiefs’ five best linemen” right now, in the words of head coach Andy Reid before the season opener. During the preseason, Chiefs offensive line coach Andy Heck said the coaching staff “could see [Benson] had dominant physical traits.” He has shown that off on run plays early on. Chiefs talked about Kahlil Benson showing dominant traits during the summer It's the effortless power in his hands. Look how easily he puts 30 on the ground pic.twitter.com/pdjHra1b7q — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) September 21, 2026 Benson shows off effortless power with his hands after climbing to the second level to nonchalantly pancake a Colts safety. The power he brings to blocks has stood out throughout practice and game observations. Moves people off the line pic.twitter.com/OFV2cu3bp9 — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) September 21, 2026 He fires off the ball and uses that huge frame — 6 feet 6 inches tall with 34 1/2-inch arms — to create space for the Chiefs’ running backs. Running back Kenneth Walker had 10 carries to the left side of the line against Indianapolis; he totaled 69 rushing yards (6.9 yards per attempt) on those runs. After the game, head coach Andy Reid acknowledged the rookie’s efforts. “Yeah, there are a couple hiccups in there, but he was going against a good player,” Reid said to reporters. “And I thought he did a decent job… (General Manager Brett) Veach, great eyes, great eyes. I mean, to bring him in here, and then (Offensive Line Coach) Andy Heck believing in him and coaching him up, the kid believing in himself. “I think he’s winning over a lot of people,” Reid said. Is he winning over the coaching staff enough to keep him in the starting lineup? With Simmons’ return on the horizon, should we expect Benson to slide over to the right side? Or does Benson stay in Simmons’ place regardless of the injury report? Right tackle Jaylon Moore didn’t allow a pressure over 51 pass blocks against the Colts, per PFF . He had a rougher performance in Week 1, but either way, the Chiefs will soon have to make decisions about their starting five up front.
