title: Miami Dolphins Fans Sound Off On Game Two
summary: Following yesterday’s predictably ugly game between our Miami Dolphins and the San Francisco 49ers, I asked: What is your overall take on today’s second game of the season for your Miami Dolphins under the new coaching staff and with the overhauled roster? What are the positive and negative takeaways from this afternoon’s game, both as […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins runs against Upton Stout #20 of the San Francisco 49ers in the second quarter of a game at Levi's Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Following yesterday’s predictably ugly game between our Miami Dolphins and the San Francisco 49ers, I asked: What is your overall take on today’s second game of the season for your Miami Dolphins under the new coaching staff and with the overhauled roster? What are the positive and negative takeaways from this afternoon’s game, both as a team and with individual players? Below are some of your thoughts on our Dolphins and yesterday’s loss- I Hate Sports predicts more of the same for week three. Dolphins have KC at home next week at noon. Another 38-13 loss incoming. Olddolphin points to the lack of pass rush thus far. The Defense hasn’t shown any pass rush in two games. Without a pass rush no way to evaluate the secondary. Austin Jackson is terrible. He hasn’t blocked anybody in two games. Unless Willis is given some time, there is no way to evaluate him or the receivers. SOD1961 just pointed out that we could be getting blown out even worse. On the bright side, the cumulative score after 2 weeks in 2019 was 102-10. Lefty5150 points out that it’s bad on both sides of the ball at this point. I saw a bad offense and a bad defense. Do they have some building blocks…….yes. Oline is ok Achane is great but they need a big time TE and another Wr for starters. On D they need pass rushers and another corner and safety. 100M will fill a lot of these holes. Wolfpack1 sees a top draft pick coming. Hello Jeremiah Smith, welcome to south Florida! Zen4Phins sees inconsistency that will only get better. Thought they played a team way ahead of them in every way. Oline moves the dline on one play beautifully, then misses completely the next. Kinda sums up what we’re likely gonna get used to. Dline is struggling in pass rush and our secondary against that offense is blessed that Miami was able to run clock in the 1st half. Malik holds on a little too long frequently but can’t tell if its recievers issue or hesitation on his part or likely combo of. Looked pretty good against run though. The offense didn’t turn the ball over and got a lucky bounce early from Herman and there was Pinion who probably won’t let that happen again. Looked good on return coverage and we weren’t punting the whole game. Overall, the 9ers are just way too good at this time and this place on this day for us. But next week, next week we FEAST! AquaAndOrange shows how it could always be worse. Well, on the bright side, we scored more than the rams did. USMCFinPhreak wishes he had not spent the fortune on NFL Sunday Ticket this season. I feel your pain! This team is a mess and I blame mainly Grier. Yes, he IS to blame. I will blame him until we can get our salary cap back under control. We all knew that once we fired him, the house of cards would crumble. Sullivan and Hafley are just picking up the crappy cards that were dealt to them. They had to purge the players with the bloated contracts, just to get it under control. But the ultimate blame goes to Ross. He was the one who hired and kept Grier. We, as fans, knew Grier wasn’t making sound decisions throughout his tenure, but he handed Ross rose-colored glasses and Ross failed to take them off until it was too late. This team seems to be worse than an franchise expansion team, with a bunch of scabs haplessly scurrying about the gridiron. Yes, we do have a few promising rookies, but it will take time for them to grasp the speed of the NFL. I promised myself that I would not get the NFL Sunday Ticket this year because I know they would be horrible, but my wife encouraged me to do so. I’m sorry she did! The Pod of Dolphins knows that even the most painful seasons must come to an end. This will be over soon, there is only 15 games left on the season StanleyDoyle1 is not pleased with the offensive game planning up to this point. The offensive play-calling is abysmal. The offensive line is not the problem, and we have a great RB who can mask other weaknesses. But Willis is not a game-changing QB who will carry a team on his shoulders. He’s just not accurate enough, nor does he make decisions quickly enough. But he’s our QB and he needs help. So design a game plan around him so he can have a modicum of success. Peter j sees a bunch of kids going out there and playing hard, something that will eventually pay dividends. Omg, really??? I’m 70yrs old, been a fins fan since 69, I call them kids but they’re playing their asses off, instead of pissing on their dreams how about some encouragement?every dog has his day we’ll have ours MiamiItaliano is not sold on the new offensive coordinator. Slowik isn’t a good playcaller. They need a new voice that wasn’t from the previous regime B4Orr just sees a plan going as designed. The plan is to go 0-17 this year to get the #1 pick.. right… so all going well so far… MIAMI235 is looking forward to the offseason and what still needs to be done to this roster. Based on what is slowly unfolding….how many players do we need to replace next Season? 5, 10, 15, 20, etc. Yes, it’s still early going. Molly Polly II isn’t a fan of our QB or how the OL pass-blocks. Positive: game tix should be extremely inexpensive this year! Negatives: O-line is a trainwreck or they really hate Malik. They block their azzz off for the running game but can’t block for crap on passing plays. Malik is not a good QB, just cuz he can scramble and isn’t injury prone like Tua, doesn’t make Willis a good QB. Meanwhile defense, who knows but Purdy, not to my surprise, embarrassed us….for 3 painful Qtrs! I got it…our team is horrible due to salary cap. This isn’t all about wins n losses, we are a completely dysfunctional organization. Billionaire Steve Ross might want to consider rewarding season ticket holders a huge discount. Well, that’s our somewhat painful random selection of comments for this evening. I guess this season is starting as ugly as most of us expected. Hopefully, going forward, we can at least start to see steady growth among the younger players on this roster as the season progresses, knowing that this is not likely a one- or two-year rebuild. As always, thank you to each of you who takes the time to join us each evening, or at least most evenings, and answer our Phinsider Question Of The Day.
author: James McKinney

title: Six Questions That Will Define the Dolphins’ 2026 Season
summary: Before the season opener against the Raiders, Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley revealed that success this year won’t be defined by wins and losses: “I want to win everything that we do. I’ve said that over and over. But at the same time, we need to make sure that this foundation and the process is […]
full_text: Before the season opener against the Raiders, Dolphins head coach Jeff Hafley revealed that success this year won’t be defined by wins and losses : “I want to win everything that we do. I’ve said that over and over. But at the same time, we need to make sure that this foundation and the process is built the right way. … There’s no shortcuts because it’s bigger than that right now.” That’s a sensible approach to take with a roster this young. But even if wins and losses aren’t the primary measure of success – and a 35-13 drubbing by the 49ers only reinforces that idea – the 2026 season still needs to provide clarity on several key questions that will shape the franchise’s future. Here are six I feel need to be answered before the Dolphins start game planning the 2027 NFL Draft. Is Malik Willis a true No. 1 quarterback? First, would we even know a No. 1 quarterback if we had one? It’s been 25 years since Dan Marino’s last game (a 62-7 drubbing by Jacksonville in the 2000 AFC divisional playoffs), and we’ve had more than 20 different starting QBs in that time, including such luminaries as Ray Lucas and Tyler Thigpen. This is the biggest question by far, because it will determine whether Miami needs to spend a top draft pick on a quarterback or has the luxury of addressing other needs early. Given the range of possible outcomes, I’ve been encouraged by what we’ve seen from Willis so far. He’s shown he can run: which feels like more and more a necessity in today’s game, and he’s got some zip and accuracy on his passes . Still, one passing touchdown and one rushing touchdown in two games is a little … underwhelming. We’ll have to see if he can continue to up his game and if he’s durable enough for a full NFL season. Is Greg Dulcich the answer at tight end? Brady and Gronk. Mahomes and Kelce. Even Marino and Hardy (though let’s pause for a quick shoutout to Keith Jackson). @retrofilmz Dan Marino to Keith Jackson on a 31-Yard TD Pass in the 1992 AFC Divisional Playoff game. #nfl #miamidolphins #fyp #flashbackfriday ♬ original sound – RetroFilmz The point is, every quarterback should have a security blanket. Can Greg Dulcich be that guy, either for Malik, Kyle McCord or a QB in next year’s draft? Dulcich flashed down the stretch last season, but he’s also been placed on injured reserve three times in his career for a recurring hamstring issue. In two games this season, he caught four passes for 35 yards and a dubious taunting penalty. Is Miami picking up Chop Robinson’s fifth-year option? First-round draft picks are eligible for a fifth-year option, which allows their team to extend the player’s rookie contract for an additional season before they reach free agency. Next spring, the Dolphins will need to decide whether or not to pick up Chop Robinson’s fifth-year option ahead of the 2028 season. Robinson’s fifth-year option could cost the Dolphins somewhere in the neighborhood of $17 million. That’s a reasonable amount to pay for a quality edge rusher – especially for a team that’s been outsacked already 9-0 after two games – but only if the Dolphins get the version of Robinson they saw during the second half of 2024, not the one they’ve seen so far in 2025 and 2026. He’s reportedly looked great in camp , adding on 10 pounds of muscle and cleaning up his diet, but he was MIA against the Raiders in Week 1 and missed Week 2 with his third concussion in the past year. How close are the Dolphins to fixing their offensive line? It’s funny to suggest the Dolphins might have solved their offensive line problem after giving up four sacks, five tackles for loss and five quarterback hits on Sunday. But for the first time in years, the Dolphins may have credible long-term answers at nearly every position. If Miami can determine this season (1) if Jonah Savaiinaea fits as a long-term starter at right guard, and (2) if Kadyn Proctor projects better at left guard than right tackle, that will go a long way toward determining what the team’s draft needs are. I suppose we could also add Austin Jackson into this bucket, though he hasn’t played especially well thus far, and it’s hard to imagine he’ll re-sign with the team for 2027. Which of the Dolphins’ young players can we build around? Miami had 18 players on their roster with fewer than two years of NFL experience. Some of them flashed in Week 1 (Caleb Douglas!), most decidedly did not flash in Week 2. Figuring out what we have and who we can build around will be paramount this season. Frankly, this is one of the best parts about a rebuilding season – seeing which players can take the leap from unproven draft pick to impact starters. There are lots of storylines to follow, from the ascendancy of Jacob Rodriguez, to the appealing potential of a shutdown corner in Chris Johnson, to the possibility that a trio of rookies in Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell and Kevin Coleman Jr (2 targets, 0 catches) can emerge and turn a position of weakness into a position of strength. One player I’m intrigued by is Michael Taaffe, a fifth-round selection who led the team in tackles in Week 2 after securing an interception in Week 1. Watching these players develop is one of the most enjoyable parts of a rebuild, and it’ll go a long way toward identifying who are building blocks are headed into next offseason. Do we have the right coaches in place to take advantage of this rebuilding year? One trap NFL teams often fall into is hiring offensive or defensive “gurus” as head coaches without giving enough consideration to everything else the job requires. Yes, you have gameday tasks like calling plays, challenging rulings and signaling timeouts. But do you know how to develop players? Can you maintain a culture of accountability without turning younger players off? Can you lead a locker room? I didn’t hate the Mike McDaniel hiring, but (IMO) he proved to be in over his head pretty quickly. I’m optimistic that Jeff Hafley has the temperament and mentality to succeed in all areas of coaching, even if the defense has been lacking so far this season. But is Bobby Slowik the right coach for this stage of a rebuild? The offensive line looked like it might actually be a strength heading into the regular season, before allowing nine sacks and generating little push through two games. So is offensive line coach Matt Applebaum the right person for the job? It’s way too early to make any determinations on coaching, and those of us on the outside may not have clear insight to how well they develop players – all we really have to go on is game tape. But this is going to be a young team next year too, and presumably for a long time. It’s important our coaches know how to develop young talent into capable players. Those are the six questions I think the Dolphins need answered this season. How are you defining success for the Dolphins in 2026? Share your thoughts in the comments.

full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - AUGUST 27: Andre Jones Jr. #59 of the Buffalo Bills stands on the field with his back turned during the second quarter of a preseason game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Highmark Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. Playing a large part in the disappointing first two games is Miami’s special teams unit coached by Chris Tabor. On Monday, the Dolphins signed a player Tabor is familiar with off of the Buffalo Bills’ practice squad — linebacker Andre Jones Jr. Tabor coached Jones in Buffalo last season when he was the Bills’ special teams coordinator for the year. Prior to joining the Bills in his third season in the league, the undrafted linebacker out of Louisianna-Lafayette spent two seasons with the Washington Commanders. According to Pro Football Reference , Jones has played 294 snaps on special teams since entering the National Football League ahead of the 2023 season. We will continue to keep you updated on all things Miami Dolphins as the team prepares to welcome Patrick Mahomes, Ken Walker III, Travis Kelce and the rest of the Kansas City Chiefs to Hard Rock Stadium this upcoming Sunday. title: Fins Up, Fins Down | Winners and losers from Miami Dolphins week two loss
summary: Hello darkness, my old friend… We all knew this was going to be a rough season for our Miami Dolphins. Maybe we didn’t realize just how tough it was going to be. On Sunday, the Miami Dolphins took on the San Francisco 49ers, and despite hanging in there in the first half — they were […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - OCTOBER 20: Austin Jackson #73 of the Miami Dolphins runs off the field at half time against the Indianapolis Colts at Lucas Oil Stadium on October 20, 2024 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello darkness, my old friend… We all knew this was going to be a rough season for our Miami Dolphins. Maybe we didn’t realize just how tough it was going to be. On Sunday, the Miami Dolphins took on the San Francisco 49ers, and despite hanging in there in the first half — they were down just 8 points at the break — our boys in aqua and orange came out flat in the second half and were decimated by Brock Purdy, George Kittle, Christian McCaffery and company to the tune of a 35-13 defeat. So, who did their part on Sunday and who contributed to the 22 point drubbing? It’s Fins Up, Fins Down time… FINS UP Patrick Paul gets this week’s Fins Up designation. He wasn’t perfect, but on an offensive line that really struggled versus a ferocious 49ers defense, Paul held his own all day long and ended up with Pro Football Focus’ highest grade along the offense line — earning a 75.5 grade on the day (82.0 pass blocking; 69.1 run blocking). The Dolphins will have plenty of cap space to try and get a deal done with Paul this offseason before he enters into the final year of his rookie contract. If he continues to play like the strongest member of the team’s offensive line, his payday should be a substantial one. Old friend Laremy Tunsil is the highest paid left tackle in football — averaging $30.1 million per year with the Washington Commanders. I don’t think Paul surpasses that with his new deal, but at this point, that can’t be said with any level of certainty. FINS DOWN From one offensive lineman to another, right tackle Austin Jackson is this week’s down player. After the contest — one in which he performed very poorly — the player himself admitted he needs to be better. Despite not officially being credited with a sack allowed on Sunday, Jackson finished the contest with a poor 45.7 grade from PFF. If the Dolphins deem backup Caedan Wallace ready to contribute, it may not be long before Jackson is replaced as the team’s starter at the right tackle spot. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if Jackson ends up getting traded for a half-eaten tuna sandwich and some waffle fries at the trade deadline. Regardless, I don’t think we’ll see him suiting up for Miami in 2027 and beyond.

title: The Good, Bad & Ugly from the Miami Dolphins Week 2 loss to the San Francisco 49ers
summary: Fresh off of a Week One loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, the Miami Dolphins traveled to northern California to square off against the San Francisco 49ers in Week Two. Despite a competitive first half, the boys in aqua and orange imploded in the second half — ultimately losing the game by a score of […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 20: Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins looks to pass against the San Francisco 49ers in the first quarter of a game at Levi's Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Fresh off of a Week One loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, the Miami Dolphins traveled to northern California to square off against the San Francisco 49ers in Week Two. Despite a competitive first half, the boys in aqua and orange imploded in the second half — ultimately losing the game by a score of 35-13. In a year when we weren’t expecting the Dolphins to amass a lot of wins, they’re certainly meeting those expectations. However, despite the current struggles, there are glimmers of hope to be found if your sights are set on the future and not necessarily on the here and now. Taking their lumps in 2026 could allow the team to blossom in 2027 or 2028 once the organization establishes a solid foundation and clears out the massive amount of dead cap currently on the books. Still, it still hasn’t been a pleasant experience watching the Dolphins play through two games this season. Regardless, we’re going to trudge along and bring to you the good, bad and ugly from each contest. Let’s dive in. GOOD Malik Willis connects with Ryan Miller for deep touchdown late The San Francisco 49ers defense is loaded with stars. From Nick Bosa to Fred Warner, Dre Greenlaw and others, the 49ers boast a ferocious opposition for offenses to face. They took it to Miami’s offense for most of Sunday’s clash, however, late in the contest, Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis uncorked a beautiful deep ball to wide receiver Ryan Miller — finding the pass catcher streaking up the sideline. Miller brought the ball in and took it all the way to the house — good for a 77 yard score. It’s in moments like that where you see the vision new general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan had when signing Willis to a three-year deal in the offseason. Of course, with little weaponry surrounding him besides running back De’Von Achane, it isn’t always going to look pretty for Willis this season. However, with Sunday’s bomb to Miller, Willis has now thrown his first touchdown as a member of the Miami Dolphins. Here’s hoping there are plenty more to come. BAD Dolphins defense couldn’t stop 49ers passing attack While the 49ers’ defense is loaded with talent, the Dolphins’ defense isn’t. To make matters worse, their top pass rusher, third-year EDGE defender Chop Robinson, missed Sunday’s game due to a concussion suffered in practice just a few days prior to the game. On Sunday, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy had his way with Miami’s defense to the tune of 20 completions on 22 attempts for 287 passing yards and and two passing scores. Tight end George Kittle reeled in 4 balls for 80 yards and a touchdown. Wide receiver Mike Evans tallied 3 receptions for 54 yards, while running back Christian McCaffrey added 4 catches for 43 yards. Whenever the 49ers needed a play to be made, they let Purdy go to work — and he rewarded that faith by finishing with a 149.1 passer rating against Miami. UGLY Dolphins offensive line dominated by 49ers defense While Miami’s defense faltered, San Francisco’s didn’t. All day long, 49ers defenders had their way with the Dolphins’ offensive line. Kadyn Proctor struggled. Jonah Savaiinaea struggled. Austin Jackson struggled. Patrick Paul had his share of mistakes as well. The 49ers finished with four sacks on Sunday. That’s 9 sacks through two games for this Dolphins team. If offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik wants his side of the ball to play better, he’s going to have to scheme up some help for his offensive line. Malik Willis and his mobility is propping this unit up as best as he can, but it still hasn’t been enough. ___ The Dolphins went winless on their West Coast roadtrip to open the season. The team starts off the Jeff Hafley era with an 0- 2 record with the Kansas City Chiefs coming to town next Sunday. Do you think the Dolphins can keep it close against Patrick Mahomes, Ken Walker III, Travis Kelce and company this week? Let me know in the comments below or on Twitter at @MBrave13 . Fins up.

title: Dallas Turner, Jalen Redmond, and the Vikings’ Defensive Identity
summary: Minnesota is 2-0 after a sloppy 9-3 win at Chicago, and on The Real Forno Show Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano argued that the real story is belief: a Flores defense that can close, a run game that is finally getting volume, and enough luck to survive a backup-QB weather game. Forness opened with the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 2026: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Andrew van Ginkel (43) sacks Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) on the last play of the second quarter at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois, on Sunday, September 20, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) Minnesota is 2-0 after a sloppy 9-3 win at Chicago, and on The Real Forno Show Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano argued that the real story is belief: a Flores defense that can close, a run game that is finally getting volume, and enough luck to survive a backup-QB weather game. Forness opened with the question that framed the hour: “Have the Minnesota Vikings built themself a Super Bowl foundation? I think they have.” He was careful not to crown anyone. “I’m not saying the Vikings will win the Super Bowl, but they have started a foundation.” That foundation, in their telling, is not Kevin O’Connell’s vertical offense. It is winning when the script dies. “Two years ago, this team loses that game,” Forness said of the old Soldier Field nightmares. Chicago went 0-for-3 in the red zone. Isaiah Rodgers recovered a fumble and later blocked a kick. Dallas Turner finished Tyson Bagent when Colston Loveland was left alone. Forness called Brian Flores’ last call “a genius actual play design,” then added the Super Bowl caveat: “This play doesn’t happen if it’s Caleb Williams.” Luck is part of the pitch. “You have to have luck in order to win a Super Bowl.” The offense is the open question. “I can’t tell you if the offense is good or not because we haven’t seen the offense actually play, other than 11 plays,” Forness said of Kyler Murray. Carson Wentz “proved who he is”: high variance, a few lasers to Josh Oliver and T.J. Hockenson, and the misses that keep him a backup. O’Connell has cleared Murray for Tampa. On the ground, Aaron Jones went 23-for-105 with Jordan Mason out; Forness still called the backfield “abysmal” if Jones goes down, with Demond Claiborne “borderline unplayable,” DeeJay Dallas dinged, and Jerome Ford on the practice squad. Ben Goessling’s True Media note: Minnesota is No. 1 in first- and second-down run rate (62%+). Forness: two games is not a fix. “How do these tendencies manifest with Kyler Murray?” Key points from the episode: Winning ugly builds confidence: The Vikings leaned on a 62% run rate (number one in the NFL on first and second down, per Ben Goessling) and a defense that covered while blitzing — a combination Forness called “disgusting” in the best way. Dallas Turner’s emergence: Despite criticism for not winning enough one-on-ones, Turner has 20 pressures in two weeks and is being schemed into favorable matchups. “Brian Flores continues to be a creative mastermind,” Forness said. “I think Dallas Turner is primed to have an elite season.” Defensive line depth paying off: Jalen Redmond “might be the best player on the team not named Justin Jefferson or Christian Darrisaw.” Levi Drake Rodriguez, a seventh-round pick, has become a starter. Caleb Banks and Dominique Orange are flashing elite potential. “As much as we can criticize Kwesi Adofo-Mensah for a lot of things, that calculated bet is paying humongous dividends.” Run game concerns: Aaron Jones is banged up and sore, Jordan Mason has a broken thumb, and Demond Claiborne is “borderline unplayable.” Forness flagged the backfield depth as the biggest red flag going forward. Carson Wentz is who we thought he was: “He is who we thought he was,” Forness said of Wentz, who delivers highs and lows with no consistency. Kyler Murray has cleared concussion protocol just in time. Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: If the Vikings keep finding different ways to win — and the good proves repeatable — this team has the foundation for a deep playoff run. “If it’s repeatable, then you can expect it to happen again.” Catch The Real Forno Show every Monday night on Vikings 1st & SKOL for the kind of film-level breakdown you won’t get anywhere else. Subscribe, leave a five-star review on iTunes, and join the Discord for live commentary. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . So here’s two questions, Vikings fans: Are the Vikings legitimately building a Super Bowl foundation, or is it too early to buy in? And… What part of this 2-0 start actually travels to Tampa — the front, the run rate, or Murray coming back?
author: David Stefano

title: Vikes Views: Nincompoop of the Week – Vikings at Bears
summary: The Minnesota Vikings dismantled the Chicago Bears offense to cruise to a 9-3 victory. There weren’t as many glaring mistakes as you’d typically see in such a low scoring game, but there’s always someone to blame. Here’s my nominees for Nincompoop of the Week. Ben Johnson All we hear about is the offensive genius Ben […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 2026: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Andrew van Ginkel (43) sacks Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) on the last play of the second quarter at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois, on Sunday, September 20, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) The Minnesota Vikings dismantled the Chicago Bears offense to cruise to a 9-3 victory. There weren’t as many glaring mistakes as you’d typically see in such a low scoring game, but there’s always someone to blame. Here’s my nominees for Nincompoop of the Week. Ben Johnson All we hear about is the offensive genius Ben Johnson for the entire offseason, and even more so after Week 1’s scorapalooza in Carolina. Johnson had no response for the Vikings pass rush on Sunday. I know it’s a tall task, but the last play is a microcosm of their issues. The Bears tried to block Dallas Turner with a Tight End. Turner easily pushed him back into Bagent for the game sealing sack. Some of those play calls were head-scratchers, and if Caleb Williams wasn’t as elusive as he is, it could have been a lot uglier for the Bears. Garrett Bradbury Bradbury was called for two holds and two false starts on Sunday. I believe he was a little nervous facing his previous employer. One of those was offset because Levi Drake Rodriguez was held into Caleb Williams’ feet, but the officials can’t get them all right. His poor play basically single handedly ended a very promising drive after the Vikings took the lead 6-3 in the 2nd quarter. You could nominate the entire Offensive Line, but Bradbury stuck out amongst the muck. Not the first time he’s been nominated for NOTW. D’Andre Swift Swift made a crucial mistake that likely cost the Bears the game. After a long 11 play drive the Bears were at the 1. Swift was pushing through to the goal line and allowed the ball to be punched out by Jalen Redmond. It was a great play by Jalen Redmond, but ball security has to be the priority at the goal line. Points were at a premium and he likely cost the team there. Caleb Williams The stat line wasn’t terrible, but the interception to Byron Murphy gave the Vikings points in a game where every possession mattered. Flores had him uncomfortable all afternoon and his only answer was to take off from the pocket. Theo Jackson Another rought day for Jackson. He’s been given a larger opportunity and he’s responded with missed tackles and blown assignments. He’s the weakest link in a very strong defensive chain. Honorable Mentions K OC – emphasis on the OC. The offense looks terrible. If the Bears didn’t fumble at the 1 and the Vikings had to respond, we’d likely be talking about a loss today. Bears OL – the entire line looked confused all day, but most OL do against the Vikings Carson Wentz – he didn’t make the big mistake, or got lucky it was dropped when he did. The lack of offensive production will likely mean he’s headed back to the bench this week (or whenver Murray is cleared).
author: Craig Williams

title: Vikings Week Two Stock Market Report
summary: The Minnesota Vikings won an ugly game at a rainy and sloppy Soldier Field on Sunday 9-3, making it a 2-0 start to the season- both against division opponents. Stock Up Brian Flores. His out-generaling Ben Johnson and holding the Bears to 3 points, after crushing the Packers last week with his unique blitzing scheme, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Dallas Turner #15 of the Minnesota Vikings sacks Tyson Bagent #17 of the Chicago Bears during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings won an ugly game at a rainy and sloppy Soldier Field on Sunday 9-3, making it a 2-0 start to the season- both against division opponents. Stock Up Brian Flores . His out-generaling Ben Johnson and holding the Bears to 3 points, after crushing the Packers last week with his unique blitzing scheme, is raising eyebrows around the league. Dallas Turner. He continues to show he has made the leap into the top tier of edge rushers in the league. He was credited with ten quarterback pressures against the Bears, according to preliminary PFF charting, including a sack to seal the victory. Jalen Redmond. He stepped up his disruptive play against the Bears. He was credited with 2 quarterback pressures, a batted pass, a key forced fumble on the one yard line, and four tackles- all of them stops. Those plays made a difference in the game. Will Reichard . He’s been automatic for a while now, and once again made all three field goal attempts. But he also did so in poor conditions for a kicker which added a degree of difficulty. Isaiah Rodgers . He allowed just one reception on two targets for seven yards in his coverage, with a PBU that was nearly an interception to ice the game and a blocked field goal to prevent the Bears from tying the game late. Caleb Banks. It was still a rough game for Banks overall, but he did make a few plays and showed some progress. He had four tackles- three of them defensive stops- and one quarterback pressure. Still a long way to go in terms of consistency among other things, but he did show progress in his second game. Aaron Jones. Jones ground out over 100 yards rushing (23/105, 4.6 ypa) when the Vikings needed him to be a bell cow, absorbing some big hits including a big helmet-to-helmet shot, while also holding on to the ball in adverse conditions. Defensive Secondary. On a day when one slip on a sloppy field could have cost the game, the Vikings defensive secondary provided next to nothing for Caleb Williams to capitalize on down the field. Tyson Bagent was able to take advantage of a prevent defense on the last drive to hit some shots down the field, but other than that the Bears didn’t have much success in their downfield passing game. Kevin O’Connell . While the execution was limited by Carson Wentz and the weather- in that order- KOC had the team well-prepared to win a tough road game in sloppy conditions. No turnovers, few penalties, and just enough playmaking on both sides of the ball to prevail. It wasn’t pretty, but 2-0 with both wins over division opponents starting a backup quarterback is impressive. Stock Down Demond Claiborne . Claiborne was active for the Bears game but seems to have been eclipsed by DeeJay Dallas on the depth chart. He only played two snaps on offense. Buy The Vikings ability to leverage situational football, special teams, and turnovers to make up for otherwise poor offensive production. The Vikings are 2-0 despite an offense that ranks last in total yards and most yards-based metrics. Sell The Vikings offensive production. Granted it was poor conditions in Chicago on Sunday, but for the second straight week the Vikings offense has been fairly anaemic in its ability to drive the field and score touchdowns. The Vikings rank last in total yards after two weeks. That’s not a recipe for success the rest of the season. Buy Carson Wentz as a capable backup quarterback. Sell Carson Wentz as a starting quarterback. Buy Playing on grass. I’m not a zealot when it comes to grass or turf, but most players prefer a well-prepared grass surface and I get that. Slide once on turf and you understand the difference. Sell Playing on a soggy, rain drenched Soldier’s Field. I’m not that nostalgic for old-school football when it comes down to it, at least the bad weather variety. It makes for a frustrating, lackluster game most of the time. And this type of field adds to injury risk. They say hamstring injuries are more likely on this type of field and guess what- there was a high profile hamstring injury. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

title: Vikes Views: Sunday King – Vikings at Bears
summary: The Minnesota Vikings visited the Chicago Bears and the result was the same as it has been for quite a while now: a Vikings victory. Minnesota has now won seven consecutive games at Soldier Field, a stadium that used to be a house of horrors for Vikings fans. The offense never really found its rhythm, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 2026: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Dallas Turner (15) chases Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) out of the pocket in the fourth quarter at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois, on Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) The Minnesota Vikings visited the Chicago Bears and the result was the same as it has been for quite a while now: a Vikings victory. Minnesota has now won seven consecutive games at Soldier Field, a stadium that used to be a house of horrors for Vikings fans. The offense never really found its rhythm, but the defense more than made up for it. Brian Flores’ unit was all over Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent from start to finish. The pass rush consistently disrupted the pocket, the secondary kept everything in front of them, and the Bears struggled to generate any explosive plays. It wasn’t flashy; more like an old school NFC Central matchup. The Vikings played great defense, won the field position battle, controlled the line of scrimmage, and found a way to leave Chicago with another win and that’s all that matters. Dallas Turner Turner finished with four quarterback hits and two sacks, and those numbers hardly tell the whole story. He lived in the Bears’ backfield all afternoon, and if not for Caleb Williams’ ability to escape pressure, Turner might have added two or three more sacks to his total. This is exactly what the Vikings envisioned when they selected him in the first round. His game-clinching sack of Tyson Bagent was the perfect ending to another dominant performance. Jalen Redmond Redmond’s third-quarter play may have been the biggest moment of the game. His forced fumble on D’Andre Swift completely changed the momentum and prevented what looked like a potential scoring drive. Redmond continues to be a disruptive force in the middle of the defense, creating opportunities for others while making plenty of plays himself. His impact doesn’t always show up on the stat sheet, but it was impossible to miss in this game. Isaiah Rodgers Rodgers delivered two of the biggest plays of the afternoon. His blocked field goal in the fourth quarter helped preserve the Vikings’ lead at a critical moment. Earlier, he recovered the fumble forced by Redmond near the goal line, preventing the Bears from capitalizing on a scoring opportunity. He also turned in another strong performance in coverage against an offense that had put up impressive numbers the previous week. Brian Flores I had high expectations for this defense entering the season. I had no idea it could be this good. Flores has built one of the most disruptive defenses in football. The pass rush comes from everywhere, the secondary is disciplined, and opposing quarterbacks rarely look comfortable. The unit has been so dominant that there are times I feel more confident when the defense takes the field than when the offense does. The Vikings’ defense has become the identity of this team, and Flores deserves enormous credit for what he has built. It’s hard to imagine anyone doing a better job than he has this season.
author: Craig Williams

title: Vikings vs. Bucs odds: Opening lines for Week 3 matchup
summary: With their trip to Soldier Field for this season firmly in the rear view mirror, the Minnesota Vikings will start preparing for their second road trip of the 2026 season as they will head to central Florida to face off with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 3. They’ll be heading to much warmer climates, […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Caleb Banks #95 of the Minnesota Vikings walks off the field as he celebrates the 9-3 win against the Chicago Bears following the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images With their trip to Soldier Field for this season firmly in the rear view mirror, the Minnesota Vikings will start preparing for their second road trip of the 2026 season as they will head to central Florida to face off with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 3. They’ll be heading to much warmer climates, and they’ll be traveling as a road favorite as the week begins. Our friends from the FanDuel Sportsbook have opened up the lines for this week, and they currently show the purple as a 2.5-point favorite over the Buccaneers, with the over/under currently resting at 43.5 points. Chat live throughout the game Enjoy fewer ads Jump easily between communities Comment and post faster Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . The Vikings are one of just four teams in the NFC who currently sit with a 2-0 record after Week 2 (though the New York Giants can join them if they win on Monday Night Football this evening). They held the Chicago Bears out of the end zone on Sunday afternoon, as three Will Reichard field goals and a last-second defensive stop were enough to help them escape from Soldier Field with a 9-3 victory. That also gives them a 2-0 mark in the NFC North after their first two games, as they defeated the Green Bay Packers in Week 1 at U.S. Bank Stadium. Minnesota will likely have Kyler Murray back at quarterback by the time the face off with the Buccaneers. Murray played just 11 snaps in the opener against Green Bay before departing with a concussion and did not clear the league’s concussion protocol before the Chicago game. Carson Wentz has stepped in and engineered victories in each of the past two weeks. The Buccaneers have gotten off to an 0-2 start, losing in consecutive weeks to AFC North opponents. They lost to the Bengals in Cincinnati in Week 1 by a final score of 33-27, and followed that up on Sunday by losing their home opener to the Cleveland Browns, 23-19. The Bucs/Browns game had some odd circumstances, as Tampa had an opportunity to drive for a game-winning score, and had gotten inside the Cleveland 30 with all three. Then, at the two-minute warning, the game went into a weather delay that stretched for over two hours due to thunderstorms in the Tampa area. After the game resumed, the Tampa Bay drive stalled out, and when Baker Mayfield’s pass on fourth down fell incomplete, the Bucs took their second straight loss to start the season. The weather certainly doesn’t appear that it will be a factor this Sunday. Initial forecasts are pointing to temperatures in the upper 80s in central Florida for this one under partly cloudy skies. The Vikings are favored to move their record to 3-0 this coming Sunday against what could be a desperate Tampa Bay Buccaneers team, folks. Do you agree with that assessment?

title: Patriots vs. Steelers snap counts from Week 2
summary: The New England Patriots entered their Week 2 game against the Pittsburgh Steelers with the task of replacing A.J. Brown, who had suffered a high-ankle sprain in the season opener. Among the candidates to fill Brown’s spot as a starting outside receiver was second-year man Kyle Williams, the speedster who looked good in preseason and […]
full_text: The New England Patriots entered their Week 2 game against the Pittsburgh Steelers with the task of replacing A.J. Brown, who had suffered a high-ankle sprain in the season opener. Among the candidates to fill Brown’s spot as a starting outside receiver was second-year man Kyle Williams, the speedster who looked good in preseason and entered the year poised for a bigger role. He keeps waiting for it, however. Versus Pittsburgh, after all, Williams’ role remained unchanged: he served as a rotational package player on offense, taking the. field for just 11 of 55 offensive snaps — a similar share than last week versus the Seahawks. Williams did manage to reel in a 10-yard pass on a 3rd-and-6 in the third quarter for his first catch of the season, but other than that and an incomplete target in the fourth period was quiet. To replace Brown, the Patriots instead relied on a three-receiver package of Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas and Mack Hollins. It was the same grouping they used down the stretch in Week 1. Even though the season is still long and Brown reportedly expected to miss five more games after this one, it seems Williams’ position on the depth chart is set in stone for now. Here is our full snap count report from the Patriots’ 20-3 win at Gillette Stadium . Offense Total snaps: 55 | Time on the field: 26:16 | *denotes starter QB Drake Maye* (55; 100%), LT Will Campbell* (55; 100%), LG Alijah Vera-Tucker* (55; 100%), C Jared Wilson* (55; 100%), RT Morgan Moses* (51; 93%), TE Hunter Henry* (50; 91%), RG Greg Van Roten (40; 73%), WR Mack Hollins (39; 71%), WR Romeo Doubs* (37; 67%), RB TreVeyon Henderson (33; 60%), WR DeMario Douglas* (26; 47%), RB Rhamondre Stevenson* (20; 36%), FB Reggie Gilliam (20; 36%), RG Mike Onwenu* (15; 27%), TE Cameron Latu (14; 25%), WR Kyle Williams (11; 20%), TE Eli Raridon* (11; 20%), WR Efton Chism III (10; 18%), RB Corey Kiner (4; 7%), RT Caleb Lomu (4; 7%) Injuries were one of the biggest stories of the game, and the Patriots offense suffered two of them. The most significant was starting right guard Mike Onwenu, who exited the game in the late first quarter due to what was later reported as a broken ankle. With him out, veteran Greg Van Roten — who arrived in training camp — was moved into the top lineup between center Jared Wilson and right tackle Morgan Moses. The other injury was suffered by rookie tight end Eli Raridon, who suffered a tight injury in the first half and was later ruled out for the remainder of the game. This means increased opportunities for Cameron Latu, another late addition to the roster. Latu played his first 14 snaps on offense against the Steelers, primarily serving as an in-line run blocker. Speaking of firsts, Caleb Lomu also played his first offensive snaps. The first-round draft pick replaced the aforementioned Morgan Moses for the final four snaps of the game. As opposed to Onwenu and Raridon, Moses was not removed from the game due to injury. Elsewhere on offense, TreVeyon Henderson out-snapped Rhamondre Stevenson following the latter’s first-quarter fumble. Efton Chism, meanwhile, played his first 10 snaps of the year after being a healthy scratch in Week 1; another byproduct of the A.J. Brown injury. Defense Total snaps: 70 | Time on the field: 30:51 | *denotes starter LB Robert Spillane* (7o; 100%), LB Christian Elliss* (7o; 100%), CB Christian Gonzalez* (7o; 100%), S Kevin Byard III* (7o; 100%), CB Marcus Jones* (69; 99%), CB Charles Woods (60; 86%), ED Elijah Ponder* (54; 77%), ED Gabe Jacas (49; 70%), S Craig Woodson* (46; 66%), DT Milton Williams* (44; 63%), DT Christian Barmore* (36; 51%), DT Cory Durden* (34; 49%), S Jaylen Reed (28; 40%), DT Joshua Farmer (24; 34%), ED Dre’Mont Jones* (18; 26%), ED Quintayvious Hutchins (16; 23%), DT DaQuan Jones (10; 14%), CB Channing Canada (2; 3%) New England’s safety depth was tested against the Steelers. Under normal circumstances, Craig Woodson would have played more than his 46 snaps, but the shoulder injury he suffered in the third quarter forced him to exit the contest. The nominal next man up, Dell Pettus, had already exited the game at that point: Pettus suffered an ankle ailment in the second period. This meant that Jaylen Reed saw his first defensive snaps since arriving in Foxborough via trade in late August. The team also had to rely on its youth on the edge. With Dre’Mont Jones being lost for the game in the second quarter, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas ended up playing 54 and 49 snaps, respectively. In the meantime, Qunitayvious Hutchins also saw his first career reps on defense. The same was true for Channing Canada, who briefly replaced fellow cornerback Marcus Jones in the late second quarter. Outside of his brief injury scare, however, Jones was on the field for every snap; with Carlton Davis inactive due to injury, the Patriots made the veteran slot their No. 2 cornerback opposite Christian Gonzalez. In base sets, he lined up outside while kicking in in nickel and dime looks while Charles Woods was brought onto the field. Elsewhere, recently-signed DaQuan Jones played 10 snaps in his Patriots debut. Special teams Total snaps: 25 | Time on the field: 2:53 TE Cameron Latu (21; 84%), LB Namdi Obiazor (20; 80%), S Jaylen Reed (18; 72%), LB Darius Muasau (16; 64%), CB Channing Canada (16; 64%), FB Reggie Gilliam (14; 56%), CB Karon Prunty (13; 52%), ED Gabe Jacas (12; 48%), LB Erick Hunter (12; 48%), CB Charles Woods (11; 44%), K Andy Borregales (10; 40%), DT Cory Durden (9; 36%), ED Elijah Ponder (9; 36%), ED Quintayvious Hutchins (9; 36%), LS Julian Ashby (9; 36%), P/H Mitch Wishnowsky (9; 36%), WR Efton Chism III (8; 32%), CB/PR Marcus Jones (8; 32%), S Dell Pettus (8; 32%), OT Will Campbell (5; 20%), OT Caleb Lomu (5; 20%), OL Alijah Vera-Tucker (5; 20%), OL Greg Van Roten (5; 20%), OL Ben Brown (5; 20%), S Craig Woodson (5; 20%), DT Milton Williams (4; 16%), DT Christian Barmore (4; 16%), LB Robert Spillane (2; 8%), WR/KR Kyle Williams (1; 4%), WR Mack Hollins (1; 4%), OL Mike Onwenu (1; 4%) The Patriots used five players on their core-four special teams units, with Cameron Latu, Namdi Obiazor, Jaylen Reed, Darius Muasau and Gabe Jacas the only ones playing on kickoff return, kickoff coverage, punt return, and punt coverage. Latu, Obiazor, Muasau and Jacas all registered tackles among them, with the latter adding his special teams performance to an already strong defensive showing. New England’s injuries also impacted the kicking game personnel. One position stands out in that regard: Dell Pettus (1), Craig Woodson (2) and Jaylen Reed (1) all saw snaps as the personal punt protector. Did not play QB Tommy DeVito While the Steelers decided to insert their backup quarterback, Mason Rudolph, in the late fourth quarter, the Patriots did not use their QB2 on Sunday. For a second straight game, Tommy DeVito remained on the bench throughout the contest. Inactive QB3 Behren Morton, TE Tanner Arkin, OT Dametrious Crownover, OL Walter Rouse, DT Leonard Taylor III, CB Carlton Davis III With only one practice squad elevation — punter Mitch Wishnowsky — the Patriots declared just six players as inactive for Sunday’s game. Two of those were ruled out because of injury: Dametrious Crownover and Carlton Davis were unavailable for the contest due to their respective knee and neck injuries. The other four were all healthy scratches, including Tanner Arkin and Leonard Taylor; both were on the game day roster in Week 1 but demoted against the Steelers.

title: Patriots position grades from Steelers win in Week 2
summary: Thanks to a 20-3 win over the visiting Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, the New England Patriots are in the win column for the first time this season. They got there on the back of an excellent defensive performance: the unit outscored Pittsburgh’s offense on the day and had future Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers […]
full_text: Thanks to a 20-3 win over the visiting Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday, the New England Patriots are in the win column for the first time this season. They got there on the back of an excellent defensive performance: the unit outscored Pittsburgh’s offense on the day and had future Hall of Fame quarterback Aaron Rodgers post an abysmal -0.416 expected points added per play, 31st in the league in Week 2. Needless to say, and like we already discussed previously, there were some standout performances. After watching the tape, however, here are our film review notes and position grades from the Patriots’ victory. Patriots film review from NFL Week 2 Quarterback: Did Drake Maye play the best game of his career on Sunday? No. Is it time to hit the panic button, though? Far from it. While he statistically once again failed to perform at his 2025 Pro Bowl level — 14-of-22 (63.3%), 208 yards, 1 INT — the third-year quarterback still had some good moments despite being under pressure on a whopping 51.9% of dropbacks and the Steelers throwing some curveballs his way in terms of blitz usage and man coverage rate. He managed to minimize unnecessary risk while also extending plays, keeping his eyes downfield, and delivering some explosive throws. Coming off a disastrous season opener and despite a rough interception off his back-foot in the third quarter, this was a step in the right direction. | Grade: C + Love these "dash" passes the #Patriots are running to get Maye on the move. Looks like they flooded the quarters side of cover six for a 63-yarder to Doubs. Getting Maye on the move and answers to cover six. 👌 pic.twitter.com/HcF5BpGJb0 — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) September 20, 2026 Running back: Rhamondre Stevenson’s first-quarter fumble after a short reception was a disappointing start, but the Patriots’ running back group as a whole actually performed well in Week 2. Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson and Corey Kiner combined to gain 119 yards on 24 carries for a healthy average of 5.0 yards per rush. Henderson’s 39-yard touchdown was the group’s biggest play and the highlight of a successful overall season debut, but the player to find the most consistent success — outside of his turnover and a quarterback hurry given up — was actually Stevenson: he was the only member of the group to finish with a positive EPA per carry number (0.30) in his six rushing attempts. | Grade: B+ Wide receiver: The first game without A.J. Brown was a mixed bag for New England’s wide receiver group. Relying mostly on Mack Hollins, Romeo Doubs and DeMario Douglas, the group finished with eight catches for 131 yards — among them a 63-yard pickup from Doubs in the second half — but was also unable to create consistent separation or make impact plays on a steady rate. In fact, its best moment outside of the Doubs big play actually might have come in the blocking department: Douglas managed to take out two defenders in one key block on TreVeyon Henderson’s long touchdown run in the first quarter. The Patriots also need more from Kyle Williams, who continues to play a limited role even with Brown unavailable. | Grade: C – Tight end: Combining to catch four passes for 70 yards, Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon both had big plays against the Steelers. The former hauled in a 29-yarder on New England’s first drive, while the latter caught a 30-yarder in the late first quarter to help set up a field goal. Unfortunately, for the group, it also had some issues. Henry had a rough time as a blocker both in the run game and on an unsuccessful screen pass to Efton Chism, while Raridon was unable to finish the contest because of a thigh injury. Third tight end Cameron Latu had some ups and downs in the blocking department as well, which might have prompted the Patriots to bring four free agents in for workouts at the position. | Grade: B Offensive line: The Patriots made sure not to let Pittsburgh’s talented outside linebacker group take over the game, and they did so by using plenty of chips and double-teams on the edge. Will Campbell and Morgan Moses both performed well in that setup, even though the latter missed a cut block on the sack that got Mike Onwenu hurt in the late first quarter. Speaking of Onwenu, his departure with a reported ankle fracture was a watershed moment for the line. The group had looked mostly okay before he left, but his replacement Greg Van Roten had issues in what was admittedly a challenging setup. An exacerbating factor was Jared Wilson not playing his bet football at center, particularly in pass protection. On the bright side, Alijah Vera-Tucker bounced back from his Week 1 struggles and played with some tenacity as a run blocker. | Grade: C+ Hello Alijah Vera-Tucker. pic.twitter.com/M6DdIwl1le — Matt St. Jean (@mattstdream) September 21, 2026 Defensive line: With Dre’Mont Jones departing due to a shoulder injury , depth remains a question along New England’s edge (to a point where even Milton Williams even was asked to line up in a two-point stance). At least on Sunday, however, the group’s youngsters — mainly Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas — were mostly up to the challenge and made multiple big plays: Ponder had a sack and fumble recovery for a touchdown, while Jacas hurried quarterback Aaron Rodgers on multiple occasions and picked off a pass that popped up in the air. On the interior, Christian Barmore and Milton Williams were only credited with one pressure each, but they managed to free up gaps for second-level blitzes and repeatedly collapsed the pocket up the middle. Barmore and Joshua Farmer also registered sacks, with the former forcing the fumble that was recovered by Ponder for the score. | Grade: B + Linebacker: Defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr used an aggressive plan against Aaron Rodgers and the Steelers offense, and it included sending the off-ball linebackers on blitzes on several occasions. Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss finished with a combined 22 pass rush reps, and they notched with five quarterback pressures including an Ellis strip-sack along the way. They also limited the damage in pass coverage — in fact, Spillane even ran with DK Metcalf down the seam at one point — and where active pursuing ball carriers in the run game. Both looked decisive with their reads and quick pulling the trigger when attacking downhill. It was a promising outing from the two. | Grade: A- Spillane running with DK Metcalf on the seam-splitter as the pole runner in cover two to force a check down. A linebacker running with DK Metcalf. pic.twitter.com/lVc1qbQ7cL — Evan Lazar (@ezlazar) September 21, 2026 Cornerback: Even though Carlton Davis missed the game with a neck injury, the Patriots continued to play their fare share of man coverage against the Steelers. This speaks for the coaching staff not being afraid of Pittsburgh’s receiving talent, but also for the trust it has in Christian Gonzalez to simply remove whoever he is going up against. On Sunday, that was DK Metcalf, and Gonzalez had him flustered all day to a point where he dropped a pass on one of the rare reps he managed to get a step on the Pro Bowl cornerback. Other than that, the highest-paid cornerback in football was in lockdown mode throughout the day. The other cornerbacks were not quite as successful — Germie Bernard in particular had some wins against Charles Woods and Marcus Jones — but the performance as a whole was still very good. | Grade: A- Safety: Losing Craig Woodson two thirds into the game and Dell Pettus also not being able to finish it put pressure on New England’s safety corps , and forced late-August trade acquisition Jaylen Reed into the lineup. The Patriots like Reed’s progression , but his lack of experience in the system and chemistry with his fellow defensive backs is evident. He also missed a tackle while filling in for Woodson, who had looked good before his injury. Kevin Byard was solid as well, but he did get flagged for pass interference to negate a third-down stop. | Grade: C+…
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: Mike Vrabel admits he ‘blew it’ on uncharacteristic penalty against Steelers
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers managed just three points in the Patriots’ 20-3 victory on Sunday. The lone field goal came, in part, due to a coaching mistake by Mike Vrabel. Near the end of the first half, Patriots cornerback Marcus Jones stayed down with an injury, which triggered an automatic timeout for New England. Before the […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Foxborough, Massachusetts, USA; New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel talks with officials in the second half of the game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Bob DeChiara-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Pittsburgh Steelers managed just three points in the Patriots’ 20-3 victory on Sunday. The lone field goal came, in part, due to a coaching mistake by Mike Vrabel. Near the end of the first half, Patriots cornerback Marcus Jones stayed down with an injury, which triggered an automatic timeout for New England. Before the following snap, Vrabel called a consecutive timeout, resulting in a delay of game penalty. Jones was injured on a play that Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth appeared to be tackled inbounds at the Patriots’ 47-yard line. However, Freiermuth was ruled out of bounds. The penalty then moved the Steelers to the 42-yard line, where a four-yard pass with 12 seconds left in the half set up a 56-yard field goal by Chris Boswell. “I blew it,” Vrabel said Monday morning. “Injury timeout. I was all caught up on the fact that they should’ve been winding that play, which again, I don’t understand. Clearly his shin came down in bounds, and so in my haste to try to correct the officials, the injury timeout under two goes on us, and then we were going to see what they ran and I called timeout. “So yep, I blew it, and I was hoping to try to convince the official to run the clock, and then the injury stopped the clock. So, that went in as a team timeout under two minutes.” While a similar penalty could hurt the Patriots in a more competitive game moving forward, all it did on Sunday was cost the defense a chance at a shutout. It was otherwise a dominant showing from New England’s defense, which blitzed Aaron Rodgers at nearly a 50% rate to help generate four sacks and a pair of turnovers. “Our identity needs to be about affecting the quarterback. It needs to be about creating turnovers and being able to force teams into longer yardage situations,” Vrabel said. “If that, each week, requires us to pressure, then I think that’s what we’ll try to do. If we feel like it doesn’t, I think we’re multiple enough to be able to do that based on what we feel like it is each week. So, we know that you have to affect the quarterback, you have to be great in the red zone, and you have to be able to create some turnovers.”

full_text: And just like that, the second week of the 2026 NFL regular season is coming to an end. The New England Patriots, of course, entered the action on Sunday by beating the visiting Pittsburgh Steelers at Gillette Stadium, one of 16 total games on the menu over the weekend. title: Patriots bring four tight ends in for workouts following win over Steelers
summary: On the heels of the home opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers, four tight ends visited Gillette Stadium. The New England Patriots had free agents Devin Culp, Tanner Conner, Lance Mason and Patrick Murtagh in for workouts on Monday, according to the NFL transaction wire. Culp, 26, was selected by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 11: Devin Culp #82 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers scores a third quarter touchdown against the Atlanta Falcons at Raymond James Stadium on December 11, 2025 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images) | Getty Images On the heels of the home opener against the Pittsburgh Steelers, four tight ends visited Gillette Stadium. The New England Patriots had free agents Devin Culp, Tanner Conner, Lance Mason and Patrick Murtagh in for workouts on Monday, according to the NFL transaction wire. Culp, 26, was selected by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in the seventh round of the 2024 draft at No. 246 overall. The Washington product, who ran the 40-yard dash in 4.47 seconds while at the NFL Scouting Combine, has since appeared in 18 career games. His Bucs stay brought six receptions for 94 yards and one touchdown before before briefly being retained on the practice squad after August’s 53-man roster deadline. The 6-foot-3, 237-pound Culp has seen 97 snaps on offense and 160 snaps on special teams. Conner, 28, entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent in 2022. The 6-foot-3, 232-pound Idaho State alum made the Miami Dolphins’ 53-man roster as rookie and went on to appear in 33 games while in the AFC East. He finished 2025 on the practice squad of the New York Giants and was released from his futures contract at the league’s cutdown deadline last month. Through 251 snaps on offense and 413 snaps on special teams, Conner’s career has featured one start along with 12 catches for 107 yards. Mason, 23, went undrafted in 2026 after transferring from Missouri State to Wisconsin, where he caught 30 passes for 398 yards and four touchdowns as a senior en route to second-team All-Big Ten honors. Mason was in the fold for the Seattle Seahawks from spring into summer. The 6-foot-3, 243-pound rookie was claimed off waivers by Pittsburgh amid training camp before being part of the NFL cutdown at the end of August. Murtagh, 26, joined the NFL International Player Pathway in 2023. The 6-foot-6, 250-pound tight end by way of Australian rules football made his initial stop with the Detroit Lions that May. He then spent 2024 on injured reserve with the Jacksonville Jaguars after being waived with an injury designation. And last campaign, Murtagh went wire-to-wire as an exempt member of the Denver Broncos’ practice squad before his contract expired in February. No. 95 overall pick Eli Raridon exited in the second quarter of Sunday’s 20-3 win over Pittsburgh with a thigh injury and did not return. With fellow rookie Tanner Arkin among New England’s inactives 90 minutes prior to kickoff, the depth chart was left in the hands of team captain Hunter Henry and waiver claim Cameron Latu. No tight end currently resides on the practice squad in Foxborough after veteran Shane Zylstra was released last week.

(Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Mitch Wishnowsky officially reverted to the New England Patriots’ practice squad on Monday after serving as a standard elevation for the home opener at Gillette Stadium. Sunday’s 20-3 win over the Pittsburgh Steelers marked the second appearance in as many weeks for the veteran punter. Wishnowsky, 34, was called upon for four punts during his latest call-up. The right-footed specialist averaged 46.3 yards per punt with a net of 41.0 yards per. Along the way arrived a long of 54 yards and one effort downed inside the opposing 20-yard line. Holding duties were also part of the afternoon as kicker Andy Borregales went 2-of-3 on field goals and 2-of-2 on extra points. With incumbent punter Bryce Baringer beginning the regular season on injured reserve , the 6-foot-2, 220-pound Wishnowsky signed to the practice squad in Foxborough at its formation. He has since seen 16 snaps on special teams, including no touchbacks, and previously posted 44.3 yards per punt in his 2026 debut versus All-Pro Seattle Seahawks returner Rashid Shaheed. Selected in the fourth round of the 2019 NFL draft at No. 110 overall, Wishnowsky spent six years with the San Francisco 49ers before making stops with the Washington Commanders and Buffalo Bills. Among the league’s 53-man roster cuts in August, the former Ray Guy Award winner by way of Australia, Santa Barbara City College and the University of Utah stands 107 games in. His career has spanned 352 punts for 16,182 yards and a long of 74, plus 236 kickoffs. For Wishnowsky, a third and final standard elevation remains this campaign before a move to the active roster would be required to take the field. The Jacksonville Jaguars host the 2025 AFC champions next Sunday at EverBank Stadium. Kickoff between the 1-1 sides is set for 1 p.m. ET.

title: Patriots’ safety depth to be tested after Craig Woodson, Dell Pettus injuries
summary: Amid a handful of injuries, the New England Patriots lost a pair of safeties in Craig Woodson and Dell Pettus during Sunday’s win over the Pittsburgh Steelers. Woodson appeared to suffer his shoulder injury with 9:54 remaining in the third quarter as he lowered his left side to tackle Steelers running back Rico Dowdle. A […]
full_text: Amid a handful of injuries, the New England Patriots lost a pair of safeties in Craig Woodson and Dell Pettus during Sunday’s win over the Pittsburgh Steelers. Woodson appeared to suffer his shoulder injury with 9:54 remaining in the third quarter as he lowered his left side to tackle Steelers running back Rico Dowdle. A heavy collision left Woodson dangling his left arm. After playing the next third down snap to end the series, he left the field and visited the blue medical tent before departing to the locker room. He was ruled out and was then seen wearing a sling in the post game looker room. Pettus, meanwhile, suffered his ankle injury on a second quarter punt. As the Patriots now begin their preparation for the Jaguars, head coach Mike Vrabel noted the team will likely need safeties on the practice squad to step up. “We have guys on the practice squad. I think some of the veteran practice squad guys are going to factor in this week,” Vrabel said. “I know that Mike Brown has been with us since the spring, and I think that’s the balance that you weigh with the practice squad. We’ve talked about that. You have some young guys that you’re looking to develop, some veteran guys that have played in games that are preparing as a starter and that’ll be ready to go. “So as the week unfolds, we’ll have to make sure that everybody’s ready to go. If guys can’t end up making it, then however we sign guys or elevate guys.” Brown is one of the Patriots’ most experienced practice squad players, signing with New England this offseason with 38 career games under his belt. That included playing in 9 games at safety for Vrabel’s Titans in 2023. New England’s developmental team also includes second-year safety Elliott Davison, who originally joined the team following training camp. With Woodson and Pettus leaving Sunday’s game early, safety Jaylen Reed was thurst into a larger role. After being acquired in a trade for Kayshon Boutte this August, Reed did not play a defensive snap in the season opener. The 23-year old, who has seen an increased comfort level in the defense, was called upon to play 28 snaps (40%) against the Steelers. “I think Jaylen has done a nice job. He’s worked hard,” Vrabel said. “He got put in there – again, we have to be ready to go. He had some plays that were good. He’s helped us in the kicking game. He would go in there at PP [punt protector], that’s not an easy thing to do, so I’m glad that he was prepared and ready to go.”
author: Brian Hines

title: The good, the bad, the s—t that gets you beat from Patriots vs. Steelers
summary: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. The New England […]
full_text: Ahead of his first training camp as Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories: the good, the bad, and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, we shall follow his lead. The New England Patriots have finally broken their five-year streak of losing their home opener. Hosting the Pittsburgh Steelers at Gillette Stadium in Week 2, they managed to outlast their opponent thanks to a stout defensive effort and an offensive display that did enough to secure the eventual victory. With that all being said, let’s dive into our weekly breakdown of the good and the not-so-good from the 20-3 victory on Sunday . The good: Big plays No two game plans are alike, but there was a notable change in the Patriots offense’s ability to generate chunk plays between Weeks 1 and 2. After the longest play against the Seahawks went for just 19 yards, the unit had six plays longer than that versus the Steelers — including a 39-yard TreVeyon Henderson touchdown run and a 63-yard Drake Maye pass to Romeo Doubs that helped set up a field goal. “We talked about creating X-plays offensively, you need great execution and extra effort,” said Vrabel on Sunday. The Patriots got both versus the Steelers, and not just on offense. The defense also followed suit by creating some big plays of its own. Coordinator Zak Kuhr’s group registered its first two takeaways of the season, scoring a touchdown on an Elijah Ponder fumble recovery and later registering a red zone interception courtesy of fellow edge defender Gabe Jacas. In the meantime, the unit managed to prevent Pittsburgh and star quarterback Aaron Rodgers from hitting any explosives of their own. A 26-yard catch-and-run in the fourth quarter was the Steelers’ only gain of 20-plus yards on Sunday. The bad: Maintaining momentum New England’s offensive performance on Sunday can best be summed up with one word: inconsistent. While Drake Maye and company did manage some big plays, they rarely were able to string together multiple positives to consistently keep the chains moving and put pressure on Pittsburgh. For Vrabel, that was a definitive issue. Not just from a performance perspective, but also in terms of the urgency the Patriots showed. “We have to be able to get into a rhythm,” he told WEEI on Monday. “We cannot have mistakes. Once you get to the red zone, negative plays are guaranteed field goals. We learned that. We’ve known that for a long time. The mindset that we want to create is when we make a positive play — like, we had a couple good runs in a row — we need to keep going. “We need to be sprinting back into the huddle, we need to be sprinting out of the huddle to continue that momentum. Or we hit a big play down the field to [Doubs], and it’s like, ‘How do we get a delay of game?’ Guys, get back in the huddle. We want to celebrate, but we also we have to continue the drive and the momentum.” The s—t that gets you beat: Ball security We are probably not going out on too big a limb when we say that the Patriots very well could have won their season opener in Seattle if not for three consecutive interceptions in the fourth quarter. And while the result was a different one on Sunday, their ball security issues reared their ugly head again. Rhamondre Stevenson, who had not fumbled the ball in 13 straight games entering Week 2, put the ball on the ground on the Patriots’ fourth play in the first quarter. The fourth play in the third quarter then saw Drake Maye throw an interception while unsuccessfully targeting a bracket-covered Hunter Henry. Those two turnovers plus the three against the Seahawks means that New England now ranks tied for second-worst in the league in both giveaways (5) and turnover percentage per drive (25.0%). Versus a Steelers team unable to capitalize, those issues were ultimately not consequential to the outcome of the game. Still, with games against the Jaguars and Bills coming up, the Patriots need to clean up their act. “Those things are going to end up costing us,” said Vrabel on Sunday.

title: Are the Saints contenders after beating the Ravens?
summary: It’s time to start taking the New Orleans Saints a little more seriously. That might sound like an overreaction after just two games, but beating the Baltimore Ravens on the road is the kind of win that gets a team’s attention. The Saints entered Baltimore as underdogs and found themselves trailing 14-3 in the second […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints looks to pass while pressure by Trenton Simpson #32 of the Baltimore Ravens in the fourth quarter of a game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s time to start taking the New Orleans Saints a little more seriously. That might sound like an overreaction after just two games, but beating the Baltimore Ravens on the road is the kind of win that gets a team’s attention. The Saints entered Baltimore as underdogs and found themselves trailing 14-3 in the second quarter. Instead of folding, New Orleans completely flipped the game after halftime, scoring the final 15 points to secure a 24-17 victory. Tyler Shough continues to show why there is growing excitement surrounding him as one of the NFL’s next star quarterbacks. He completed 27 of 34 passes for 252 yards and a touchdown while also rushing for 23 yards on nine carries and the game-winning score with under two minutes remaining. Chris Olave added eight catches for 86 yards and a touchdown, while the defense held Lamar Jackson and the Ravens to only three points after halftime. Those are the types of complementary performances that can make a team dangerous. But this is where the overreaction comes in. The Saints are just two games in, and one road victory doesn’t suddenly erase every question surrounding a team that is still figuring itself out. New Orleans also trailed by double digits for the second consecutive week, meaning the team has plenty to clean up despite its ability to respond. Still, there is something different about beating a team like Baltimore in its own building. The Saints now return home for their first game at Caesars Superdome against the 2-0 Las Vegas Raiders. If they can carry the momentum from Baltimore into that matchup, the conversation around this team could change quickly. Are the Saints contenders? It is probably too early to say. But after Sunday, it is no longer unreasonable to ask the question.
