title: Saints LT Kelvin Banks Jr. expected to miss significant time
summary: New Orleans Saints standout second-year tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. is expected to miss significant time after suffering a high ankle sprain in the team’s win over the Baltimore Ravens, per Ian Rapoport. Banks will undergo surgery in the coming days. Banks is a big loss for the Saints, as the former first-round pick has been […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Kelvin Banks Jr. #71 of the New Orleans Saints is carted off the field after an injury against the Baltimore Ravens during the third quarter of the game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images New Orleans Saints standout second-year tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. is expected to miss significant time after suffering a high ankle sprain in the team’s win over the Baltimore Ravens, per Ian Rapoport. Banks will undergo surgery in the coming days. #Saints OT Kelvin Banks Jr suffered a severe high-ankle sprain and is now expected to have surgery to repair it, tests revealed today. He is out indefinitely. Banks, one of the top young OTs, has a chance to return late in the season if all goes well. But a significant loss. pic.twitter.com/Yp0g5hfHha — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 21, 2026 Banks is a big loss for the Saints, as the former first-round pick has been a critical piece of their young core. With Banks set to miss time, Asim Richards is expected to sub in his place. Richards was solid taking over for the starting left tackle in the second-half of Sunday’s game. Banks is expected to miss around 10 weeks, a significant jump from the original expected 4-6 weeks, but will still have a chance to make a return late in the season. With the Saints sitting at a 1-1 record, it’s likely record-dependent if New Orleans decides to try and rush their promising left tackle back. The Saints are coming off a big win and are now reaching the supposed easiest stretch of their schedule. But Week 3 won’t be easy as they face the 2-0 Las Vegas Raiders and their superstar pass rusher, Maxx Crosby. Richards will likely be tested quickly by the Raiders, who will utilize the mismatch. New Orleans’ offensive line has already been spotty through the two weeks of the season, but Banks has been a bright spot. Now without the second-year standout, there may be more questions than answers for the Black and Gold’s offense.
author: Kyle Besson

title: Ups and downs from Saints vs. Ravens
summary: The New Orleans Saints didn’t have to wait long to get their first win of the season. The Saints took down the Baltimore Ravens 24-17, shocking the NFL. Plenty of players stood out in the win, including Tyler Shough and Chris Olave, who added to their strong season. But it wasn’t just the Saints’ stars […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - SEPTEMBER 20: New Orleans Saints tight end Juwan Johnson (83) fights for extra yards during a NFL football game between New Orleans Saints and Baltimore Ravens September 20, 2026 at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore, MD (Photo by Charles Brock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints didn’t have to wait long to get their first win of the season. The Saints took down the Baltimore Ravens 24-17, shocking the NFL. Plenty of players stood out in the win, including Tyler Shough and Chris Olave, who added to their strong season. But it wasn’t just the Saints’ stars who stood out, and lingering problems made their way back into their Week 2 win. Up: WR Devaughn Vele Wide receiver Devaughn Vele had a strong game in the team’s loss against the Detroit Lions. Then, he recorded 7 receptions for 69 yards and a touchdown. The third-year wideout followed his successful performance with a 5-reception game logging 64 yards against the Ravens. Third down has quickly been keyed the term “third-and-Vele.” The 6-foot-5 receiver has been a reliable target, and his ability to survive contact and make receptions has made him a valuable resource to the Saints’ offense. With rookie Jordyn Tyson’s return date approaching, assuming he’ll be ready in weeks five or six, Vele has made a strong case to heighten his snap count. Up: K Daniel Carlson Kicking has been a major problem for the Saints since they traded away Wil Lutz in 2023. Since then, New Orleans has tried plenty of kickers, often going with younger risers. But after Charlie Smyth and Tanner Brown each struggled in preseason and training camp, the Saints brought in veteran Daniel Carlson. Carlson missed a big kick in the team’s Week 1 loss, missing from 62 to win the game. While still a miss, 62 yards is certainly not automatic, but it still left the Saints with a bit of uncertainty at kicker. Carlson shut all of that down, however, during the team’s win over the Ravens. The veteran kicker ended the day making all three of his attempts, with makes from 23 yards, 47 yards, and 51 yards. Carlson proved to be vital in the team’s win, scoring their first nine points, and his veteran presence was what kept the team afloat as the offense finally heated up. Up: TE Juwan Johnson Tight end Juwan Johnson began a larger role with the Saints last season, and once Shough became the quarterback, he started to look like one of the better tight ends in the NFL. Johnson had a strong role in Week 1, catching three passes for 54 yards and a touchdown. While he failed to find the end zone in the win against Baltimore, falling inches short, he probably had a better day in the win. Johnson logged 4 receptions for 66 yards and made critical plays to keep the Saints offense on the field. The highlight of the day for the veteran tight end was a third and eight where Shough found Johnson short. The wide receiver turned tight end was surrounded by three defenders four yards short of the first-down line before making them miss and taking it 25 yards, leading the Saints into the redzone and ultimately to the game-winning touchdown. Down: Slow starts Despite the win, we’ll see another week of concerns about the Saints’ slow starts. New Orleans went scoreless in the first quarter for the second week in a row. The Saints now have six total points through the first half in two games, and 48 points in the second half. The Saints’ second-half adjustments are serious, but they won’t be able to sustain their luck. The offense has to start faster and find the end zone in the first half for the first time this season. The good news is, I think the Saints will be in a better position to get right against the Las Vegas Raiders at home next week. New Orleans is in a good spot right now. They’re tied at the top of the NFC South and are the favorites to win the division. Despite being the favorites, starting slow will prevent the team from winning games and force them to continue playing catchup, which isn’t sustainable. Down: RB Travis Etienne I don’t think the lack of a run game is directly due to Travis Etienne, but the newly signed running back has had a disappointing start to the season. Through two games, Etienne has logged just 17 carries for 71 yards with an average of 4.2 yards per carry. Interestingly, Etienne was outcarried by both Alvin Kamara and Shough in Sunday’s win, raising questions about his role with the team. The Saints signed the veteran running back to a $52 million contract in the offseason, so his role is bound to heat up, but his lack of impact on the game is directly tied to the Saints’ slow starts and vice versa. Once the Saints get the run game right, the offense will be even more lethal. But so far, the run game has been disappointing, and Etienne is at the front of it.
author: Kyle Besson

title: CSC Interview: Chase Daniel talks about his newest partnership, the Saints, LSU and more
summary: Last week, I had the opportunity to interview Super Bowl champion and former New Orleans Saints quarterback Chase Daniel to discuss his partnership with Cheez-It and the upcoming Cheez-It Couch Committee as well as his thoughts on college football, LSU and of course, the Saints. CD: What’s up, Anthony? AP: Hey, Chase, what’s going on, […]
full_text: Last week, I had the opportunity to interview Super Bowl champion and former New Orleans Saints quarterback Chase Daniel to discuss his partnership with Cheez-It and the upcoming Cheez-It Couch Committee as well as his thoughts on college football, LSU and of course, the Saints. CD: What’s up, Anthony? AP: Hey, Chase, what’s going on, man? I am absolutely thrilled to meet you. I’m a diehard Who Dat and I’ve been a fan of yours since you were in Missouri cutting it up, bro. CD : Let’s go. AP: I’m all here for it. So, you got something going on now with the Cheez-It Couch Committee. Tell me a little bit about that partnership. CD : Yeah, so Cheez-It has been showing up at bowl games in the college football playoff for over a decade. So, we said, hey, what’s better than getting the Cheez-It Couch Committee together? Cheez-It literally has this massive orange square couch that looks like cheese. I mean, it is like bright orange, like a Cheez-It. It’s gonna be in November. I’m gonna be sitting on that couch. We’re gonna have a tailgate, and we got fans that can enter a contest at cheezit.com/couchcommittee . And pretty much, we’re gonna talk ball. We’re gonna debate. I was a backup my whole career. I love armchair quarterbacking. I have quarterback breakdowns on YouTube. We’re on TV talking about this and that. But why not do it in person? So, it’s gonna be a massive orange couch, and we’re gonna be kicking it, eating some Cheez-Its. It’s gonna be awesome. AP: Man, that sounds amazing. So, first of all, who came up with the concept for a giant Cheez-It couch? CD: Dude, the Cheez-It team is unbelievable. And it is like the sickest couch you’ve ever heard. AP: I can’t wait to see it. AP: So, this is a rentable couch? CD : Dude, they made it. Yeah, it’s crazy. AP: So, you were literally a star quarterback at Missouri. Clearly, you understand the importance of college football, the culture, game day traditions. Why does all of that matter so much for college football? Describe it from your, from a player’s perspective. CD: You know, I spent so long in the NFL where fans are crazy, fans are fun, and games sometimes can be like a wine and cheese crowd, where they’re just going to show up, they’re just like here to be seen and to see people. College football fans are crazy in all the good ways. Like, they are diehard. Ready to go, the pomp and circumstance, the pageantry, the band, the cheerleaders, like all that stuff. In the bill doesn’t have that stuff. So as a diehard fan, dude, like getting back into college football the last two years, it’s been really cool. I’ve, like, literally become a fan all over again. And so to have this out of tailgate with Cheez-It, like, to me, it’s awesome. AP : That’s amazing. So, with that being said, the Cheez-It, the couch, college football fans… blending all these things together. Why is this such a unique situation with the couch itself being such, like, the ultimate seat centered around college football? CD : Yeah, that’s a good call, because I think if you can’t make it to the game, what do most fans that don’t go to games, what do most fans do on Saturday? They sit on a couch, and they’re always have these hot takes of I could do that. Or I could do this, and what’s this guy doing? This ref sucks, like all this stuff. And so why not bring it live and in person outside of a stadium? And you’re literally sitting on the couch, and we’re talking face to face. You’re not talking to screens like we’re doing right now. AP: Awesome. So, we’re going into Week 3 of the college football season. What has been some of the things that have stood out to you the most and what’s your biggest prediction for the rest of the season? CD: Wow, that’s tough. I think one of the things, the SEC has the deepest quarterback class in the country of any college conference. And quite honestly, it’s not even close. I’m not just talking about the top three, I’m talking about from, in general. The other thing is Sark in Texas, they’re for real. Huge win, program-defining win for Sark over Ohio State, program-or career-sort of-defining win for Arch Manning. Look, I know it’s early. But to be able to get past your demons that you had last year with Ohio State and how bad you played and how much stuff you got in the media, all this stuff, it was just, you could tell, like, it was weight lifted off of shoulders. And I would say the biggest thing at the end of the year, I’m gonna say the SEC does not go four years in a row and gets the national championship. AP : All right, since we’re on the SEC, let’s talk about the marquee matchup of the weekend that’s coming up. You’ve got Lane Kiffin, LSU. What are your thoughts on him being an LSU, and how do you think everything unfolds in Oxford this Saturday night? CD : Yeah, it’s a good call. I don’t know if Ole Miss’s secondary can handle the passing game of Sam Leavitt and Charlie Weiss Jr. and Lane Kiffin. That’s what I’m gonna be focusing on the most, because when you watch it, Sam Leavitt has not been an efficient passer this year whatsoever. Can you get the pass game going? Can the Rebels defense actually hold LSU to less than 40 points? I think Trinidad Chambliss on the other side. That’s the most intriguing matchup to me. Trinidad versus that LSU Blake Baker defense, which is blitzing left and right, has been fantastic through the first couple weeks. I, I think those are the two matchups to do. I wouldn’t be surprised if LSU wins. However, I think it’s gonna be a lot closer than you think. AP: I want to get your thoughts on Tyler Shough and the Saints. You literally were brought up under Drew Brees. You were led by a Hall of Famer. So, you have a really good perspective on this. How do you see Tyler Shough’s career going? How do you see him now entering into his second year as really the guy in New Orleans, knowing how much the Saints mean to the city? CD: They found their guy. They found their second coming. I’m not going to say of Drew Brees. No one can do that. But it’s been a hard road for Saints fans since Brees has left and retired and I think that they have found their franchise guy, without a doubt. Love how he played against the Lions, like played really bad… but there’s, you know, some stuff that goes on in the first half of the game, but then in the second half, third quarter, fourth quarter, overtime, bringing them back, driving them down the field, throwing for over 400 yards. That game, even though they didn’t win, I love the fact that they went for two. Even though they didn’t win, I think that they ended up with a feeling in that sort of team that, hey, this is our guy, we have our guy. We’re gonna be better, the Saints are gonna be better than a lot of people think. NFC South, the whole gamut’s 0-1. They’re gonna be better than people think. And so, how do we continue to build on that performance? AP: And finally, Missou, Eli Drinkwitz, got a stacked running backfield. What are your expectations for your alma mater this season? CD : Man, they gotta win some games. They gotta win games that they’re not supposed to win, but they gotta win games that they’re SUPPOSED TO win. There’s a big difference in that. That’s how you end up at the season with eight, nine, ten wins. When you pull some out that you’re really not supposed to, but then you win all the ones that you’re supposed to. A lot of, you know, questions about the offensive line, defensive line. We’re gonna get that sorted out going into, to SEC play, but I’m super excited about seeing what’s happening. AP : Chase, what else do you have to say about Cheez-Its, your partnership with them, and the rest of college football? CD: Yeah, remember cheezit.com/couchcommittee. If you’re a college football fan with friends who love to debate, just enter the contest at cheezit.com/couchcommittee . It’s gonna be awesome. AP: Awesome, man. Thank you so much for your time, Chase. I look forward to seeing everything you and the Cheez-It brand have…

title: Game Recap: Saints visit Ravens in Week 2 clash
summary: The New Orleans Saints were looking to grab their first win of the 2026 regular season on Sunday as they paid a visit to the Baltimore Ravens. Here’s a full recap of all the action. First Quarter The hosts began the game by going three-and-out, but the Saints only managed a short series of their […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Devontez Walker #81 of the Baltimore Ravens catches a pass against Martin Emerson #22 of the New Orleans Saints during the second quarter of a game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints were looking to grab their first win of the 2026 regular season on Sunday as they paid a visit to the Baltimore Ravens. Here’s a full recap of all the action. First Quarter The hosts began the game by going three-and-out, but the Saints only managed a short series of their own as Tyler Shough was sacked on 3rd down in his own half. Lamar Jackson and the Ravens offense got going after that. He found Mark Andrews, Derrick Henry, and Rashod Bateman for big gains en route to the red zone. Henry did the rest of the work on the ground from there, capped off by a 1-yard touchdown run to give Baltimore a 7-0 advantage. Penalties hampered the visitors’ efforts on their ensuing drive, but Shough did find Devaughn Vele to move the drive near midfield before the quarter’s end. Second Quarter The Saints were quickly in 3rd-and-long territory back in their own half after having to recover their own fumble and were forced to punt. Jackson then connected with Devontez Walker for 47 yards to overcome poor field position, before finding LaJohntay Wester for 14 more. But a big sack from Chase Young helped limit the series to a field goal attempt from 49 yards out, which Carl Granderson was able to block to keep the score at 7-0. Shough had his first chunk play of the afternoon on the ensuing possession, finding Vele for 29 yards. A few plays later, he found Olave for 11 more, as Alvin Kamara also had a few short gains on the ground in his season debut. The Ravens defense was able to keep New Orleans out of the end zone, but a 23-yard chip shot from Daniel Carlson got the visitors on the board. With less than 4 minutes on the clock as they regained possession, Jackson and Henry began to run at will. The Saints defense was quickly pegged deep into their own territory before Bateman caught a 22-yard touchdown pass to extend the hosts’ lead to 14-3 just before the half. However, despite having just 24 seconds to work with, Barion Brown returned the kickoff near midfield to give the Saints a chance. Shough would then connect with Vele to reach field goal range, and Carlson was good from 47 yards as time expired. Third Quarter Travis Etienne Jr began the half with an 8-yard run, and a 25-yard pass a few plays later from Shough to Juwan Johnson moved the Saints into Baltimore territory. New Orleans had no luck from there, though, and settled for another field goal. Carlson’s 51-yard kick cut the lead to 14-9. After nearly fumbling on the kickoff return, Baltimore embarked on a mammoth 14-play drive that went for just 37 yards. A mix of third-down conversions and offensive penalties resulted in an extended possession that never got near the end zone. Chase Young and Nathan Shepherd split the sack that forced Baltimore into a field goal, which Tyler Loop converted from 49 yards. With the score at 17-9, both teams proceeded to go three-and-out, with a big sack from Pete Werner on Jackson helping the Saints defense win the ball back for the offense as the third quarter ended. Fourth Quarter Shough completed his first four passes on the ensuing drive for 31 yards as New Orleans drove down near the red zone. His fifth attempt was the touchdown strike, finding Olave for a 21-yard score. The two-point conversion attempt to tie the game was initially unsuccessful, but a defensive holding penalty gave the Saints another go at it. The second time around, they got it done as Etienne ran it in to tie the game at 17-17. Baltimore proceeded to go three-and-out at a bad time, giving New Orleans the opportunity to take their first lead late in the game. Shough continued to find a variety of receivers, including a 15-yard pass to Olave and a 7-yard connection with Kevin Austin Jr. Etienne and Kamara also had a few short runs, and Vele caught a few short passes of his own. And on 3rd-and-8, Shough came up with the big play of the drive on a 25-yard pass to Johnson to set up 1st-and-goal. Johnson was found again by Shough but was marked just short of the goal line. Shough then tried to run it himself and was marked short before finally, on 4th down, the quarterback just barely broke the plane to score the game-winning touchdown for the black and gold. The Ravens had 88 seconds with which to respond, but Julian Blackmon picked off Jackson to secure the 24-17 comeback victory for New Orleans. Kellen Moore’s squad now heads home 1-1, where they’ll finally host the Las Vegas Raiders in their home opener this weekend.

title: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly from the Saints win against the Ravens
summary: The Good: Tyler Shough and Chris Olave Shough and Olave once again had a great day, as Shough threw for 252 yards and Olave went for 86 yards while the pair connected for the game tying touchdown. Juwan Johnson and Devaughn Vele also had very good days, as they each converted a few tough third […]
full_text: The Good: Tyler Shough and Chris Olave Shough and Olave once again had a great day, as Shough threw for 252 yards and Olave went for 86 yards while the pair connected for the game tying touchdown. Juwan Johnson and Devaughn Vele also had very good days, as they each converted a few tough third downs and had 60+ receiving yards in their own right. Shough is the NFL’s passing yards leader through two games and Olave trails only Jaxon Smith-Njigba in receiving yards. This combination is only going to continue to get better as the season goes along, as after two tough road games to start the year the Saints now have three very winnable games in the Superdome over the next three weeks before they head to New York and then Paris. The Bad: Rushing offense The Saints trailed much of the game, so they did not need to rely on the ground game that much, but even still they did not produce much in that area this week. As a team they ran 27 times for 65 yards which is an average of 2.4 yards per carry. This is going to be a problem if they manage to get a lead early in some of their next few games against weaker opponents and need to milk the clock a bit, as so far through two weeks the Saints and new addition Travis Etienne Jr. are averaging just 3 yards per carry on the ground. The Ravens and Lions both have above average run defenses, but still we need to see a bit more considering how good we know Etienne and Alvin Kamara can be. The Ugly: Another slow start The Saints started slow again on Sunday, thankfully not as slow as they did last week in Detroit but they still eventually needed a +15 point fourth quarter to secure the win. The defense kept it close throughout as they had a very good day and deserve a lot of recognition for the win. The offense managed just three field goals through the first three quarters before turning it on in the fourth. They did not have any turnovers like last week but only had one drive of more than 50 yards before the fourth quarter. While exciting, this is a dangerous game to be playing week in and week out, and lets hope that the Saints returning home against lesser competition will have them take and hold a lead throughout a game rather than having to rely on fourth quarter comebacks most of the time.

After opening the 2026 season with back-to-back road games, the Saints will make their long-awaited return to the Caesars Superdome on Sunday afternoon when they host the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 3. And they are returning home with plenty of momentum. New Orleans comes into this game after getting a shocking 24-17 victory over the Baltimore Ravens, a matchup that very few expected the Saints to win. After trailing 14-3 in the first half, the Saints once again showed their resilience and battled back to score 15 unanswered points in the fourth quarter to secure their first victory of the season. Quarterback Tyler Shough continued to show why the Saints have so much confidence in him, completing 27 of 34 passes for 252 yards and a touchdown. He then delivered when it mattered most, scoring the go-ahead touchdown on a 1-yard quarterback sneak with 1:28 remaining in the fourth quarter. Chris Olave caught eight passes for 86 yards, including a 21-yard touchdown that tied the game at 17. But it was Julian Blackmon who sealed the Saints’ victory, intercepting Lamar Jackson on Baltimore’s final drive with just 20 seconds remaining. Now sitting at 1-1 after two difficult road games, the Saints finally get the opportunity to play at home in front of the Who Dat Nation, with kickoff against the Raiders set for 3:25 p.m. CT on Sunday. There will also be a familiar face on the opposing sideline, as former Saints offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak returns to New Orleans now as the head coach of the Raiders. According to FanDuel, the Saints are currently 3-point favorites against the Raiders, with an over/under of 43.5 points. However, those odds could move as kickoff approaches. title: Jaxson Dart injury, Rams provide NY Giants with a reality check
summary: The big thing everyone connected with the New York Giants is thinking about in the wake of Monday’s lopsided 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams is the health of quarterback Jaxson Dart. The Giants appear to have dodged the worst possible news, with the expectation that imaging on Tuesday will confirm a sprained MCL. […]
full_text: The big thing everyone connected with the New York Giants is thinking about in the wake of Monday’s lopsided 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams is the health of quarterback Jaxson Dart. The Giants appear to have dodged the worst possible news , with the expectation that imaging on Tuesday will confirm a sprained MCL. Monday’s outcome, though, exposed a number of things about the 2026 Giants that we have to talk about, and that they have to be concerned about. Let’s look at some of the ‘things I think’ as the Giants try to move on and get ready for a Week 3 game against the Tennessee Titans. We have to start with Dart. Not the worst case, but not good “We’ll know more when we find out more,” Giants coach John Harbaugh said after the game. Harbaugh did allow that there was “no question” that seeing Dart moving around on the sideline after the game and believing his injury wasn’t season-ending was comforting. “The fact that it’s not that outcome that you’re talking about, the devastating outcome, is really good news,” he said. Dart’s injury had nothing to do with all of the ongoing chatter about him not being willing to protect himself by sliding or getting out of bounds when he runs, something he actually did do in Week 1 against the Dallas Cowboys. Dart got hurt in the pocket, which, thanks to the NFL rulebook, is actually the safest place for quarterbacks. There is nothing the rules can do, though, to prevent getting sandwiched between two pass rushers and getting your knee inverted in a manner in which it’s not meant to bend. Maybe Dart misses two weeks. Maybe he misses six. The Giants, driven hard by Harbaugh this spring and summer, are about to best tested in a way they hoped not to be this season. Giants players have seen and dealt with injuries before. They were saying the right things after the game. Winstn did admit losing Dart was a “gut punch” in the moment. “You get ready to play another one,” Winston said of what the Giants do now. “You got another opponent and they don’t care.” “We’re going to continue to practice hard, get out there, be more intentional about what we’ve got to do, what we’ve got to accomplish. Rally around Jameis ,” said Malik Nabers. “For us to come in here and … get punched in the face, you have to get back up and keep going,” right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said . “There’s still 15 more rounds.” The bigger issue, beyond how long Dart will be out, is that Monday night exposed many truths about the 2026 Giants. Let’s get to them. Pump the brakes on expectations I have been warning for months not to expect a New England Patriots-like turnaround from 4-13 one year to 13-4 and a Super Bowl-berth the next. The most optimistic outcome I could summon for the 2026 Giants when asked to make a prediction was 9-8. Yet, after an impressive season-opening victory over the Dallas Cowboys national analysts were jumping the bandwagon and fans were dreaming big dreams. The Rams brought those out-sized expectations crashing down to earth. Matthew Stafford, Davante Adams, Aaron Donald, Sean McVay and the rest of a supremely talented Rams’ roster showed the Giants and a national football audience what a Super Bowl-contending teams looks like. It ain’t the Giants. The floor has been raised with the accomplished John Harbaugh as head coach. The eventual ceiling? Unknown, but the Rams exposed a number of things that have to be dealt with to find out. What are some of those things? Running the ball without Dart The Giants averaged 2.5 yards per rush Monday night. Through two games, they average 3.7 yards per carry, 22nd in the NFL. Take out Dart’s 11 carries for 54 yards in Week 1, that average dips to 3.5 yards. The Giants’ longest non-Dart run in two games is 13 yards. The Giants are built to be a run-first team, and that has to get better. After a turnover games the Giants the ball on the Rams’ 11-yard line they ran four times (including a 3-yard loss negated by a Los Angeles penalty), got nowhere, and settled for a deflating field goal when down 14-0. Do they have the interior blocking or the backs to make that better? Maybe, but they need to be better than they were Monday. The Andrew Thomas injury might complicate matters. The Giants were outclassed up front by the Rams. Plus, they had several plays where the timing and execution were off, with players running into each other. The pass rush The simple question is, where is it? This is an incredible stat: Per @NextGenStats the Rams had a pressure rate of 58.6% tonight. The Giants, after all of their investment in the Edge group over the years, somehow ended up at 15.2% — Brett Kollmann (@BrettKollmann) September 22, 2026 The Giants have just one sack and five quarterback hits in two games. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson wants to rush just four, which isn’t a horrible goal considering the state of the secondary, but through two games Dak Prescott and Matthew Stafford have stood in the pocket and done basically whatever they wanted to do. The Giants’ sack percentage of 1.52 is worse than every team in the league except the Miami Dolphins. With Brian Burns injured, fixing that quickly won’t be easy. About that secondary Who knew at the start of training camp that the Giants would miss Tae Banks as much as they did last night? Cornerbacks Colton Hood and Greg Newsome, along with safety Tyler Nubin, were not up to the task of defending Davante Adams. The linebackers and safeties weren’t up to the task of covering tight end Terrance Ferguson. There are no easy fixes. Dream about a Joey Porter trade if you must, but the Giants really need an offseason where they can add talent via free agency and the draft. Run defense One week after an impressive performance vs. Dallas, the Giants allowed the Rams to run for 163 yards on 28 carries, 5.8 per rush. Through two games, the Giants are giving up 5.0 yards per rush, 28th in the NFL. Talent-wise, this is another area the Giants are going to have to Band-Aid, duct-tape, and scheme around until they can get to the offseason and try to add more young talent. It was disturbing to see 2025 second-round pick Darius Alexander, who simply does not seem to be improving as a run defender, inactive. The Giants used journeyman Josh Tupou, a practice squad player who appeared in six games with the Ravens the past two seasons, and C.J. Okoye, a Nigerian-born defensive tackle who knew nothing about football until 2023, instead of Alexander. Not a good sign. The upcoming schedule Not that long ago, the upcoming four games (vs. the Tennessee Titans, vs. the Arizona Cardinals, at the Washington Commanders, vs. the New Orleans Saints) was looked at a stretch where the Giants might be able to run off some victories. Now? Maybe it is still a softer part of the schedule, but there isn’t any certainty that the Giants will be able to take advantage of it. My last thought is this: Months of good vibes that began when Harbaugh was hired crumbled on Monday night with the Dart injury and the reality check provided by the Rams. The season, as Eluemunor indicated, will be defined by the next 15 rounds. Do the Giants have the ability to punch back? We’ll find out.

title: 4 things we learned from the Giants’ 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams
summary: A few years ago, John Mara warned Head Coach Brian Daboll after his surprising first season as Giants head coach that it doesn’t take long to go from Bono to Bozo. Daboll found out how true that was the next season and beyond. John Harbaugh has something much closer to Bono’s portfolio, and his team’s […]
full_text: A few years ago, John Mara warned Head Coach Brian Daboll after his surprising first season as Giants head coach that it doesn’t take long to go from Bono to Bozo. Daboll found out how true that was the next season and beyond. John Harbaugh has something much closer to Bono’s portfolio, and his team’s resounding opening week victory over Dallas had fans singing, “It’s a beautiful day.” But in the NFL, it’s what have you done for me lately? Would Giants fans be singing again after facing the Super Bowl-contending Los Angeles Rams, or would they be saying, “I still haven’t found what I’m looking for”? Bozo it is. The Rams brought the Giants back down to earth with a 28-6 victory that wasn’t as close as the score indicated. What did we learn from this thrashing? The game is won in the trenches. Part I The Rams’ defensive line wasted no time letting the Giants’ offensive line know what a real pass rush looks like. The Giants took the opening kickoff, and they did move the ball for a little while, but only in fits and starts. Right from the start, Dart felt pressure. He did complete a (poorly thrown) pass to Isaiah Likely, who made a nice adjustment for a 5-yard gain, and on the next play Dart went to Malachi Fields with another poorly thrown pass for 14 yards that Fields made a great play on to catch. That’s the sign of a quarterback who is afraid to step into his throws. After an incompletion to Theo Johnson (a recurring theme tonight and in every game, it seems) and a short Skattebo gain, Dart threw long but incomplete to Theo again. He had an excuse for that, though, because both Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor were beaten, by edge defenders Josaiah Stewart and Byron Young. The Rams’ rushers made a Dart sandwich and Dart’s knee was pushed inward, causing him to leave the game. Overall the Rams pressured Dart on half of his dropbacks, and that was without Aaron Donald doing very much…except stopping Skattebo near the goal line the one time the Giants threatened. Of course the double teams he faced helped the rest of the Rams’ defensive line win their one-on-one battles. The Giants used to have a guy called Dexter Lawrence who did that. As a result of this, the pressure wasn’t just coming from the outside. It came up the middle too, so much so that after Jameis Winston entered the game he looked afraid to really step into his throws, leaving many of them short. This wasn’t the good Jameis we saw in Detroit last year. It was the bad Jameis, short-arming and throwing right to defenders. Getting beaten by the Rams’ defensive line wasn’t restricted to the passing game. The Giants rushed 21 times, for only 52 yards. Cam Skattebo did his best trying to bounce off the first defender to hit him, but he only gained 36 yards on 12 rushes. Najee Harris, seeing his first action, gained only 6 yards in four carries. Inexplicably, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy had him in there carrying the ball the one time the Giants got inside the 10 instead of Skattebo. On third-and-2, Harris was tackled for a loss by Aaron Donald. And this suggests what might be a theme for the entire season. This is not a Giants team that is built to play from behind. Last week they were able to dictate to the Dallas defense, stay ahead of them most of the night, and use the running game to grind the Dallas defense down. Falling behind early against the Rams, we saw that the Giants’ receivers didn’t get open much. It didn’t help that Winston was short-arming the ball or throwing off his back foot, but this looks like a team that needs to win the first half to thrive. The game is won in the trenches. Part II Correct me if I’m wrong, but I believe the Giants were supposed to have a fearsome pass rush this season. Abdul Carter did get one sack, but that was it. Matthew Stafford was able to sit back there in the pocket and look at tourist photos from Australia if he’d wanted to. Meanwhile, the Rams’ running backs carried the ball 24 times for 164 yards. Much of it early on was between the tackles, but as the game wore on, the Giants’ old problems of setting the edge reared their ugly head again. To make matters worse, Brian Burns came off the field with an ankle injury late in the game. Was Dennard Wilson the defensive coordinator tonight, or did they bring Shane Bowen back? The inability to get to Stafford, or even put pressure on him on a consistent basis, led to the realization of the Giants’ worst fear… The Giants’ secondary is not up to the task Granted, any secondary is up against it when the pass rush doesn’t pressure the quarterback. But the Rams’ receivers, even with Puka Nacua sidelined, embarrassed the Giants’ secondary. Davante Adams had 8 receptions in 10 targets for 195 yards and 2 TDs, and on most of them he was so wide open it was ridiculous. Tight end Terrance Ferguson caught six balls in nine targets. There were occasional good plays, including another interception plus two forced fumbles by Jevon Holland, and even passes defensed by Tyler Nubin and Greg Newsome II, but more often, Rams receivers were catching the ball with no Giant within five yards of them. In particular, when you see Adams downfield and Nubin the one defending, you know it’s not going to end well. The secondary gets a bit of a pass because Deonte Banks and Paulson Adebo were out with injuries, but it’s not as if either one is considered a Pro Bowl threat. The bottom line is that any game in which the Giants’ front seven does not dominate this season is probably going to be a loss. At least the Giants have a kicking game After making all 4four extra points in his first game, kicker Dominic Zvada made both of his field goal attempts tonight, including a 52-yarder, and both were pretty much down the middle. Meanwhile, Jordan Stout averaged 52.5 yards on his (unfortunately) six punts, three of them inside the 20 and one of them for 78 yards. Hopefully there will be games this season in which they can be a factor in a Giants win. That may be as soon as next week, when the Giants face a Titans team that was looked at as an easy W but which doesn’t look that way anymore.
author: Anthony Del Genio

title: Brian Burns, Andrew Thomas injuries add to Giants’ misery
summary: As if the New York Giants needed more bad news on Monday night, star players Brian Burns and Andrew Thomas suffered injuries late in the Giants’ lopsided 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Thomas, the team’s left tackle, suffered a groin injury. Burns was helped off the field with what appeared to be a […]
full_text: Brian Burns | Getty Images As if the New York Giants needed more bad news on Monday night, star players Brian Burns and Andrew Thomas suffered injuries late in the Giants’ lopsided 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. Thomas, the team’s left tackle, suffered a groin injury. Burns was helped off the field with what appeared to be a left ankle injury. Per John Harbaugh after the game, Burns has a low ankle sprain. Jordan Raanan of ESPN reports that Burns was wearing a boot and being driven to the team bus on a golf cart. The good news is that Burns was able to leave the field under his own power, which demonstrates that his ankle was stable enough to walk on and bear his weight. That suggests either a Grade 1 or Grade 2 sprain, per Harvard Health . A Grade 1 low ankle sprain has a recovery time of 1 to 3 weeks, while a Grade 2 sprain has a recovery time of 3-6 weeks. Typically treatment for a low ankle sprain involves a RICE (Rice, Ice, Compression, Elevation) regimen, resting the ankle as much as possible for the first 24 to 48 hours, and icing regularly. Given that the Giants need to travel from Los Angeles to New Jersey, the use of a boot isn’t much of a surprise and shouldn’t be particularly alarming at this point. As with Jaxson Dart , we’ll get more information on his prognosis as the week unfolds. Thomas has had an injury-plagued career, but has been healthy all spring and summer until now. Burns is coming off a career-best season. He was seen at the end of the game on the bench with a wrap on his left ankle. The Giants also had an injury scare with wide receiver Malik Nabers in the second quarter, but he returned to action after having his shoulder checked. These are all cornerstone players for the Giants that they cannot afford to be without. We will get more information on all of the injuries, especially Dart’s, as soon as it becomes available.
author: Ed Valentine

title: Rams 28, Giants 6: Instant position-by-position grades for New York
summary: The New York Giants lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart on their first offensive drive, and they failed to gain much offensive rhythm after Dart’s seven offensive plays that went for 27 yards. New York failed to get anything going on the ground, and Jameis Winston looked overmatched in relief of Dart. The Giants only had 182 […]
full_text: The New York Giants lost starting quarterback Jaxson Dart on their first offensive drive, and they failed to gain much offensive rhythm after Dart’s seven offensive plays that went for 27 yards. New York failed to get anything going on the ground, and Jameis Winston looked overmatched in relief of Dart. The Giants only had 182 yards on offense, and the Rams rumbled for 481 yards, while averaging eight yards per play. Los Angeles went 5 of 9 on third down and the Giants 3 of 14. The Rams had the football for five minutes and ten seconds more, but their explosive plays complied, as the Giants’ offense sputtered all night after Dart’s injury. The Giants suffered multiple injuries in the loss, but they’ll have to quickly regroup on a short week. Brian Burns hurt his ankle late in the fourth quarter. It was just a brutal game for the Giants from many perspectives. Here are the grades. Quarterback The Giants lost Jaxson Dart on their first offensive drive. Dart was ruled out in the second half, and it was a devastating blow to the Giants’ nation. Jameis Winston looked lost through the first half. He went 4 of 12 for 58 yards with a terrible interception in the red zone. Winston didn’t improve until the Rams were up by three-plus scores well into the second half. Winston finished 11 of 27 for 111 yards while suffering two sacks and throwing an interception. It was the worst I’ve seen Winston as a Giant. Dart was 3 of 5 for 20 yards before the injury. Grade: D Running back Jevon Holland forced a fumble late in the first half, which gave the Giants excellent field position and a chance to split the Rams’ lead in half. Matt Nagy decided to roll out a package with Najee Harris on second and third down, with the third down play being in 11 personnel. It was a handoff, too, and it was a massive tackle for a loss that led to a Dominic Zvada 24-yard field goal. With no Jaxson Dart, Nagy kept his best running back on the bench in a critical situation – that’s a HIGHLY questionable situation. The Giants averaged a measly 2.5 yards per carry. Skattebo finished with 12 carries for 36 yards; he added four catches for 19 yards. There was no room on the ground, and the backs couldn’t get much goiung. Grade: C Wide receiver The loss of Dart hurt the offense, and Malik Nabers battling a shoulder injury that held him out for several plays didn’t help the overall chances of the Giants to win the game. The Giants offense went into a shell once Winston entered the game. Darnell Mooney had a few plays over the middle of the field, but the receivers were not receiving quality looks from Winston. Mooney led the Giants with 48 receiving yards on two catches, while Fields hauled in two balls for 30 yards. Odell Beckham Jr. was not targeted, and Malik Nabers caught one of his four targets for one yard, and left in the first half with a shoulder injury. He returned, but the game got out of hand. Grade: C – Tight end Dart’s injury stifled their passing attack. Theo Johnson had an opportunity to secure a Dart pass on the play he was injured. Johnson did an excellent job high-pointing the football over two defenders, which was very impressive, but, unfortunately, Johnson could not secure the football. Isaiah Likely was targeted ten times and caught five for 33 yards. Grade: C – Offensive line Jon Runyan’s holding penalty ended an early potential scoring drive for the Giants. The offensive line struggled all night. They opened a few lanes for Cam Skattebo and the Giants’ rushing attack, and their pass protection was suspect. Obviously, the injury to Dart changed the Giants’ game plan, but the offensive line was just getting beat by the Rams’ front. John Michael Schmitz, just like last week with Devin Singletary against man coverage, was late to his assignment at the second level and a screen ended in a loss, when a massive gain was attainable if that block was executed. Jermaine Eleumunor was beat bad by Byron Young on a valuable third-down in the third quarter, which led to Zvada’s second field goal of the game. Grade: D Defensive line Chauncey Golston forced a holding penalty and had a few disruptive plays up front, and the Rams weren’t establishing the run too well for much of the game, but Stafford had too much time to pass too often. A lot of the Rams’ rushing success was to the outside, and D.J. Reader had a few nice STOPs near the line of scrimmage. Still, the line didn’t do enough to make a difference. Grade: C + Edge Matt Stafford had WAY too much time in the first half. He sat comfortably in the pocket and delivered too many passes beyond 20-yards. New York HAS to receive more from their pass-rush. Carter did sack Stafford by splitting a double-team, but the Giants’ surrendered 21 yards on the following play to Terrance Ferguson. The Giants were also shaky on the edge against the heavier personnel packaged Rams. Kayvon Thibodeaux lost contain on a 21-yard Williams scamper in the third quarter. New York surrendered the edge several times in the second half. What’s possibly most consequential from the game is the injury to Brian Burns, who got rolled up on in garbage time. The Giants need to get more from this position group. Grade: F Linebacker Kyren Williams caught a touchdown as the third receiver releasing to the boundary toward the two receiver side. Arvell Reese stayed tight toward the in breaking route of the No. 2 receiver, and Reese allowed Williams to find a soft-spot between himself and Colton Hood, where Williams caught the ball for an easy score. This was Reese’s second mistake in coverage that resulted in a touchdown. The Terrance Ferguson touchdown was over the head of Tremiane Edmunds. The middle of the field was more vulnerable versus the pass as well. Stafford found back side dig routes and other in-breaking routes in front of over-pursuing safeties, but just behind linebackers. The coverage was an F for the Giants’ linebackers, but they were adequate against the run. Edmunds did, however, knock a pass away as a blitzer late in the third quarter. Grade: D Cornerback Matt Stafford and Davante Adams were having success against quality cover plays by Greg Newsome III and other Giants’ cornerbacks. Colton Hood wasn’t terrible, but there were plays where he looked like a rookie, specifically the Davante Adams touchdown pass in the third quarter in the red zone. Greg Newsome III was forced to shadow Adams after Hood surrendered the touchdown. Grade: C – Safety Tyler Nubin had a beautiful tackle at the line of scrimmage early in the first quarter, but he was the defender that contacted Davante Adams on the veteran’s first quarter touchdown. Nubin was then toasted in coverage on Matt Stafford’s long 64 yards third-and-nine conversion; the third-year safety bit on an Adams’ double-move. Nubin lost leverage and over-pursued on several other coverage snaps. Jevon Holland, however, was one of the biggest difference makers for the Giants’ defense. He intercepted Matt Stafford as the middle-of-the-field closed safety and then punched the football loose from Kyren Williams on the subsequent Rams’ drive. Holland is living up to the off-season hype. Holland than forced a fumble against Blake Corum in the fourth quarter. It’s strange to give a grade to the safety position with Holland having a great game but Nubin having one of the worst by a Giants’ safety in some time. Let’s split the diff and give the position a C. Nubin was attacked all game, but he did knock one pass away from Ferguson late in the third quarter, although Nubin was beaten on the play. Grade: C Special teams Jordan Stout is an asset. Poor blocking up front forced Stout to punt it into the end zone on the Giants’ second drive, but he was lucky to get the football off; his third punt, though, sailed for 61 yards. Stout also booted a 58-yarder after the Giants’ failed first drive of the second half. Field position becomes more important when injuries take effect on offense. Unfortunately for the Giants, that…
author: Nick Falato

title: NY Giants-Rams winners and losers: Well, Jevon Holland and Jordan Stout had good nights
summary: As much as we may not want to, let’s review the New York Giants’ humbling 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night in our unique ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ style. Kudos to … Jevon Holland — The veteran safety had an interception and then a forced fumble/fumble recovery on back-to-back snaps in […]
full_text: Jameis Winston vs. the Rams. | Getty Images As much as we may not want to, let’s review the New York Giants’ humbling 28-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night in our unique ‘Kudos & Wet Willies’ style. Kudos to … Jevon Holland — The veteran safety had an interception and then a forced fumble/fumble recovery on back-to-back snaps in the first half. The fumble recovery gave the Giants the ball at the Rams’ 11-yard line, but they could only convert that into a field goal. Holland forced another fumble in the fourth quarter. Jordan Stout — Yes, this is one of those games where we end up talking about what an amzing weapon the Giants’ punter is. But, well, he is an amazing weapon. Stout punted six times for an average of 52.5 yards per put. He had a 78-yard punt from deep in his own end zone and a 61-yard punt, as well as three punts downed inside the 20-yard line. He was ridiculously good Monday night. Dominic Zvada — The rookie placekicker made the first two field goals of his NFL career, the second of which was from 52 yards. Wet Willies to … Jameis Winston — The Giants’ backup quarterback wasn’t good at all in relief of the injured Jaxson Dart. He looked unsettled all night. He was off target and unsure. He looked a lot like a quarterback who had worked very little with the first team, which he hadn’t. Winston finished 11 of 27 for 111 yards passing and an interception. If Dart is going to miss time, which seems likely, Winston needs to be better than that. Much better. If not, the Giants are going to have a difficult time winning games. Pass protection — Dart got hurt in the pocket, which is supposed to be the safest place for a quarterback, when he got sandwiched between defenders. Winston never looked like he was sure he would be protected in the pocket, and sometimes he wasn’t. The Rams had just two sacks of Giants’ quarterbacks and eight overall hits, but there was disruptive pressure all night. The running game — The Giants managed just 52 yards on 21 carries, 2.5 yards per attempt. They desperately need a running game, especially if Dart is sidelined, and couldn’t generate one Monday. After taking over following a Jevon Holland fumble recovery at the Rams’ 11-yard line, the Giants ran the ball four times (including a play that didn’t count because of a Los Angeles penalty), got to the 6-yard line, and kicked a field goal when trailing 14-0. Not good. The interior of the Giants’ offensive line seemed overmatched much of the night. The secondary (other than Holland) — Thank goodness Puka Nacua didn’t play! The Giants couldn’t cover the star wide receiver who did play for the Rams, Davante Adams. He educated rookie Colton Hood, and was too much for everyone who tried to cover him. Adams finished with 8 catches for 195 yards and 2 touchdowns. The Giants couldn’t cover tight end Terrance Ferguson, either. He finished with 6 catches for 54 yard, and a touchdown. Pass rush — Abdul Carter got a sack. That was about it for the Giants’ pass rush. In fact, that is about all the supposedly terrorizing pass rush has done in two games. Matthew Stafford threw the ball 31 times Monday night. The Giants sacked him once and hit him two other times. That’s it. And, that’s not nearly enough. The Football Gods — Are the Giants simply not supposed to have nice things? Are there fans not supposed to be allowed to have more than fleeting feelings of optimism? Jaxson Dart, Andrew Thomas, Brian Burns, and Malik Nabers all getting hurt in the same game is ridiculous. Maybe none of these things is, as Harbaugh said, “life-threatening.” Still, though, an awful night for a team that has generated such good vibes thus far. title: Jaxson Dart injury: NY Giants’ QB suffers left knee injury vs. Rams
summary: New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart went down with a left knee injury on the team’s first drive Monday night against the Los Angeles Rams. Initial reports are that the injury is believed to be a sprained MCL. Dart will undergo an MRI on Tuesday. “We’ll know tomorrow,” head coach John harbaugh said after the […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart comes off the field after suffering a knee injury Monday night. | Getty Images New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart went down with a left knee injury on the team’s first drive Monday night against the Los Angeles Rams. Initial reports are that the injury is believed to be a sprained MCL . Dart will undergo an MRI on Tuesday. “We’ll know tomorrow,” head coach John harbaugh said after the game. “That’s [MCL sprain] in the neighborhood of it, I would say.” Dart was sandwiched between Rams defenders Byron Young and Josaiah Stewer on a third-and-8 incompletion to Theo Johnson from the Rams’ 41-yard line. Dart did walk slowly off the field under his own power. Dart has been ruled out. GM Joe Schoen told ESPN that the quarterback is “going to be OK.” ESPN’s Jordan Ranaan reported that Dart wanted to return to the game . After the game, Giants running back Cam Skattebo confirmed that Dart wanted to get back into the game. He added that he thinks Dart will be back on the field ‘In the next few weeks’. "He told me he wanted to get back out there and the doctors kind of told him no… he told me what was happening. I'm going to leave that to him and the doctors and stuff. I think he'll be alright here in the next few weeks." – Cam Skattebo on Jaxson Dart's injury pic.twitter.com/kLLHVpY3xe — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) September 22, 2026 We’ll know more once Dart has his MRI on Tuesday. Per the Cleveland Clinic , MCL tears usually heal well on their own without surgery, provided there’s no other damage. That Dart was able to walk off and stand on the sideline without crutches is a good sign. If his MCL sprain was a Grade 1, he could be back in 1 to 3 weeks, with a Grade 2 sprain needing 4 to 6 weeks to heal with treatment. Hopefully it was a Grade 1 sprain and there was no other damage, and he’ll be back sooner rather than later. Jameis Winston took over at quarterback for the Giants on their second offensive series. Dart protecting himself from big hits and concussions has been a constant story. This, though, was a hit from the pocket after which his left knee appeared to bend in an awkward manner. Dart limped slowly to the locker room after being checked in the medical tent. John Harbaugh had this to say about Dart’s injury during a brief halftime interview: “We’re just focused on the second half, trying to find a way to win the game. We’re not thinking about that right now.” Dr. David Chao, a former NFL team doctor who goes by @ProFootballDoc on X, offered a quick take on the injury. Not expecting season ending Hard to return but not surgical injury Foot off the ground saves him🙏 https://t.co/qXROCLhts9 — David J. Chao – ProFootballDoc (@ProFootballDoc) September 22, 2026 Here’s more from Dr. Chao: Good news for Jaxson Dart: By video, I do not believe he suffered a season-ending ACL tear. The concern is an MCL sprain, an injury likely measured in weeks, not months. The MRI will determine the severity. pic.twitter.com/6uS1bteswL — David J. Chao – ProFootballDoc (@ProFootballDoc) September 22, 2026 Several starting quarterbacks have already suffered injuries this season. That list includes Sam Darnold of the Seattle Seahawks, Jayden Daniels of the Washington Commanders, and Caleb Williams of the Chicago Bears. We will have more on Dart’s injury when it becomes available.

summary: Former New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton signed with the Indianapolis Colts on Monday evening. You might have missed the news due to Monday Night Football, but the Colts have rekindled the relationship between Daniel Jones and Slayton. The Colts needed a big, athletic deep threat following the injury to Alec Pierce on Sunday, […]
full_text: Former New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton and quarterback Daniel Jones. | Getty Images Former New York Giants wide receiver Darius Slayton signed with the Indianapolis Colts on Monday evening. You might have missed the news due to Monday Night Football, but the Colts have rekindled the relationship between Daniel Jones and Slayton. The Colts needed a big, athletic deep threat following the injury to Alec Pierce on Sunday, and quickly turned to the former Giants’ receiver. Slayton and Jones were both drafted by the Giants in 2019 and had an immediate chemistry, and Slayton led the Giants in receiving in four of his first five seasons (2019, 202, 2022, and 2023). Even apart form his pre-existing chemistry with Jones, Slayton would be a solid replacement for Pierce, thanks to his uncommon blend of size and speed. The Colts could use a deep threat to open things up for TE Tyler Warren and RB Jonathan Taylor. Meanwhile, the Giants could use the wide receiver depth with Malik Nabers playing through a shoulder injury.

title: Jets vs. Packers: When will we see the progress?
summary: So frequently over the last decade and a half, the definition of success for a Jets season has been nebulous. With regime after regime attempting rebuild after rebuild, the team has frequently begun a season with low expectations. The 2023 and 2024 seasons with Aaron Rodgers are the only from the last decade where the […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 20: Skyy Moore #23 of the Green Bay Packers celebrates after scoring a touchdown during the second half of the game against the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on September 20, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images So frequently over the last decade and a half, the definition of success for a Jets season has been nebulous. With regime after regime attempting rebuild after rebuild, the team has frequently begun a season with low expectations. The 2023 and 2024 seasons with Aaron Rodgers are the only from the last decade where the Jets were viewed as a team that had a legitimate chance to make noise in the AFC heading into Week 1. Phrases, “You can’t judge this team solely by its record,” and, “We need to see progress,” have become staples of Jets preseason analysis in recent years. In broad strokes, these statements have largely been fair. The rosters the Jets have put on the field just haven’t been very good. They have been full of holes and flawed young players hoping to develop with extensive game reps. What has bothered me is that over and over the concept of rebuilding has been used as a blanket excuse to rationalize all of the team’s shortcomings. If we are judging the Jets on progress, shouldn’t there actually be tangible progress throughout the season? There’s a pretty large middle ground between expecting the Jets to immediately go from the bottom of the league to the Super Bowl and accepting any and all failures because the team isn’t a contender. That brings us to Week 2 as the Jets fell to the Green Bay Packers 20-17 in overtime. On paper it was easy to pencil this game in as a loss. Green Bay has been one of the league’s most consistent franchises recently with trips to the Playoffs in six of the last seven seasons. Surely the Packers should be expected to handle a rebuilding team. That’s logical enough in theory, but the Packers were dealing with pretty significant injury issues. They also were not in top form, looking shaky in their Week 1 loss to the Vikings. And the Jets got Green Bay in their home opener at MetLife Stadium. The Jets were never going to be favored over the Packers at any point when these two teams play in 2026, but it’s tough to imagine this matchup happening at a more favorable time for New York. Making progress for a rebuilding team isn’t just about winning the few games you are expected to win like Week 1 against Tennessee. It means occasionally punching above your weight class and stealing a game you aren’t expected to get. Heading into the day, the Packers appeared potentially ripe for the picking. By the time the game started, it was clear this was the case. Green Bay was anything but sharp. The Packers committed 14 penalties and otherwise were sloppy with miscue after miscue. Simply put, it felt like they were trying to hand the Jets this game. The Jets weren’t exactly sharp themselves. They had to work around two wasted timeouts in the first half and a bad challenge that left them without a timeout in an end of half situation where the time expired on them while driving. The offense struggled to gain traction, struggling in the trenches. There wasn’t much room for Breece Hall to run, and Geno Smith was erratic. The Jets had their own penalty issues, and couldn’t so much as jump on fumbles right in front of them. Still, they cobbled together enough production when combined with Green Bay’s struggles to gain a 17-7 lead in the fourth quarter. What better way for the Jets to show progress than closing this game out? What followed can only be described as a classic late game collapse. It began with the Packers backed up on a first and 25 due to two penalties. Matthew Golden got a step or two on Azareye’h Thomas. Jordan Love fired deep. The ball was underthrown. Golden pulled up. Thomas extended his arms and tapped Golden. Golden fell. If Thomas turned his head, it wasn’t much of a head turn. If he contacted Golden, it wasn’t much contact. Still, that’s a situation in the modern NFL where a flag is almost always thrown. The few instances it isn’t, fans of the offensive team scream about the injustice. It was a shame because Thomas was otherwise playing a strong game. Then he was central at the point where the game began to unravel. The Packers scored a touchdown to cut it to 17-14. The Jets got the ball back with around 8:00 left and a chance to put the game away with a long scoring drive. They quickly were forced to punt, and their vaunted special teams failed, allowing a 63 yard return which immediately put the Packers into range for a game-tying chip shot field goal. The Jets got it back with 3:00 left and a chance to win the game. The Jets got to midfield where the drive stalled, stuffed on runs on third and fourth and short. From there, the defense actually came through, tackling Christian Watson short of the sticks after a 5 yard reception on a fourth and 10 with over 40 seconds left. This should have given the Jets an opportunity to win the game in regulation after a Green Bay punt. However, Aaron Glenn inexplicably did not call a timeout after the stop, allowing the Packers to run the clock down with the aid of a delay of game penalty and a rules loophole. The clock went down to 2 seconds, which allowed Green Bay to attempt a low risk Hail Mary. Glenn robbed his offense a chance to win it in regulation. Instead he gave the Packers a chance, even if it was a longshot that failed with a sack. Overtime came. The Jets took the ball, but two of their three plays resulted in sacks, resulting in a punt and a net of -8 yards. From there the result seemed predestined. The Packers drove 58 yards in 5 plays, aided by an undisciplined 15 yard penalty on a late hit by Jarvis Brownlee, Jr. Rookie Trey Smack converted a chip shot 26 yard field goal, and the Packers had an improbable win. After a meltdown like this, I have one simple question to ask. Where is the progress? The Jets let a golden opportunity to start 2-0 for the first time since 2015 slip through their fingers. A victory would have given them a cushion with a challenging two game road trip on the horizon. Beating Green Bay would have guaranteed the Jets entered their Week 5 home date with the Cleveland Browns .500 at worst. Perhaps it could have been a springboard to bigger things. Seven of the sixteen teams in each conference now make the Playoffs. Having one of the top seven records doesn’t require a team to be great or even necessarily good. Opportunistic rebuilding teams sometimes arrive in the postseason ahead of schedule by taking advantage of the chances like this. It would be one thing if the Jets had maintained their level of play from their Week 1 win over the Tennessee Titans. The Packers are objectively a better football team right now. There were scenarios where the Jets played a strong game, but Jordan Love just hit a bunch of tight window passes under duress. Then you’d just have to tip your cap and move on. It’s tough to argue the Jets did anything other than give away a game on this September Sunday in the Meadowlands. Normally a hallmark of progress is young players shining. You can live with losses as a rebuilding team if your future cornerstones play strong games. Again, this wasn’t the case for the Jets. Two of the team’s four highly drafted rookies didn’t play due to injury. Of the other two, David Bailey did register an early sack on a nice play where he first identified a screen, but he was largely ineffective as a pass rusher looking as raw as one might expect a rookie playing his second game to look. Kenyon Sadiq was essentially a nonfactor. Of second year players, Armand Membou struggled, and Mason Taylor was invisible. Thomas had some moments, but that pass interference loomed large. Of course nobody should argue that one bad game should be used to make sweeping judgments on these players. Membou in particular has shown great promise in his…

title: Eagles-Titans Film Review: A very good offense is hiding in here
summary: The Eagles won 24-20, and I came away feeling much better about the passing game than I did after Week 1. The Eagles found answers against the Titans’ coverage, attacked the weaknesses I flagged in my preview (which is always great to see), and repeatedly converted third-and-long. However, the offense cannot keep making life this […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Tank Bigsby #8 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Tennessee Titans with Jalen Hurts #1 during the first quarter of the game at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles won 24-20, and I came away feeling much better about the passing game than I did after Week 1. The Eagles found answers against the Titans’ coverage, attacked the weaknesses I flagged in my preview (which is always great to see), and repeatedly converted third-and-long. However, the offense cannot keep making life this difficult for itself. The Eagles went 11-of-18 on third down, which is an absurd 61.1% conversion rate. That’s why they sustained drives despite averaging only 4.7 yards per play, turning the ball over twice and rushing for 89 yards on 32 attempts. Winning on third down is obviously good. Needing Hurts to repeatedly deliver elite throws on third-and-long isn’t a sustainable offensive identity. The early-down numbers are wild. I mean, come on… The Philadelphia Eagles have the largest difference in early down offensive success rate vs. late down offensive success rate to start a season since 2022, per @SumerSports Early downs: 31.5% (3rd percentile) Late downs: 60.6% (96th percentile) — Shawn Syed (@SyedSchemes) September 20, 2026 The contrast between the pass and run games could not have been clearer. The Eagles produced +0.17 EPA per passing play but -0.20 EPA per rushing play. This was not a perfect offensive performance. But the passing game looked excellent for long stretches. Jalen Hurts and DeVonta Smith were elite. Now Sean Mannion and the rest of the offensive staff must find a way to stop wasting early downs before asking them to rescue the offense. Offense This opening play might be the most Eagles run of all time. The offense comes out in 12 personnel, condenses the formation and invites the Titans to load the box. There is no numbers advantage, no misdirection and no obvious way to manipulate the second level. The Eagles simply run straight into it. What could possibly go wrong? Pretty much everything. Johnny Mundt goes to the ground in hilarious fashion, Dallas Goedert is asked to climb to a linebacker he has little chance of reaching, and the combination between Tyler Steen and Drew Kendall is messy. Because the interior double-team never develops properly, Cam Jurgens cannot work up to the linebacker. Lane Johnson then runs into the traffic created inside and cannot generate movement on his block. It is a calamity of errors, but the design makes every error more likely because the defense can attack downhill immediately. I refuse to post 20 versions of the same failed run, because you all watched the game. The more important question is why this keeps happening. The Eagles ran 79.2% of their offensive snaps from 11 personnel and only 19.4% from 12 personnel. I think that needs to change. Long one. Eagles' Offense All22 Thread vs. Titans. 1) The Eagles start off the game, in the most Eagles way imaginable. I laughed out loud of this. 2 TE, stacked box, failed run. Who saw that coming? Mundt falls over and gets destroyed (in quite amusing fashion). They are… pic.twitter.com/c9T67bccVH — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 21, 2026 I am ready to set fire to the swing-pass section of the playbook. This is not just about one bad play. The whole operation looks slow. Hurts does not have the quickest release on these throws, and the ball often reaches the receiver when he is flat-footed or moving sideways rather than already attacking upfield. That delay gives zone defenders, who are facing the play, plenty of time to trigger and rally to the football. Most modern defenses are playing zone these days, so this look is common Perimeter blocking doesn’t save the concept either. Dallas Goedert is blown up by a cornerback here, and the play has nowhere to go. The Eagles do not currently have a group of dominant perimeter blockers who can consistently turn these throws into efficient gains. They also lost five yards on the swing to Makai Lemon immediately before Hurts’ second interception, transforming second-and-7 into another third-and-12. Screens and swings can be useful answers against pressure or aggressive fronts, but this version threatens no one. Burn it. At least until the Eagles can change the timing, blocking angles, or presentation enough to make it functional. 2) A lot of talk about why the Eagles swing/screen game sucks so much. Lots of the reasons on show here. Hurts doesn't have a particularly quick release, and it takes too long to get it out. The receiver catching the ball often isn't running upfield, which slows him down. And… pic.twitter.com/i0HvBwhw82 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 21, 2026 Now for the fun part. The Eagles loved dagger in this game, and it gave Hurts a clean answer against the Titans’ zone coverage. Marquise Brown runs the vertical clear-out with real intent, forcing the deep coverage to honor his speed, while Dontayvion Wicks pushes his intermediate route beyond the linebackers and settles in the void. That route depth is really good. The linebackers sit around the sticks on third-and-12, so a shallow in-breaker runs directly into them and leaves Wicks short of the line to gain. By getting vertical first, he creates space behind the second level. The offensive line gives Hurts time, and he hits the top of his drop and layers a perfect throw into the middle of the field. The touch is outstanding. Brown deserves credit too. He did not play in Week 1, but he ran these clear-out routes hard and looked fast. Very fast! He also carried the ball twice for 12 yards. I am not demanding he suddenly becomes a featured player, but speed changes the defense even when the ball doesn’t come his way. I would like to see more of him. Is that crazy to say? 3) One of many Jalen Hurts' dimes on 3rd and long. The Eagles loved running Dagger in this game, and shoutout to Hollywood Brown who looked fast as hell on these clear-out routes. For someone who didn't play last week, he ran these hard. The Eagles' OL does a fantastic job, and… pic.twitter.com/cq4xQq6MHm — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 21, 2026 The first interception is a mistake by Hurts, but it is also a fantastic play by Amani Hooker. Both things can be true. The Eagles are trying to isolate Smith by having Goedert pull the middle safety away, and Lemon occupy the flat defender. They create a window, but it never becomes as clean as Hurts appears to expect. Goedert does not remove the safety far enough with a pretty poor route, Smith’s route could be sharper, and Hooker recognizes the concept and drives on the throw brilliantly. Hurts is slightly late and should turn it down. In the red zone, especially, he cannot give the safety this opportunity. It was an enormously costly decision, but I can somewhat understand why he made the throw based on the pre-snap look. What I loved was the response. Hurts did not become conservative or hesitant after the interception. He continued attacking tight windows, trusted what he saw, and played aggressively. Quarterbacks will make mistakes. The good ones don’t let one mistake ruin everything that follows. 4) A rare Hurts INT in the red zone, but it's also a fantastic play by Amani Hooker. Credit where credit is due. The Eagles are trying to create space for the throw to DeVonta Smith by using Goedert to draw the middle safety away, and Lemon to draw the flat CB away. It works… pic.twitter.com/QsxJrTZNU4 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) September 21, 2026 Look at what happens when the Eagles spread the defense out and run away from the strength of the box. This outside zone rep is not revolutionary, but it gives the blockers a chance. The motion forces the Titans to flow in the opposite direction, and Goedert becomes eye candy rather than being asked to execute another difficult block. Steen…
