title: Romello Height becomes the latest 49ers’ rookie to suffer an injury
summary: San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan provided injury updates Monday afternoon. Wide receiver Mike Evans will be managed throughout the week with a hip injury: “Mike’s gotten a lot of work here in the last couple weeks. He’s been able to practice each day since us going down to Australia and last week, but […]
full_text: (Photo by Martin KEEP / AFP via Getty Images) | AFP via Getty Images San Francisco 49ers head coach Kyle Shanahan provided injury updates Monday afternoon. Wide receiver Mike Evans will be managed throughout the week with a hip injury: “Mike’s gotten a lot of work here in the last couple weeks. He’s been able to practice each day since us going down to Australia and last week, but no, I also think they’re two really good players, so usually when you have two really good players who are both instinctive guys, they gel together pretty fast.” Evans pulled himself mid-game in Week 2 after it was evident something had bothered him. The practice reps for Evans were going to be limited regardless. It wouldn’t be surprising if we saw him sit out of multiple practices, or at least have a limited designation, only for him to suit up on Sundays throughout the season. Shanahan confirmed the high-ankle sprains for wide receiver Demarcus Robinson and defensive tackle James Thompson Jr. Those two could miss anywhere from three to six weeks. Shanahan said that Robinson is a potential candidate to land on the Injured Reserve. The 49ers are going to need to get creative if they keep losing players, as there are so many spots that you can designate to return from the Injured Reserve list during the regular season: “Anytime it’s a high ankle, we don’t have a timeline, but just high ankles in general are anywhere from three weeks at the best, which is very rare, to six weeks. So, we’ll see how it goes, but most likely will be an IR candidate here.” So if Thompson Jr. is closer to three weeks than six, the Niners may have to bite the bullet and have him inactive on game days without using an IR spot. Thompson Jr. played 34% of the snaps in Week 2. There were five teams that held tryouts on Monday, but the 49ers weren’t among them, per the NFL’s transaction wire. That may change on Tuesday, unless the 49ers are content with the options on their practice squad. Those are Sebastian Valdez, Kevin Givens, and the recently added McKinnley Jackson. Rookie edge rusher Romello Height broke his hand and will need surgery. Shanahan didn’t rule out Height being able to play as soon as Sunday. The injuries aren’t 1-for-1, but we’ve seen Talanoa Hufanga (torn wrist ligaments), CJ West (broken thumb), and Jimmie Ward (broken hand) all play with some sort of protective casts. Height played over half of the snaps in Week 2 . He is not a player the 49ers’ defense can afford to miss, especially with Sam Okuayinonu and Mykel Williams sidelined. Speaking of Mykel, he’s eligible to return to practice this week. The new PUP rules allow players to practice with their teams after Week 2. However, the 49ers are holding Williams and Christian Kirk out of practice this upcoming week. Shanahan is hopeful those two can practice in Week 4. Shanahan specifically said Kirk is not there yet, so they’ll need to wait another week on him, “at least.” That would give them a week of practice under their belts for a potential Week 5 debut against the Seattle Seahawks.
author: Kyle Posey

title: Who should the 49ers look to bring in at wide receiver?
summary: The good: The San Francisco 49ers had a dominant 35-13 victory over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday. The bad: They lost another wide receiver to injury. Demarcus Robinson was carted off with what Kyle Shanahan says is a high-ankle sprain. Mike Evans also left due to a hip issue, but Shanahan didn’t seem too concerned. […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The good: The San Francisco 49ers had a dominant 35-13 victory over the Miami Dolphins on Sunday. The bad: They lost another wide receiver to injury. Demarcus Robinson was carted off with what Kyle Shanahan says is a high-ankle sprain . Mike Evans also left due to a hip issue, but Shanahan didn’t seem too concerned. Shanahan says they are going to look into signing a wide receiver this week. And no, Brandon Aiyuk is not a possibility; Shanahan was very quick to shoot that down. Considering Robinson’s injury and Mike Evans’ hip thing (which we won’t know about until later Monday), what do the 49ers have? Their current rostered wide receivers are as follows: Jacob Cowing Mike Evans KhaDarel Hodge Deebo Samuel Jordan Watkins They have both Robinson and De’Zhaun Stribling out with injuries. Of those names left, we can probably guess both Cowing and Watkins might have expanded roles in Week 3 against the Arizona Cardinals. Watkins was a healthy scratch against Miami, and it’s fair to think that won’t be the case when the Cardinals roll around. He and Hodge both went through training camp and know the offense, meaning it’s easier to game plan for. In turn, the 49ers will be needing someone for depth and possible special teams help—but might not suit up on game day. On the practice squad, the 49ers have Wesley Grimes and Will Pauling. Both are rookies. Obviously, they can call up either of them. Between those two, Pauling had a bit more chatter during training camp. The question is whether they are ready for the NFL game, and only the coaching staff knows that. Again, if either of them were to be called up to the main roster, the chances of seeing anything from them are small. So that’s what might be the free agent they bring in. Sure, there are big names like Tyreek Hill, Darius Slayton, Brandin Cooks, and JuJu Smith-Schuster, but that’s a bit too expensive given the 49ers’ predicament. If they wanted to go a veteran route and get someone who wouldn’t break the bank, Ray-Ray McCloud is available. Don’t get too excited; McCloud was placed on IR with the Chicago Bears before the season began and was released with an injury settlement. The big question is if he’d be healthy enough to come back to the 49ers. I mention McCloud simply because of his familiarity with Shanahan’s offense—but this situation is almost certain not to happen. He could fill the role left by Robinson, as well as be a backup punt returner in case Cowing goes down—but all of that depends on whether he’s healthy. It also takes away development from Watkins, who the 49ers might want to see what they have with a small sample size/window available. The 49ers are not in the position to spend a ton of money on a veteran wide receiver. Should they lose Mike Evans, then that’s the time to look at the big-hitters. For now, they need to add some depth while some other guys get a bit more of a role. We don’t know the extent of Robinson’s injury, or even when Stribling will be back (they said 10 weeks, but you never know); that suggests they aren’t targeting a big name. If you have ideas for who they should bring in, Spotrac has a good list of available wide receivers. Keep in mind, some of these names are retired, like DeAndre Hopkins —he ain’t coming. Who would you bring in for depth?
author: Patrick Holloway

title: 8 winners that helped the 49ers beat up on the Dolphins: There are no losers when you win by 22
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have outscored their opponents by 42 points through two weeks. That’s at least two touchdowns better than the next team. The Miami Dolphins did their best to play keepaway in the first half, but they couldn’t control the ball in the second half, and that’s when things got out of hand. […]
full_text: Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have outscored their opponents by 42 points through two weeks. That’s at least two touchdowns better than the next team. The Miami Dolphins did their best to play keepaway in the first half, but they couldn’t control the ball in the second half, and that’s when things got out of hand. How do you have a “loser” in a game that you controlled wire to wire? Dolphins didn’t reach 200 yards passing. They didn’t score a touchdown on either red zone trip. The 49ers scored on all five red-zone attempts and had only seven third downs across 49 plays. It was a playoff team versus a rebuilding one, and it showed on the field. Here are the winners and losers from the 49ers’ thrashing of the Dolphins. Winners Brock Purdy Twenty-eight of Purdy’s 30 rush yards came on one drive, and they resulted in a pair of first downs. Purdy’s legs went well beyond the box score, though. He bought time in the pocket for his receivers on numerous plays — most of them resulting in 10+ yard completions. Purdy’s aggressiveness remains one of his best traits. Credit Kyle Shanahan for calling plays that required Purdy to push the ball downfield. Purdy converted 83% of his late-down throws into first downs or touchdowns. He had a 24% explosive play rate. The farther the ball was thrown downfield, the better the result. Against the blitz, Purdy was 6-for-8 for 121 yards and two touchdowns. Purdy had three 20+ yard completions in the third quarter, which added significant EPA to his ledger. He was in the zone all game. It was Purdy’s eighth career start with a 140+ passer rating. That ties this guy named Joe Montana for the second-most in 49ers history. Purdy needs five more to tie Steve Young. Since Purdy entered the league in 2022, only Lamar Jackson has more games with a 140+ passer rating. George Kittle Kittle became the third-fastest tight end in NFL history to reach 600 career receptions. He did it in 126 games, only trailing Travis Kelce (110 games) and Jason Witten (125 games). On a third-quarter play, the 49ers tried to run “leak,” but the Dolphins sniffed it out. Kittle adjusted on the fly, broke his route inside, and turned it into a 26-yard reception. It was a heady play that could’ve easily resulted in an incompletion. Kittle had three impact plays. It’s somewhat miraculous to see him run after the catch. Kittle added 30 yards after the catch to his 80 receiving yards. Kittle topped 17 miles per hour on the GPS tracker. He also forced a missed tackle and caught his one contested target. Raheem Morris Morris had a completely different defense against the Dolphins than he did against the Rams. As we highlighted in the snap counts , the 5-man fronts used an extra defensive tackle instead of a linebacker. There’s no arguing with the drastic difference in the quality of the passing attacks and quarterbacks. Still, the 49ers had the fifth-lowest passing success rate allowed in Week 2 and only allowed one rush for 10+ yards. The 49ers had the highest sack percentage of the week at 14.3%. Morris only blitzed the Rams four times. He blitzed Miami 39.3% of the time. Yet, the 49ers still ran zone coverage 90% of the time. Last week it was primarily a 2-high shell on the back end. This week? Nearly 70% of the time, there was a single-high safety. Morris showed he’s not married to one scheme, coverage, or personnel usage, despite the injuries. It’s been impressive. Gracen Halton Halton is a ball player. He should’ve had a sack on the first play. That play highlighted Halton’s awareness and overall football IQ. Halton’s 21.4% pressure rate was eighth among all defensive tackles this week with at least double-digit pass-rushing snaps. His run defense was more impressive. Halton was fourth among all defensive tackles in run-stop percentage. On one play, Halton stood up his blocker, peeked one way after steering and locking out the lineman, then peeked the other way, disengaged, and made a play. If the first play of the game doesn’t impress you, this one will grab your attention. Halton is playing like a first-rounder. He’s beating first-rounders. He will be even better once Mykel Williams returns. Ji’Ayir Brown and Marques Sigle Credit where it’s due. Had it not been for Halton, Brown would have given up a touchdown on the first play of the game. But it was forgotten, and there were no issues for the rest of the game. Brown was aggressive against the run. Brown’s three run stops were the third most of any safety this week. He did so without missing a tackle. He had only four solo tackles compared to nine assists, but Brown did a job well, making plays around the line of scrimmage and playing fearlessly around offensive linemen. Marques Sigle looked more confident and got into some throwing lanes. There might be something to using Sigle as a blitzer after a sack. That speed around the line of scrimmage could be problematic. Sigle fits the run as aggressively as anybody on the roster. I think it’s a credit to Morris that the safeties played better in Week 2. Morris will keep fine-tuning their roles as the competition stiffens. Upton Stout Stout was a bit confused about the touchdown he gave up, but less than three minutes remained in a 35-6 game at that point. I’m going to forgive the second-year pro for not being focused at that point in the game. Stout topped 20 miles per hour on the GPS, which was the second-fastest time on the team this week. That speed, paired with his intuition, is how you end up with a tackle for loss and a pass breakup in the same game. Aside from the touchdown, Stout allowed 39 yards in coverage on six targets. He has a lot on his plate, and it’s not slowing Stout down, literally or figuratively. He’s a keeper who hasn’t come close to reaching his ceiling. The pass protection I say this a lot, but Trent Williams gets dozens of reps in a game and looks bored. If you could caption the plays where he’s unchallenged, it comes off as, “Really, this is the best y’all can throw at me?” Williams allowed no pressure on 25 blocking snaps, despite the Dolphins throwing six different players at him. 49ers fans’ favorite pinata Jake Brendel had a clean sheet, as did Dominick Puni. Connor Colby allowed only one pressure, but made up for it with a pair of impact plays. The same is true for Colton McKivitz. When your quarterback throws the ball downfield as often as Purdy did and finishes the game with two incompletions, you’re doing a disservice when you don’t mention the offensive line. We are a couple of weeks away from this unit being truly tested against the Broncos and Seahawks’ fronts. That’ll tell us more about Colby than anything. But you can only play who is in front of you, and so far, so good for the offensive line. Parting thoughts When you’re expected to win by multiple touchdowns, and you exceed those expectations, you are a dominant team. Early season results can be tricky . This is the fifth time the 49ers have begun the season 2-0 since 2019. They’ve made the playoffs in each of those years (’19, ’21, ’23, and ’25). The offense produced like a juggernaut. It was the first time they scored five consecutive touchdowns to begin a game since 1981. The 49ers’ 761 total net yards through two weeks are the third-highest since 2019. Everything feels easy, which is a good sign considering the injuries at the skill positions. The two different game plans on both sides of the ball in each game could foreshadow this season’s potential dominance. You don’t want to make any grand proclamations after eight quarters of the season. But Mykel’s return should shore up some of the run-defense issues. The offense’s exceptional production feels like an outlier, but it’s really not. They’re loaded with great players at every position. This is a team that is supposed to play like they’re destined for the NFC Championship. That’s what it looks like after two weeks.
author: Kyle Posey

title: 2 games into the season, here’s what the tape is telling us about the 49ers
summary: Whenever we go over a San Francisco 49ers loss (which hasn’t happened yet this season), I like to say it’s not that they lost, but how they lost. The same can be true about winning, and the 35-13 victory over the Dolphins is a perfect game to look at how they won, especially when you […]
full_text: (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images) | Getty Images Whenever we go over a San Francisco 49ers loss (which hasn’t happened yet this season), I like to say it’s not that they lost, but how they lost. The same can be true about winning, and the 35-13 victory over the Dolphins is a perfect game to look at how they won, especially when you want to make some conclusions about this team for the long haul. Two games in, there are some things that we’ve seen in both that might raise an eyebrow. Overall, the 49ers look terrific. How can you not when Brock Purdy nearly gets the best single-game QBR in history? Stats lie, tape doesn’t, and both seem to be unanimous in how effective the quarterback—and the offense by extension—is. It’s two games, and if history has taught us anything, we can identify a few things. We’ve said over and over again that making any conclusions about what a team in the NFL is after Week 1 is inaccurate. Week 2 isn’t much better, but after a second week, you can see a few things that will be there for the long haul due to the larger sample size. 2023: The 49ers opened against the Pittsburgh Steelers, followed by the Los Angeles Rams. The 49ers walloped the Steelers—in Pittsburgh—30-7. We knew that offense was going to be a problem for the league; we also saw hints of the 49ers’ two-minute defense. The Steelers scored their only touchdown due to the (soon-to-be predictable) defensive brain farts thanks to late hits and soft coverages. A week later against the Rams, the defense didn’t crumble in the two minutes, but they had some really strange coverages against the Rams. The 49ers managed to win both games, but the strange calls against the Rams and the two-minute break in the Steelers game were something we’d see more prominently. 2024: The 49ers opened against the New York Jets and beat them convincingly. Many saw new defensive coordinator Nick Sorensen as a breath of fresh air after the aforementioned issues with Steve Wilks. That breath was quickly turned into seething through gritted teeth in Week 2 when the 49ers faced the Minnesota Vikings. You knew something was very, very wrong once then-Vikings quarterback Sam Darnold threw a 97-yard touchdown pass out of his own end zone in the second quarter. It wasn’t just the fact that it was a touchdown; it was Justin Jefferson being covered by two safeties . What was that coverage? Things didn’t get much better from there, as the offense struggled to move the ball downfield. Brock Purdy fumbling and throwing an interception didn’t help. Yes, the offense was an issue, but the defense (aside from stars like Fred Warner, who notched an interception) looked lost on several plays. Things didn’t get awful until much later in the season, but the cracks certainly showed here. 2025: The 49ers opened with victories both in Seattle and New Orleans. Wins on the road at either of those places are nothing to sneeze at. Both came down to a Nick Bosa sack. The Seahawks went on to win the Super Bowl that year and beat the 49ers twice after that: once in Levi’s Stadium and again in the NFC Divisional. Both of those wins were after injuries decimated the team. Unlike the Seahawks, the Saints were not a good team, finishing the season 6-11. With Spencer Rattler at quarterback, the Saints managed 21 points, and Rattler had a 118 passer rating—not exactly a defensive masterpiece. This is with Robert Saleh as defensive coordinator and before Nick Bosa, Fred Warner, and others were out with injuries. The 49ers were not bad, but that second game went a little too close for comfort. Then again, the 49ers were favored by only three points, thanks to injuries on the offensive side of the ball, so maybe this was expected. And now we’re into 2026. What have we learned? What could be a problem or benefit with this team? Well, the 49ers are consistent on offense, gashing both the Dolphins and the Rams. However, those come with asterisks; the Rams had an injured Myles Garrett, no Aaron Donald, and jet lag. The Dolphins were seen as a bad team before the coin toss. It’s not an overreaction to ask if the 49ers are the best offense in the league, but it’s also not incorrect to point out they still need a Seattle-like defense as a litmus test. Then there’s the defense. Outside of the touchdown in garbage time, they clamped down pretty well in the second half after the Dolphins’ run game gave them trouble in the first. And the run game problems the 49ers had were an issue for the Rams too. Fortunately, both the Rams and Dolphins moved away from it as their respective games progressed. It doesn’t remove the issue. There’s a point to be made that if Brock Purdy is going to play like he’s played the last two weeks and the 49ers can stay healthy, they don’t need a running defense since opposing teams are going to be playing catch-up. At the end of the day, it’s not the 49ers beating the Dolphins. That is expected. They did what they should have done. They were favored by nearly two touchdowns anyway. It’s how they beat the Dolphins. This wasn’t a nail-biting last-minute go-ahead field goal. Nor was it the offense making mistakes while the defense just held down the fort. This was an offense playing near-perfect on every drive and a quarterback having one of the best games of their career back-to-back. On the offensive side of the ball, the 49ers very well might be the best. On the other side, they benefited from a bad Dolphins offense, but also a bad Dolphins offense that managed to win time of possession in the first half. On the defensive side, that’s where there’s worry. Right now, the 49ers defense looks like a second-half defense. I’ll take that. Yes, the Dolphins were holding like crazy, but so do the Kansas City Chiefs and other teams. That first half may have ended in just six points for the Dolphins, but what happens when a more capable offense is in that position? Do they walk away with six points or 14? Or 21? The defensive backs looked terrific, but the Dolphins don’t have much in the vein of wide receivers to begin with. At the end of the day, the 49ers got the job done, and they are positioned to wreck the NFL this year. That said, while we can say the offense is one of the best in the league, we’ve seen enough to question whether the run defense will be an issue in the future. More games will give us answers.
author: Patrick Holloway

title: 49ers snap counts: Raheem Morris is adapting to his personnel
summary: The San Francisco 49ers dominated the Miami Dolphins. It’s not often the scoreboard tells the full story, but they beat up on the Fins as much as 35-13 indicates. It was a relatively clean game for the Niners in all three phases. Any concerns about jet lag and an emotional letdown were quelled after the […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers dominated the Miami Dolphins. It’s not often the scoreboard tells the full story, but they beat up on the Fins as much as 35-13 indicates. It was a relatively clean game for the Niners in all three phases. Any concerns about jet lag and an emotional letdown were quelled after the offense’s first drive. Brock Purdy capitalized on an aggressive game plan from Kyle Shanahan. The Dolphins offense couldn’t keep pace, and that’s how you end up winning by three touchdowns. Let’s look at the snap counts from this game and see what they mean for the depth chart hierarchy and what we can ascertain moving forward. Quarterback Brock Purdy: 42 Mac Jones: 7 You know things are going your way when you can put in a backup quarterback in the fourth quarter. That’s because the starter had an 80% passing success rate, which would be tough to do in practice. Purdy faced a blitz on 40% of his dropbacks, but you’d never know by his results. He had a “wow” throw and a couple of other impact plays. He rushed for 30 yards, which aided the offense when nobody was open. Purdy knows when to pick and choose his spots. He wasn’t perfect, but he wasn’t far off. Running backs Christian McCaffrey: 27 Kyle Juszczk: 23 Kaelon Black: 15 Jordan James: 7 McCaffrey led the team with 10 carries. This was a game where you don’t need to give CMC a bunch of touches, so credit the coaching staff for using a player like James in the fourth quarter. None of the running backs averaged more than four yards per carry. Here’s a funny stat: Black ran for 25 yards, with 28 of those coming after contact. McCaffrey ran for 23 yards, with 27 of those coming after contact. The 49ers didn’t need to run the ball because they were averaging a first down almost every time they dropped back to throw. Pass catchers Deebo Samuel: 30 Mike Evans: 28 George Kittle: 25 Luke Farrell: 25 Jacob Cowing: 22 KhaDarel Hodge: 17 Demarcus Robinson: 16 Brayden Willis: 11 Deebo ran more routes than anybody. Deebo and Kittle were the most targeted, but it was Kittle who ran away with most of the production. The average yards of separation numbers are silly. Kittle’s was 5.4. Deebo’s was 5.1. Robinson’s was 4.7. Evans was the only player under three. The scheme took advantage of a bunch of rookies. We’ll see how the 49ers replace Robinson, who clearly had built a rapport with Purdy. Maybe it’s more Deebo? Do they trust Cowing in that role? The better football shape Kittle gets in, the more he’ll be used, too. Offensive line Connor Colby: 49 Colton McKivitz: 49 Dominick Puni: 44 Jake Brendel: 42 Trent Williams: 42 Jarett Patterson: 7 Vederian Lowe: 7 Carver Willis: 5 Patterson came in for Brendel—Lowe for Trent, and Willis for Puni. The 49ers allowed only three pressures in the afternoon—one from Colby, McKivitz, and Williams. Every lineman was credited with at least two impact plays, save for Puni. Williams had three impact plays. No penalties of any kind for this group. Only 7.4% of their carries were stuffed, which was the fourth-best mark of the week. This unit will be underrated for most of the season. Defensive tackles Osa Odighizuwa: 37 (66.1%) Gracen Halton: 30 (53.6) CJ West: 26 (46.4%) James Thompson Jr.: 19 (33.9%) Around the third quarter in Week 1, it was obvious that rookie Gracen Halton was the best option at defensive tackle next to Osa Odighizuwa: I'm finding a way to get Gracen Halton on the field more after that drive. He had a couple of disruptive plays. Something the 49ers have been lacking at DT outside of Odighizuwa today. — Kyle Posey (@KP_Show) September 11, 2026 Technically, Halton started. The 49ers came out in a true man-front to begin the game. Morris replaced one rookie with another: Jaden Dugger off, Halton in. Morris stayed with that front in the first drive. Thompson Jr. subbed in for Halton after a handful of plays. On third and long, Odighizuwa was the only defensive tackle on the field. He doesn’t have many options at the position, but Morris is adapting to his personnel. It’s telling that Halton has already jumped West in snaps. It’s not surprising, though. Halton had a pressure rate of 21.4%, which was seven percentage points higher than Odighizuwa. Halton had a stuffed run and three run stops. None of the other defensive tackles had any. Halton looks like the real deal. EDGE rushers Nick Bosa: 36 (64.3%) Keion White: 30 (53.6%) Romello Height: 29 (51.8%) Ogbo Okoronkwo: 16 (28.6) Khalid Kareem: 11 (19.6%) White didn’t start, but still outsnapped Height. He outplayed the rookie, too. Height had one more pressure, but White added a run stuff and was in the backfield more. Both players notched sacks, which is what you want from your depth players. Life is much easier when Bosa is on the field. Bosa’s pressure percentage was 27.8%. He won at a 22.2% clip, which is hilariously high. Bosa added a pair of run stops. You’d have no idea that Bosa is coming off a season-ending ACL injury. Linebacker Fred Warner: 46 (82.1%) Dre Greenlaw: 39 (69.6%) Jaden Dugger: 18 (32.1%) Garret Wallow: 11 (19.6%) Luke Gifford: 1 (1.8%) For the second week in a row, Wallow replaced Greenlaw at WILL linebacker when Morris was expecting the offense to pass. In the fourth quarter, once the game was out of hand, Wallow was the lone dime linebacker on the field. It’s evident that Morris views Wallow as an asset in coverage, based on his usage. That might be because Greenlaw allowed all five of his targets to be completed for 40 yards. Greenlaw missed one tackle, but had two run stops, a run stuff, and continues to be aggressive on run plays. Warner had a “hustle” stop and one other. He also notched a half sack and a quarterback pressure on four pass rushes. He was the only linebacker to rush the passer. Warner extended his forced fumble streak to two games. And yes, we will track that all season. Dugger is mostly a run-first player early on in his career. He played 12 run-down snaps compared to six coverage snaps. He’s still making plays. Per Sumer Sports, Dugger’s three impact plays were one more than Warner and Greenlaw. Cornerback Renardo Green: 55 (98.2%) Deommodore Lenoir: 52 (92.9%) Upton Stout: 30 (53.6%) Jack Jones: 9 (16.1%) Morris used dime personnel 10.7% of the time in Week 2, which was the seventh-highest rate. As he continues to tinker with his personnel, Jones on the field with Lenoir and Stout on the inside remains the 49ers best coverage unit. On six plays, they averaged -0.24 EPA per play. That’s with the touchdown allowed, which skews the stats. Still, the Niners had a sack in this package and allowed 21 total yards on the other plays. Green was only targeted once. He had a pair of run stops, including one “hustle” stop — which is when you chase down a play from 20 yards away. In my mind, it’s more impressive when you’re not targeted. That tells me you are forcing the quarterback to look elsewhere because the receiver isn’t open. Stout had one of those as well. Stout allowed the touchdown, but had a pressure on his only pass rush, and chipped in for three run stops. Stout will be one of the most important defenders on the team this season. The theme is the cornerbacks tackle, as Lenoir also had three run stops. He gave up a first down, but when you’re only allowing 12 yards in a game, you’re doing plenty in coverage. Jones allowed one of his two targets to be completed. He joined Stout in the pass breakup category. Safeties Marques Sigle: 55 (98.2%) Ji’Ayir Brown: 52 (92.9%) Malik Mustapha: 3 (5.4%) Mustapha played the final series of the game once it was out of hand. Brown comes off the field when the 49ers are in their goal-line package. Sigle’s speed showed up on a sack. It seems like Sigle’s main priority in Raheem Morris’s defense is to take routes away before they can be thrown. He was only targeted once all game. Sigle had six tackles, but had three run stops. The team leader in run stops for the game was Brown,…
author: Kyle Posey

title: The 3 biggest stars from the 49ers’ home opener: No rust for George Kittle
summary: The San Francisco 49ers took care of business, and that’s all you need to know about their home opener on Sunday. The 49ers demolished the Miami Dolphins 35-13 in a game the Dolphins never had a chance in. Miami opened the game with a field goal, but the 49ers went on to outscore them 35-10 […]
full_text: (Photo by Robin Alam/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers took care of business, and that’s all you need to know about their home opener on Sunday. The 49ers demolished the Miami Dolphins 35-13 in a game the Dolphins never had a chance in. Miami opened the game with a field goal, but the 49ers went on to outscore them 35-10 over the remaining 55 minutes. San Francisco avoided a letdown spot after an impressive Week 1 win over the Rams and now carry the momentum of a 2-0 record into Week 3 against the Arizona Cardinals. These are the three players most responsible for the 49ers’ second win of the season: 3rd Star: TE George Kittle Allow me to be the first to mention that George Kittle tore his Achilles just nine months ago. He emphatically announced he’s healthy against Miami. Kittle led all pass-catchers with his 80 yards on four receptions, scoring one of two passing touchdowns for the 49ers on Sunday. But it was one drive in specific that helped Kittle en route to his monster day. With the 49ers up eight to start the second half, San Francisco was looking to extend that lead early in the second half. That’s when Kyle Shanahan smashed the George Kittle button. The offense opened the third quarter with a quick strike to a wide-open Kittle for 40 yards, teleporting the 49ers into plus territory. Three plays later, Kittle scored his touchdown on a 12-yard pass to put the 49ers up 15 yards. Kittle’s quick turnaround from such a devastating injury will continue to become more impressive with each week. If Week 1 was the first test of how Kittle could handle a real-speed game again, Sunday showed he can return to the level we’ve grown to expect from the tight end. 2nd Star: DE Nick Bosa He didn’t collect a sack on Sunday, but Bosa wreaked havoc in the Miami backfield, forcing others to get to Malik Willis. Osa Odighizuwa matched Bosa with four pressures against the Dolphins’ offensive line, but Bosa’s pressure caused issues for Willis. His first pressure of the game forced Willis to pass earlier than he wanted, resulting in an Upton Stout pass breakup. Later on the drive, Miami faced a third-and-goal, but when Bosa quickly got after Willis, the play quickly fell apart, and Bosa’s pressure led to Romello Height’s first-career sack. His next pressure would result in Marques Sigle’s first career sack. With the 49ers up 21-6, the defense looked to put Miami away. Bosa beat Miami right tackle Austin Jackson off the snap and wrapped around the tackle, getting behind Willis. Willis stepped up in the pocket, but in the gap Bosa left, Sigle came through to finish the play and force the third down. Bosa was effective in the run game in Week 1, but on Sunday, Bosa showed that pass-rush ability we’re familiar with. 1st Star: QB Brock Purdy Miami’s secondary was leaving 49ers pass-catchers open all game, and Purdy happily took advantage. Purdy threw an incomplete pass to Deebo Samuel with 9:20 left in the first quarter. He then completed his next 18 passes. In those 18 passes, Purdy threw for 275 yards and two touchdowns, attacking the Dolphins’ defensive weaknesses. You could tell we were in for a good Purdy day on his fifth pass attempt of the game. With the 49ers offense facing a third-and-5, Miami pressure forced Purdy into a scramble drill. As usual, Purdy excelled on the off-script play. He kept the play alive with his feet before settling and hitting Mike Evans along the sidelines (with Evans making an acrobatic catch) for the first down. Purdy would have to wait for the second half for his touchdown pass when he connected with Kittle, and he’d close his scoring with a six-yard pass to Kyle Juszczyk to put the 49ers up 22 in the third quarter. Oh, and did I mention Purdy led the 49ers in rushing yards? He gained all 30 yards on the same drive, with a 10-yard gain on his first carry followed by an 18-yard gain. His feet would close the drive, finishing his day on the ground with a two-yard score to put the 49ers up 14-3 in the second quarter. Purdy took what Miami was giving, and it resulted in a big day for the 49ers quarterback. Throughout the season, we will track the three stars of the season by tallying points for each star award using a complex scoring system: three points for being the first star, two for the second, and one for the third. Through Week 2, the standings are: QB Brock Purdy – 5 points LB Fred Warner – 3 points DE Nick Bosa – 2 points

title: Around the AFC South Week 2
summary: It has been a tough start for the teams in the AFC South. The Houston Texans, who were considered by most to be the heavy favorites to win the division, have started 0-2. They lost a shootout to the Buffalo Bills in Week 1. This week, despite C.J. Stroud throwing for 353 yards with no […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 20: Head coach DeMeco Ryans of the Houston Texans reacts during a preseason game against the Las Vegas Raiders at Reliant Stadium on August 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images It has been a tough start for the teams in the AFC South. The Houston Texans, who were considered by most to be the heavy favorites to win the division, have started 0-2. They lost a shootout to the Buffalo Bills in Week 1. This week, despite C.J. Stroud throwing for 353 yards with no interceptions, they only scored 6 points in a 20-6 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals. It’s usually a tough road for a team that starts 0-2 to make the playoffs, but the Texans are still in pretty good position in the division. The Jacksonville Jaguars are leading the division at 1-1. They lost 20-13 this week to the Denver Broncos. I know the jury is still out on the Cam Ward pick for the Tennessee Titans, but it still looks better than the Travis Hunter pick the Jaguars made in the same draft at #2 overall. The Jags gave up picks number 5, 36, and 126 in the 2025 draft and pick 24 in the 2026 draft to get to pick 2. Hunter, who was supposed to be a two-way star, has just one catch for eight yards this season and has not had an interception in his NFL career. The Indianapolis Colts also find themselves at 0-2. Their schedule has been tough to start the season, facing the Baltimore Ravens at home in Week 1 and the Kansas City Chiefs on the road in Week 2. They took the Chiefs to overtime, but ultimately lost the game 33-30. There weren’t many people who expected the Tennessee Titans to have a chance at winning the AFC South, but if they can find a way to knock off the New York Giants this week, they will only be, at worst, a game back of the division leader.

title: Titans QB Cam Ward showed real progress in Week 2
summary: The Tennessee Titans endured a tough loss in Week 2, losing 24-20 to the Philadelphia Eagles. Sophomore quarterback Cam Ward showed real growth. Ward was way better than he was in Week 1 versus the Jets, and that progress is good news for the Titans. Ward finished 13-of-20 for 183 yards. The second-year No. 1 […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Cam Ward #1 of the Tennessee Titans drops back to pass the ball during the fourth quarter of the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans endured a tough loss in Week 2 , losing 24-20 to the Philadelphia Eagles. Sophomore quarterback Cam Ward showed real growth. Ward was way better than he was in Week 1 versus the Jets, and that progress is good news for the Titans. Ward finished 13-of-20 for 183 yards. The second-year No. 1 overall selection was better than the box score indicates. Ward was very accurate and decisive. Ward also rushed for two touchdowns. His playmaking ability on 3rd-and-goal set the offense up for 4th-and-goal from the half-yard line. A QB sneak got Ward into the end zone. Ward completed 65% of his passing attempts. He only bested that mark in four individual games last season. Ward also averaged an explosive 9.2 yards per pass. That would have been a single-game high during his 2025 rookie campaign. Ward’s only “miss” was a throw into the end zone for Ayomanor. Poor footwork led to an inaccurate ball behind Ayomanor. It was still catchable, but it should have been a straightforward completion. Ward’s footwork is still in work-in-progress mode. The former Miami standout made up for it with the aforementioned third-down scramble that led to his first rushing score on fourth down. Ward’s average depth of target (7.1) was also significantly better than his Week 1 aDOT (5.3). Titans offensive coordinator Brian Daboll did a good job removing some of the concepts Ward struggled with in Week 1. He played with confidence, throwing the ball with anticipation while finding the explosive plays that lacked versus the Jets. The Titans’ 2026 season is all about Ward’s progress. Week 1 was a discouraging showing, but Ward already looked significantly more comfortable in Daboll’s offense against a stout Eagles defense. Hopefully he continues taking positive steps forward versus the New York Giants in Week 3 .

title: The play call Brian Daboll probably wants back
summary: Against all odds, the Tennessee Titans had a chance to beat the Philadelphia Eagles late in the 4th quarter. Jeffery Simmons got pressure on Jalen Hurts and forced an underthrow on what would probably have been a Devonta Smith touchdown. The ball was picked off by Marcus Harris. That gave the Titans the ball at […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Joey Slye #6 of the Tennessee Titans kicks a field goal against the Philadelphia Eagles during the second half of the game at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images Against all odds, the Tennessee Titans had a chance to beat the Philadelphia Eagles late in the 4th quarter. Jeffery Simmons got pressure on Jalen Hurts and forced an underthrow on what would probably have been a Devonta Smith touchdown. The ball was picked off by Marcus Harris. That gave the Titans the ball at their own 17-yard line with 6:00 left to play in a tie game. The drive started off perfectly. Tony Pollard ripped off back-to-back 9-yard runs, followed by a 41-yard pass from Cam Ward to Elic Ayomanor. The drive stalled a bit with a holding penalty, a negative run, and an illegal formation penalty. A short pass set up 3rd and 22 from the Eagles’ 36-yard line. At this point, I’m thinking the Titans are just going to hand it off again and attempt a field goal. Well, they did just hand it off, but Tyjae Spears ripped off a 27-yard run to set up 1st and goal from the 9-yard line with 2:37 left. The Eagles had two timeouts remaining. The smart thing to do here, as Austin Stanley detailed here , would have been to hand it off on first down. You don’t really want to score on the first play because then you have to kick the ball back to the Eagles with them having two timeouts and the two-minute warning. Why not hand it off on first and second down? That would force the Eagles to use both of their timeouts and still give you a third down with a shot to take the lead. Instead, Brian Daboll called a bootleg that ended in a sack back at the 18-yard line. JC Latham whiffed on Jalen Carter, who had apparently picked up a tell from Ward when watching tape: Unheralded play of game in Eagles win over Titans: Jalen Carter sack on 1st and goal from 9. Carter told me he noticed Cam Ward tendency to dip shoulder with slow bootleg fakes, went full attack & made 1st sack of year. Mental 💎 Titans had 79% win probability at this stage. pic.twitter.com/x5CJNBbNyT — Cameron Wolfe (@CameronWolfe) September 21, 2026 Now, if Latham makes his block and the Titans score a touchdown on the play, no one would be complaining today, even if the Eagles did end up getting a touchdown when they got the ball back, but it sure seems like Daboll called the wrong play here. What do you think? Is this just a case of hindsight being 20/20, or did Daboll mess up by calling that play?

title: Future Hogs – Week 3: College football players who could help the Commanders
summary: It did not look like the premier matchup of Week 3 of the college football between LSU and Ole Miss would live up to the hype. Quarterback Trinidad Chambliss looked like a Heisman front-runner in the first half, converting all his third downs and leading the Rebels to a 24-7 lead at the half. Lane […]
full_text: Jan 8, 2026; Glendale, AZ, USA; Mississippi Rebels defensive tackle Will Echoles (52) against the Miami Hurricanes during the 2026 Fiesta Bowl and semifinal game of the College Football Playoff at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect It did not look like the premier matchup of Week 3 of the college football between LSU and Ole Miss would live up to the hype. Quarterback Trinidad Chambliss looked like a Heisman front-runner in the first half, converting all his third downs and leading the Rebels to a 24-7 lead at the half. Lane Kiffin motivated the Tigers at halftime as they rallied to tie the game at 24-24 in the fourth quarter. Chambliss had a little magic left as he led the Rebels to the go ahead touchdown and two-point conversion. A tipped pass in the end zone on LSU’s final drive resulted in an interception of LSU quarterback Sam Leavitt that sealed the win for Ole Miss. The other ranked-on-ranked games were competitive games. Louisville and SMU was a back and forth affair with Louisville taking the lead in the fourth quarter and holding on to it for the win. A failed two-point conversion allowed Texas Tech to escape an upset by Houston. Who didn’t escape being upset this weekend? Texas A&M. Despite being tied with Kentucky at halftime, 21 unanswered points in the third quarter was enough for a Wildcats win. Virginia will fall from the AP Top 25 after a loss to West Virginia. Week 4 will feature a pivotal matchup between #10 LSU and #23 Texas A&M. A second loss for either team could end their chances for the College Football Playoff. #1 Texas will go on the road to #14 Tennessee in each team’s first SEC action. Several Big Ten teams will begin conference play. This includes #18 Michigan as they welcome #17 Iowa, a team that may finally have some offensive firepower, and #20 Oregon who will go on the road to face #12 USC who are looking to keep their playoff hopes alive. Here are a few players who had a good week and might be able to help the Commanders. Let me know what you think about these prospects and feel free to comment with players that stood out to you. Aidan Chiles | QB | Senior | Northwestern It was tough to see Jayden Daniels injure his elbow for a third time in the past year. While he has the talent of a top NFL QB, his health has to be a consideration with regards to his future in Washington. While I’m not at the point where the team should consider an early draft pick to replace him, it shows why it’s always important to continually look for talent at the position. Aidan Chiles has played at Oregon State, Michigan State, and now Northwestern. He’s had an up and down career. He was benched last season at Michigan State as he and the team struggled. He decided to transfer to Northwestern and, so far, it looks like a good decision. Chiles is 6’4”, 225 pounds, so plenty of size for the position. When Chiles has times, he has good mechanics and delivers accurate passes. When he has to get rid of the ball quickly, those mechanics change and his accuracy can dip. While Chiles can run, he is more of a pocket passer with a strong enough arm for NFL throws. Chiles went 17 of 22 for 241 yards and three touchdowns and two touchdowns on the ground. Aidan Chiles has given the Northwestern offense a real spark this season His dual threat skill was the primary factor in The Wildcats beating Colorado 41-7 See more Chiles 🏈🧵⬇️ https://t.co/cPR0zje7I2 pic.twitter.com/KTNFVBPEID — Durst (@Durst_NFLDraft) September 20, 2026 Keyjuan Brown | RB | Senior | Louisville David Blough might have felt pressure to pass with how effectively Dallas scored, but there were moments in the run game. Although more attention has been given to his teammate and backfield-mate Isaac Brown, Keyjuan Brown looks more like a complete NFL back. He’s densely built at 5’10”, 215 pounds, but he has superb burst and speed at that size. Those qualities along with his vision make him a productive back in a zone blocking scheme. While he can lower his shoulder and deliver punishment, he’d much rather use his quick feet to juke tacklers. Where he isn’t much of a contributor is in the pass game since he only has 18 receptions in his career. Louisville got the win over SMU behind Keyjuan Brown’s 163 yards and two touchdown on 10 attempts. Junior Sherrill | WR | Senior | Vanderbilt The receivers for the Commanders were a mixed bag against Dallas. While Stefon Diggs had a respectable game, Terry McLaurin struggled. Dyami Brown made a few plays, but had a costly fumble. Antonio Williams made three catches, but wasn’t as impactful as he was in Week 1. Junior Sherrill fits the mold of receivers like Williams and Diggs. His route-running creates separation against defenders thanks to his nuance and attention to detail. His hands are reliable both as a receiver and a kick returner. After the catch, he has both elusiveness and toughness thanks to his 5’11”, 200 pound frame. My biggest question about his game is deep speed; he’ll make deep catches, but just doesn’t look like a burner. Sherrill had six catches, 108 yards, and two touchdowns in Vanderbilt’s win over NC State. “Want more of the Vanderbilt WR Junior Sherrill connection with Jared Curtis” 6 catches, 108 yards, 2 TD. Thank you pic.twitter.com/aTDMvo154x https://t.co/blrfslHR57 — Clint Goss (@NFLDraftDome) September 19, 2026 Luke Reynolds | TE | Junior | Virginia Tech With Chig Okonkwo hurt for the matchup with Dallas, the tight ends were not factors in the pass game. Luke Reynolds could change that. He followed James Franklin to Blacksburg from Penn State and he has shined in an increased role this season. It is hard to believe a tight end this athletic and quick is 6’4”, 250 pounds. Quickness and agility allows him to create separation when running routes and eluding tacklers after the catch. Reynolds adjusts easily to passes thanks to above-average body control. The blocking needs work. He will try to block, but his technique needs improvement in order for him to sustain blocks. Reynolds made 12 catches for 107 yards and a touchdown in the Hokies win over Maryland. Virginia Tech strikes first for a touchdown! pic.twitter.com/bbEII3ytoS — College Football Zone (@CollegeFBonX) September 20, 2026 Hokies TE Luke Reynolds looks like a Sunday player to me. Super athletic, big TE. Makes plays after the catch. Tech looks way better prepared than Md in the early going. pic.twitter.com/10yQqxIiLq — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) September 20, 2026 Ridiculous grab by Luke Reynolds 😳 pic.twitter.com/Hc8uTsSZfE — SleeperCFB (@SleeperCFB) September 20, 2026 Kade Pieper | OG | RS Junior | Iowa It looked like the interior offensive line struggled opening holes in the run game early, but improved as the game went on. Pass protection was better than last week, but there is still need for improvement. Enter Kade Pieper. Now 6’3”, 293 pounds is small for an offensive lineman, but he is an athlete. He’s got elite quickness, an attribute necessary to play center. It also helps him in the zone blocking game reaching his landmarks. While he might be a smaller offensive line, Piper is strong. He anchors well against power and drives his legs to get movement as a run blocker. Iowa put up 55 points and over 600 yards against Northern Iowa behind Pieper and the offensive line. Kade Pieper locating linebackers He has a good chance of becoming the 1st C drafted in R1 since former Hawkeye Tyler Linderbaum in 2022 pic.twitter.com/mmaZ6Tczrt — Mike Renner (@mikerenner_) July 28, 2026 Will Echoles | DL | Junior | Ole Miss The Commanders’ run defense was a bright spot, but they need to add more to the defensive line. Daron Payne is in a contract year and Johnny Newton, who is recovering from a pectoral injury, has not impressed. A lot of attention is given to Trinidad Chambliss and the Ole Miss offense, but Will Echoles may be the Rebels best draft prospect. Echoles has the size to play anywhere on a…

title: Washington Commanders Whiteboard: Notes and observations from Week 2
summary: Before the advent of media devices, football coaches at all levels used simple whiteboards to outline plays, map out player positions and explain schemes in real time. Nowadays digital playbooks and tablets have taken over, but coaches still use whiteboards on occasion to impart information quickly and effectively. The following are some quick notes and […]
full_text: Before the advent of media devices, football coaches at all levels used simple whiteboards to outline plays, map out player positions and explain schemes in real time. Nowadays digital playbooks and tablets have taken over, but coaches still use whiteboards on occasion to impart information quickly and effectively. The following are some quick notes and observations from the Washington Commanders’ disastrous 20-37 loss to the Cowboys in Arlington, Texas . Coaching has been substandard It is not just on head coach Dan Quinn. Defensive coordinator Daronte Jones did not have his squad ready to go for this one. Quarterback Dak Prescott and the Dallas offense completed numerous uncontested completions in the first half, including easy touchdowns to CeeDee Lamb and Jake Ferguson. Dak Prescott (3) to CeeDee Lamb (2) Dallas Cowboys 3 yards pic.twitter.com/HIDTEsICbx — NFL Touchdown Videos (@NFLTDsVideos) September 20, 2026 Even when the defense isn’t getting beat there seems to be a hole in the plan and opposing offenses have identified it early https://t.co/haawU17I9C pic.twitter.com/Rmoh0bPSnN — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) September 21, 2026 Washington can not continue to spot teams multiple early touchdowns before starting to play competitive football and expect to win. There is also still plenty of blame to place on Quinn. While the decision to go for it from the 1-yard line with three seconds left on the road versus a division opponent may be debated, his poor clock management leading up to the call cannot be. Washington’s head coach had all three timeouts heading into the last minute of the first half, and didn’t use the first one until there was 29 seconds left. The net result of Quinn’s attempt to manage the clock meant that, instead of using Kaytron Allen to pound the ball into the end zone, the team opted to have Jayden Daniels pass at the goal line. Overall, the team has failed to execute. While assistants should shoulder some blame, that lies with the head coach. Roster evaluation has been substandard Concerns regarding the secondary and the offensive line called out by fans before the season have become key weaknesses in the first two games and have contributed to the 0-2 start. Mike Sainristil has been a complete disaster and general manager Adam Peters and the coaching staff appear to have no viable backup plan for one of last season’s worst cornerbacks. They are also trying to shoehorn Jeremy Reaves into a coverage role that does not fit his skill set. Again, the team appears to have few other options available. Don't think Daronte Jones was particularly happy with Mike Sainristil after this rep… pic.twitter.com/3aFSl0o5QK — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) September 21, 2026 On Lamb's first touchdown, Jeremy Reaves back is toward Dak. Not covering a soul. Nick Cross bites on the play-action, so 0 has no inside help from his safeties. Void created, TD. pic.twitter.com/FJtsLV7suP — Jamual (@LetMualTellit) September 21, 2026 The loss of Laremy Tunsi l was clearly a blow to one of the most important units on the team, but with over a month to adapt to the loss, Peters brought in no significant additions. In fact, one of his few depth signings in D.J. Humphries was released shortly before the opener with no replacement added for the oft-injured Brandon Coleman. The result was Andrew Wylie taking snaps at a position he has clearly shown in the past he is not capable of handling. Also, the team has failed to provide an answer for Chris Paul starting at left guard after Coleman shifted to tackle. Paul made third-round rookie Jaishawn Barham look like an All-Pro on Sunday. Coleman left the game with an injury. Wylie comes in at LT and this is what he does🤦🏻‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/5MiCs4X41a — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) September 20, 2026 Jaishawn Barham shapeshifting around blocks, forcing fumbles, puking, etc pic.twitter.com/Z2pfhBxX5E — James Foster (@NoFlagsFilm) September 21, 2026 The team also continues to carry seven wide receivers, designating Luke McCaffrey inactive two straight weeks in a row. Dyami Brown has played a significant number of snaps over the first two games, and saw more time on the field than both Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams on Sunday. Dyami Brown was on the field more than Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams pic.twitter.com/qWEZvWZ9Jy — Commanders on Real (@WSHOnReal) September 21, 2026 Has the team mismanaged Jayden Daniels’ elbow injury? Full elbow dislocations stretch the tendons and make the joint unstable, but for first time displacement with no evidence of tears or fractures, as was the case in Daniels’ first injury, surgery is usually not indicated . Jayden did aggravate the injury when he returned later that same season versus the Vikings. There was some question if he should have returned all, and the decision was ultimately made after that game to shut him down for the year. At the time, Quinn said that he could have returned to the game and Daniels was wearing a brace. He was not wearing one on Sunday and while, in hindsight, he should have been, Dan Quinn said there wasn’t a discussion regarding one by the coaching staff. Fans and the team will wait for specialists to examine imaging taken on Monday, but ultimately it might be best for Daniels to have surgery due to the repetitive instability in the joint, but that could also possibly wait until after the season. We’re still uncertain what the team and Daniels will decide to do in this case. Jayden Daniels could return sooner than expected with an elbow brace, but he’ll likely need it for the rest of the season. Why surgery could still be considered, and why not operating after the first dislocation wasn’t a mistake. pic.twitter.com/4lhBk2dmuk — David J. Chao – ProFootballDoc (@ProFootballDoc) September 21, 2026 Is the Washington Commanders’ season over? While the loss of Daniels for any length of time and an 0-2 start should have Commanders fans resetting their record predictions for the season, a poor start was expected by many. The team finally returns home this Sunday, and quarterback Marcus Mariota looked good in the second half of Sunday’s game, going 11-of-16 for 111 passing yards and a touchdown while taking zero sacks. It is only Week 3 and Seattle is expected to come to town with a backup quarterback of their own in Drew Lock. Mariota has proven capable of winning in the past, but as Brian Mitchell pointed out in the clip below, the entire team needs to get better for him to have any chance. Can Washington climb back from an 0-2 start with Marcus Mariota at quarterback? #Commanders #NFL #Football pic.twitter.com/HvCXZwu8HO — 106.7 The Fan (@1067theFan) September 21, 2026 Quinn may very well be coaching his last season for the Commanders but is still a professional head coach in the NFL and will do everything in his power to keep this team competitive. A rebound performance from Daronte Jones and the defense, some positive news on Daniels, and a few wins between now and a return for No. 5 could keep the Washington Commanders relevant later in the season.

title: Commanders coach Dan Quinn provides Jayden Daniels injury update
summary: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels suffered an elbow dislocation during Sunday’s 37-20 loss to the Dallas Cowboys and will not play in the Week 3 contest against the Seattle Seahawks. Veteran backup Marcus Mariota will be the Commanders signal caller in the team’s next game. He played well after Daniels got hurt in the second half, […]
full_text: Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels suffered an elbow dislocation during Sunday’s 37-20 loss to the Dallas Cowboys and will not play in the Week 3 contest against the Seattle Seahawks. Veteran backup Marcus Mariota will be the Commanders signal caller in the team’s next game. He played well after Daniels got hurt in the second half, completing 11-of-16 passes for 111 yards and a touchdown. Daniels had imaging done on his elbow on Monday, but head coach Dan Quinn wouldn’t reveal any information from the results of those images. Daniels will take the next few days to consult with specialists on Tuesday and Wednesday about what comes next, head coach Dan Quinn told reporters during his virtual Monday afternoon press conference. That imaging information and the strategy derived from it will dictate Daniels’ rehab process and will reveal how long the quarterback will be out. There’s at least a possibility that Daniels has surgery to stabilize the left elbow joint, though no decisions have been made regarding what comes next. Quinn also said the Commanders have not talked about bringing in a veteran quarterback to backup Mariota. Right now, seventh-round draft pick Athan Kaliakmanis is the primary backup. Check back for further updates on this developing story

title: 2026 NFL Power Rankings: How all 32 teams stack up for Week 3
summary: How do all 32 NFL teams stack up ahead of Week 3? Plus, what we know for sure about the starting QBs around the league.
full_text:
Week 2 of the 2026 NFL season  marked a return to defensive dominance one week after record scoring numbers . This season, NFL defenses have a 35% pressure percentage (the highest through two weeks since ESPN began tracking pressures in 2009) and a 25% pass rush win rate (highest since 2017).

 How is this impacting quarterbacks around the league? In our Power Rankings ahead of Week 3, we asked our NFL Nation reporters to name the one thing we've learned so far from each team's QB situation. Which quarterbacks are handling the pressure? How are teams such as the Giants, Bears, Commanders, Seahawks and Vikings dealing with early injuries to their QB1s?

 To form the list, our power panel of more than a dozen NFL analysts evaluates how all 32 teams stack up against one another, ranking them from No. 1 to 32. And here are a few highlights from this week's rankings:

 
 The 49ers climbed into the top three, led by a near-perfect two weeks from quarterback Brock Purdy . He became the fifth QB in NFL history to record multiple games with 90% completion percentage, per ESPN Research. And San Francisco gets to stay at home for two more weeks, starting with the Cardinals next Sunday . 
 The Chargers are down to No. 22 after falling to 0-2. According to ESPN Research, they are the second team in the Super Bowl era (since 1966) to be favored by at least 6.5 points in each of their first two games and lose both. The Raiders, who most recently beat the Chargers, are at No. 20 and 2-0 for the first time since 2021. 
 Meanwhile, the Falcons and Dolphins are squarely at the bottom of the rankings. The Dolphins are the only team to not lead at any point this season, and ESPN's Football Power Index already gives them a 43% chance at the No. 1 pick. Atlanta is hoping to rebound with quarterback  Michael Penix Jr . back in the fold from ACL surgery. 
 
 Let's get into the full list, starting with the same No. 1 team as last week .

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Buffalo Bills (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Lions 41-31 
 Week 2 ranking: 1 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Josh Allen is going to make defenses pay either way.

 Allen has kept his eyes downfield through two games, averaging a career-best 9.7 yards per attempt on his deepest average depth of target (10.5) since 2018, his rookie season. That has led to three touchdowns on throws of 20-plus air yards. But Allen is just as dangerous when defenses bail out to protect against the deep ball. Of his 92 rushing yards on 20 carries this season, 70 have come on six scramble plays. -- Nick Suss 

 

 
 

 

 2. Seattle Seahawks (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Cardinals 31-7 
 Week 2 ranking: 2 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Drew Lock is one of the NFL's best backup QBs.

 He's not the same player who turned the ball over 25 times in 24 games over his first three seasons in Denver. Or the one who couldn't beat out Geno Smith after a  trade to Seattle in 2022. Lock has gotten plenty of help from receiver  Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Seattle's defense, but he has also played like a starter. Since stepping in for an injured Sam Darnold one series into the season opener, Lock has completed almost 73% of his passes with four touchdowns, zero turnovers and only two sacks. His Total QBR of 86.4 ranks fourth. -- Brady Henderson 

 

 
 

 3. San Francisco 49ers (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Dolphins 35-13 
 Week 2 ranking: 5 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Brock Purdy looks poised for his best season.

 Purdy has been one of the league's most productive quarterbacks since taking over the starting job in 2022. Now in his fifth season, he's completely comfortable in coach Kyle Shanahan's offense and coming off his best training camp. That hot start has teammates such as linebacker  Fred Warner openly wondering whether Purdy can compete for league MVP honors. Through two weeks, Purdy is atop the league in QBR (94.9) despite a supporting cast that has already been thinned by injury. If he stays healthy, there's reason to believe Purdy will post his best year yet. -- Nick Wagoner 

 

 
 

 4. Kansas City Chiefs (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Colts 33-30 (OT) 
 Week 2 ranking: 8 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Patrick Mahomes can deal from under center.

 With the addition of running back Kenneth Walker III , Mahomes has shown that he can be surgical when passing from under center, especially on play-action passes. On under-center plays, Mahomes threw a touchdown against the Colts and has already recorded 107 passing yards. It's one of the biggest changes from last season, when the clear majority of the Chiefs' snaps with Mahomes were in the shotgun -- 80.6% of their formations (excluding quarterback kneel-downs), third most in the league. -- Nate Taylor 

 

 
 

 5. Los Angeles Rams (1-1) 
 Week 2 result:  Beat the Giants 28-6 
 Week 2 ranking: 4 

 One thing we know about the QB1:   Matthew Stafford is still capable of playing at an MVP level.

 Stafford and the Rams' offense struggled in the season opener , but wide receiver Davante Adams said the team's Week 2 offensive performance was closer to what the group expects to look like this season. On Monday night against the Giants, Stafford, the reigning MVP, completed 22 of 31 passes for 327 yards with four touchdown passes and an interception. He had that success without wide receiver Puka Nacua , who is dealing with soreness in his groin .  -- Sarah Barshop 

 

 
 

 6. Philadelphia Eagles (2-0) 
 Week 2 result: Beat the Titans 24-20 
 Week 2 ranking: 6 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Jalen Hurts is carrying this team.

 The thought heading into the season was Hurts and the passing offense would need time to acclimate to coordinator Sean Mannion's system , meaning the Eagles would have to rely on their defense and ground game early. The defense did not dominate as expected  against Washington and Tennessee, while the running game has been spotty behind an offensive line still trying to find its footing. Meanwhile, Hurts led the team to a Week 1 win with three touchdowns and another victory Sunday via a go-ahead touchdown drive in the closing seconds. He is tied for second in touchdown passes (five) and ahead of schedule in this new scheme. -- Tim McManus 

 

 
 

 7. Baltimore Ravens (1-1) 
 Week 2 result: Lost to the Saints 24-17 
 Week 2 ranking: 3 

 One thing we know about the QB1: Lamar Jackson is facing a lot of pressure.

 Baltimore's revamped offensive line has struggled in protection. The Ravens' two lowest pass block win rates with Jackson as the starting QB have come in the first two weeks this season. Baltimore had a 38% pass block win rate at the Colts in Week 1 and a 33% win rate in Week 2. The 2027 NFL draft is still months away, but with the 2026 season underway, we're starting to track pick order in Round 1. Which teams are in position to add elite prospects in the top 10 next April? What about the top five ... or even at No. 1?

 What follows is not the current draft order based on records. It is a projection of what ESPN's Football Power Index thinks the order ultimately will be by the end of the season. Each week during the season, the FPI projects the draft order by simulating the remainder of the season 10,000 times. Game probabilities are based primarily on the model's team ratings and game locations. The draft order is determined by the records the model projects for each team after 17 games, as well as each team's average draft position across the simulations.
