title: Titans trying to 'trust the process' after tough loss to Eagles
summary: The Titans could have a 1-1 record but they're 0-2 because they didn't finish on both sides of the ball down the stretch.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. --  Tennessee Titans defensive lineman Jeffery Simmons sat at his locker still in full uniform in disbelief almost 40 minutes after watching the Philadelphia Eagles celebrate Darius Cooper 's game-winning, 3-yard touchdown reception with nine seconds left on the clock. These types of tough losses can send a team spiraling, especially a team like the Titans, who's 25.9-year-old average age is tied with the Green Bay Packers , Jacksonville Jaguar s and New England Patriots for the fifth-youngest roster in the league. Titans coach Robert Saleh isn't a believer in moral victories, but he refuses to allow the 24-20 loss to the Eagles alter his approach. 
 
 "You can't let the result affect your process," Saleh said. "There is no good job in losing. You're either winning or you're losing. But you can't let that deter you from the process at which you attack it because that's the only chance you have to win a football game, having a great process." 
 
 The Titans could have a 1-1 record, but they're 0-2 because they didn't finish on either side of the ball down the stretch.  
 
 Tennessee had a 73.7% win probability when Tyjae Spears ' 27-yard run gave the Titans the first down while facing third-and-22. The Titans got the ball to Philadelphia's 9-yard line but had to settle for Joey Slye 's 33-yard field goal to take a 20-17 lead with 1:56 left in the game. Tennessee's defense was unable to protect the lead, allowing Jalen Hurts to march the Eagles 65 yards to the end zone thanks to Cooper's catch. 
 
 
 "It's frustrating, for sure," Titans quarterback Cam Ward said. "We want to end every drive with a touchdown. That's our goal each and every time that we step on the field is to get a touchdown. And for us not to be able to help the defense in that situation, we take that upon ourselves" 
 
 The Titans hadn't won a game since last December. They were humiliated by Saleh's former team, the New York Jets in the season opener. Now the Titans have to figure out a way to flush the bad feelings after having a win snatched from their grasp. 
 
 Second-year receiver Elic Ayomanor is taking a trust the process approach to get ready for the next game, which will be on the road against the New York Giants on Sunday. Ayomanor's faith is in the hard work he put in during the offseason and what he's going to do leading up to the game. That hard work has made Ayomanor a player Saleh referenced when asked how the Titans can weather the storm of a two-game losing streak to start the season. 
 
 Saleh said that everyone would be sick once they sat down and watched the film from the loss. The film showed exactly what Saleh thought he'd see, a failure to execute in multiple phases late in the game. But there were also plenty of shortcomings throughout the day. The Eagles were able to convert a ridiculous 11 of their 18 third-down opportunities. That caused the Titans to once again lose the time of possession battle, with Philadelphia holding the ball for over 36 minutes. It was a close game, but in the end, the Titans suffered another heartbreaking loss. 
 
 Saleh said they'll learn to win games like this, and the experience last Sunday will help that. In the meantime, the players must continue preparing this week regardless of their record.  
 
 "Just because you have a good process doesn't necessarily guarantee you're going to have a good outcome," veteran defensive lineman Jacob Martin said. "But you're putting yourself in the best position to have a good outcome. And obviously, sometimes things don't go your way, but that doesn't mean you go back and change your process because the outcome wasn't good."

title: What's next for Jayden Daniels, Commanders after elbow injury?
summary: Experts weigh in on Daniels' latest injury and what it means for him, the Commanders and their collective futures.
full_text:
ARLINGTON, Texas -- For nearly an entire half on Sunday, Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels resembled the player from 2024, the one who was named NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year and mentioned as a future league MVP.

 On the final drive of the first half at the  Dallas Cowboys , Daniels provided reminders of that season: He ran for 24 yards and threw for another 27, including a strike on third-and-6 to Stefon Diggs for 10 yards.

 

 Then, on the final play of the half, the 2025 version of Daniels showed up, the one who missed 10 games with three different injuries. He suffered a dislocated left elbow, leaving the Commanders with plenty of questions about the future -- from his durability to whether they had built a good enough roster to withstand his absence for even a short period.

 Commanders coach Dan Quinn said Daniels will visit specialists Tuesday and Wednesday to determine the best course of action. It's the same injury Daniels sustained in Week 9 last season; he returned in Week 14, but after reinjuring the elbow in that contest, the Commanders shut him down for the final four games of the campaign.

 His latest injury has left Washington in a familiar spot: wondering what this means for Daniels' future and trying to piece together wins. Last season, the Commanders struggled to do the latter and finished 5-12. Washington is 0-2 now and will face the defending Super Bowl champion  Seattle Seahawks  in its home opener Sunday.

 "0-2 is not where we wanted to be, that's for sure," Quinn said. "But we also are resolute that that's not where we're going to be staying."

 Commanders reporter John Keim and senior fantasy writer Eric Karabell weigh in on Daniels' latest injury and what it means for him, the Commanders and their collective futures.

 

 

 Is the season lost? 

 It's only two games. But after last season, when injuries -- notably the one to Daniels -- derailed the Commanders, it would require a leap of faith to think otherwise at this point, particularly in the NFC East. Even if Daniels had remained healthy, Washington is now 0-2 in the division. So, the road would have been tough regardless. Also, the Commanders will next face Seattle in their home opener and in the coming six weeks will play the Giants twice, the 49ers, the Rams and the Eagles.

 If Daniels is out multiple weeks, that's a steep task. And this isn't about backup quarterback Marcus Mariota , who will start Sunday, as much as it is about what the Commanders haven't shown in other areas.

 The sad aspect for Washington is that Daniels was playing well. He was sharp and showed the dynamic ability that made him the No. 2 pick in the 2024 draft, and a player multiple high-profile coaches liked best in that class.

 
 "I loved everything about the first half, how he was playing," Quinn said of Sunday's performance, as Daniels rushed for 69 yards and threw for 96 yards and a touchdown before the injury.

 But Daniels also covers up a lot of flaws. Those flaws will now be magnified, and that's the concerning part. Washington's defense has allowed seven touchdowns in two games. A new system always brings growing pains, but the Commanders are faster and more talented in the front seven as compared with 2025's unit, and new coordinator Daronte Jones has a strong reputation. Defensive backs say his scheme requires a lot of preparation and knowledge; that also could lead to early issues in coverage until they have more games in the system.

 On multiple plays Sunday, a cornerback could be seen communicating with a safety right before the ball was snapped. In one case, there appeared to be confusion; and in another, the corner was looking at the safety when the ball was snapped. At other times, it appeared players went to the same coverage area.

 Quinn said they know what it looks like when they do it right, so after two games, "It's not good enough."

 But can that overcome all the issues? The Commanders' defense struggles unless it applies pressure. They don't create turnovers. That's a bad combination. Last season, the Bears' defense ranked 24th in scoring and 29th in yards but led the NFL with 33 takeaways (23 more than Washington).

 Washington has forced only 27 turnovers since the start of the 2024 campaign and hasn't taken the ball away in two games this season.

 If the Commanders had a proven defense and a strong, consistent run game, then they could survive for a few weeks. But their offensive line, already down left tackle Laremy Tunsil , now has right guard Sam Cosmi  -- their top remaining lineman -- in concussion protocol. Tunsil and Daniels are Washington's best offensive players. It's tough to survive those absences.

 Could they develop those other aspects? Sure. But when? And will it happen quickly enough for Washington to withstand Daniels' absence? The Commanders have lost 12 of their past 14 games dating to last season, but they changed coordinators and spent heavily on defense in the offseason. If not a new team, it should be a different one. After two games, Washington ranks 27th in yards and 25th in points. The Commanders are 28th in yards per pass attempt.

 After Sunday's game, one player, without prompting, expressed confidence in what the offense and the team could still do. He was encouraged by a lot of what he had seen by the offense, despite the loss. And he remained convinced it could get the season pointed in a better direction. Others share his belief. If that belief doesn't turn into a win real soon, then hope will once more lead to despair for Washington fans.

 

 Should the Commanders have serious concerns about Daniels' viability as their QB of the present and future? 

 If he missed another long stretch, it would be hard not to have those concerns.

 What they'll never have to worry about is his approach. Few work harder or study more; he continues to arrive at work by 5:30 a.m. every week. He organized film sessions with the receivers. He picks the brains of athletes in other sports -- Steph Curry, Draymond Green and LeBron James -- and has talked to Lakers general manager Rob Pelinka about Kobe Bryant's mindset.

 Daniels has been focused on improving and winning; he has said he doesn't care about fame and celebrity status.

 However, he has now dislocated his left elbow twice in his past four games and reinjured it in another. He has finished only four games since the start of last season and left four others early. He suffered a knee injury in one game that cost him two weeks and a hamstring in another that sidelined him for one.

 The question is: Can anything be done to prevent another dislocation? One source close to the situation said Daniels did not need surgery last year because there was no ligament damage. Quinn said surgery was not discussed and the questions for specialists will involve determining the best course of action, whether it be surgery to tighten the ligaments or if rest and rehab is enough. As of Monday surgery, was not an option, one source said, but that will ultimately be up to the specialists, as they need to determine why this keeps occurring.

 Daniels will almost certainly have to play with a brace on when he returns -- but he wore one in Week 14 last year when he returned from his first dislocation. He reinjured the elbow as he attempted to make a tackle following an interception.

 And for what it's worth, Daniels does lift weights, and he said he had added 8 to 10 pounds of muscle in the offseason. At 6-foot-4 and 215 pounds, he might be lean but isn't considered weak. Still, it could be that strengthening his elbow is one recommendation.

 He remains the quarterback of the present and the future. He is too talented and works too hard to think otherwise at this point. That said, Daniels does not have to prove he can play; he needs to prove he can be durable. That will be the primary focal point once he returns. If the Commanders finish with a poor record but Daniels plays the rest of…

title: Jayden Daniels to see specialists before Commanders form plan
